The only authorized source for NeurIPS registration and Housing is through the official NeurIPS website. Please do not share registration details with any outside party. July 23, 2026: Due to a technical issue during release, we are currently re-releasing all reviews and initial meta-reviews. Reviews will be temporarily offline during that time. AI Reviewing Experiment This year NeurIPS will be held in Sydney, Atlanta, and Paris. Author Eligibility. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The responsibility for that error is ours as an organization, and we deeply apologize for the alarm and impact this miscommunication had on our community. We have updated the link and clarified the text of our policy, which is consistent with that of ACM and IEEE, as well as other international conferences and NeurIPS in the past. As in previous years, NeurIPS welcomes submissions from all compliant institutions and individuals. We want to reiterate that NeurIPS is a community-driven event, created by and for the community, and strives to be inclusive. The NeurIPS 2026 organizing committee was particularly saddened to learn of this institutional miscommunication. The organizing committee has taken on the responsibility of running the conference this year with the goal of fostering open communication, knowledge sharing, and global scientific discourse. We thank the community for bringing this issue to our attention and working with us through this situation. Santos University of Amsterdam Mission Statement The Neural Information Processing Systems Foundation is a non-profit corporation whose purpose is to foster the exchange of research advances in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, principally by hosting an annual interdisciplinary academic conference with the highest ethical standards for a diverse and inclusive community. About the Conference The conference was founded in 1987 and is now a multi-track interdisciplinary annual meeting that includes invited talks, demonstrations, symposia, and oral and poster presentations of refereed papers. Along with the conference is a professional exposition focusing on machine learning in practice, a series of tutorials, and topical workshops that provide a less formal setting for the exchange of ideas. items.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
items.summary: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports
items.content: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. Foundry Labs Foundry Labs bridges the distance between Microsoft breakthroughs and the builders, scientists, and curious minds who can put them to work. Foundry Labs Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush. How to use 1. Use Flint in your chat Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation. Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns. 2. Build an interactive app with Flint Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas. Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa. 3. Create bespoke interactions To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks. Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes. How it works Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level: Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates. Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states. Figure 1: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable c and cost effective. This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards. Try it now! Video playback requires cookie consent Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery. App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab) . Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app. Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab) , design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. Foundry Labs Foundry Labs bridges the distance between Microsoft breakthroughs and the builders, scientists, and curious minds who can put them to work. Foundry Labs Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush. How to use 1. Use Flint in your chat Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation. Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns. 2. Build an interactive app with Flint Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas. Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa. 3. Create bespoke interactions To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks. Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes. How it works Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level: Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates. Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states. Figure 1: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable c and cost effective. This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards. Try it now! Video playback requires cookie consent Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery. App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab) . Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app. Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab) , design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary. items.content: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up. So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in. PODCAST SERIES The AI Revolution in Medicine, Revisited Join Microsoft’s Peter Lee on a journey to discover how AI is impacting healthcare and what it means for the future of medicine. Listen now Opens in a new tab Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical. Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it. How PDD Kit works PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab) , GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document. The workflow has two halves (Figure 1). First, team members review intent in plain language. PDD Kit asks the questions a careful reviewer would ask, explains the relevant code as it goes, and records the answers in an intent artifact , a document that bridges the user’s intent with the formal specification or tests. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it. Figure 1. Proof-Driven Development with PDD Kit. Team members settle intent. Verus and the test suite hold the code to it. Consequently, every result in PDD Kit says which kind of verification it rests on: Formal verification is a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every possible input, checked by a tool called a verifier. For PDD Kit today, that verifier is Verus (opens in new tab) , a proof language for Rust co-developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI-SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison and the Weizmann Institute of Science. Empirical verification checks code by running it and observing what it does. It covers what a proof can’t reach, such as a third-party cryptography library or a user interface. It uses unit and end-to-end tests, terminal automation, browser agents, and computer-use agents for anything a browser can’t drive. A passing test only shows the code worked on the inputs it tried, so PDD Kit labels it as evidence rather than proof. The line between the two is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) : the code that the proof assumes behaves as described. PDD Kit makes that line explicit and asks you to sign off on each piece. The capstone: a full-stack web app To show PDD Kit integrating with existing codebases, we built Pet Store, a full-stack web app written entirely in Rust (opens in new tab) . The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab) . Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust. For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences: Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements: You only get a token with the right password. Only admin accounts get admin tokens. We kept the request rough on purpose. Capturing the intent of the user and turning the user request into something a proof can check is PDD Kit’s job. Step 1: Questions before code PDD Kit’s planning workflow, pdd-plan, reads the code and comes back, before writing anything, with questions in a Decisions tab. When a question depends on how the code works, the card explains that part first: the goal, how the pieces fit, and the exact function involved, so you can answer without opening the source. Figure 2. The first decision card. “Only with the right password” on its own is also met by a login that refuses everyone. Proving both ways rules that out. The question looks pedantic, but it matters. “You only get a token with the right password” rules out the bad case, a wrong password getting a token, and a login that refuses everyone keeps that promise perfectly. “The right password always works” is the half that rules it out. Formally, the first is an implication (token ⇒ right password) and the second is its converse. Together they make an “if and only if.” An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways. Step 2: A human readable intent map As the conversation goes on, PDD Kit keeps a rough work section at the top of the plan current, so a user can keep track of important concepts without having to scroll back through a long chat to find what was agreed. It includes a flowchart of the login being specified, a spec landscape of what will be proved and what will be trusted, and, when a picture helps, a mental model. For login, PDD Kit drew a ticket desk (Figure 3). Figure 3. PDD Kit’s mental model for login. The field you send picks the window, the window picks the table and with it the role, and nothing prints until the password matches. Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent. Figure 4. An intent map entry after the decision: a login gets a token only with the right password for that account, and always with it. The flowchart shows every way the password check can end. The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token. Figure 5. Two readings of the same sentence. They differ in one cell, and that cell changes what the proof has to establish. Step 3: Proving the login function Before anything gets built, PDD Kit asks the team to sign off on the plan as a whole. Its first draft proved the decision at the center of login, picking the table and gating on the password, and kept the handler around it trusted and tested. That’s a sensible default, and it’s what PDD Kit recommended, but the developer wanted more. The handler is where the lookups get awaited and the token gets signed, and that glue is exactly where a refactor can quietly swap two lines. So at intent review the developer chose to give the login handler its own async spec, so the proof covers that glue too instead of trusting it (Figure 6). Figure 6. Proving more of login means trusting more small wrappers. The card says so before the developer chooses. That choice moved almost everything into the proof and left the login handler with nothing to do but unpack the request. A new async function, login_flow , carries the contract from the request’s fields all the way to the token or the HTTP error. PDD Kit then brought the revised plan back for a fresh sign-off, because matching your intent isn’t proof, and it doesn’t approve new trust or a wider scope. Step 4: Where proof stops There are plenty of things you can’t prove about a program, and login runs into most of them: Code the verifier can’t see. bcrypt’s hashing, sqlx’s queries and jsonwebtoken’s signing live in other crates, outside the proof. Facts about the outside world. What SQLite holds right now and what time the clock says are inputs to the program, not something its code can establish. Whether, and how fast, something finishes. The spec says what you get if login answers. A hung query, or a slow one, breaks nothing in it. Anything a person has to judge , like whether an error message helps or a screen makes sense. Whatever nobody wrote down. A proof covers its spec and says nothing about requirements outside it. That’s where empirical verification comes in. PDD Kit spells out the trusted boundary, the part of the TCB this proof leans on. It wraps each trusted piece in a small function with an assumed contract, using Verus’s #[verifier::external_body] or external_fn_specification , asks the developer to accept each one on its own, and writes a test for every assumed clause into the plan. For login, the developer signed off on six pieces: The two lookups, Customer::find_by_email and Admin::find_by_username . Each awaited, successful lookup returns exactly the row its own table holds for that email or username, or none. check_password , a thin wrapper around bcrypt::verify . It errors only on a stored hash bcrypt can’t read, and Ok(true) means exactly the right password. generate_token , which signs exactly the claims it is given under the configured secret and reports a signing failure as a 500. expiry_from_now , which reads the clock and writes an expiry exactly 24 hours later. database_error , which turns a failed lookup into today’s 500 with sqlx’s message. The login handler shell, which unpacks the request and passes its fields to login_flow unchanged. In the spec, a lookup keeps its code where it is and gets a contract from the outside with external_fn_specification : /// Looks up a customer by exact email. /// Trusted, not proved: the SQL query runs in sqlx, which Verus cannot check. /// Every customer promise of `login_flow` rests on it. #[verifier::external_fn_specification] pub async fn ex_customer_find_by_email(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, email: &str) -> (r: Result , sqlx::Error>) ensures // When the query succeeds, it returns the customers row on // file for exactly this email, or None when there is none. r matches Ok(found) ==> found == customer_on_file(email@), { Customer::find_by_email(pool, email).await } The clock is a small wrapper marked #[verifier::external_body] . Verus uses its ensures clause and never reads the body: /// Reads the clock and computes a token's expiry 24 hours ahead. /// Trusted, not proved: chrono's clock is outside the proof. /// It panics if the time is out of range, as today's login does; /// that panic is not promised against. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn expiry_from_now() -> (r: Expiry) ensures // The expiry is exactly 24 hours (86,400 seconds) after the clock reading. r.exp as int == r.now as int + 86_400, { ... } Figure 7 puts the three layers together: what Verus proves, what people accept and tests check, and what nobody is promising. Figure 7. Where the login proof stops. Verus proves the core for every input. People accept the trusted ring and tests check it. The plan lists what nobody is promising. Figure 8 maps what gets proved and what gets trusted. Each trust decision is its own card. It shows the clauses Verus will take on faith, what the developer is accepting, and which promise falls apart if the assumption is wrong (Figure 9). Every assumed clause then gets an empirical check in the plan’s Empirical verification section, written as Given/When/Then scenarios before any test exists (Figure 10). An entry says planned until it has run, and then it records the command’s result and the commit it ran against. Figure 8. What gets proved and what gets trusted in login. Green functions are proved by Verus for every input. Amber pieces are trusted, accepted by the developer, and checked by the planned tests in the plan’s §4.1. Figure 9. A trust card for check_password . Verus takes these two clauses on faith, so a person accepts them and two tests check them. Figure 10. A planned test for the trusted check_password , written before the test exists. The plan labels a passing test as evidence rather than proof. The plan is just as explicit about what nobody is promising: that the login future ever completes, that an out-of-range clock won’t panic, anything about the timing or rate of attempts, and how other endpoints read the role. Step 5: Reading the spec The intent artifact is what the team reviews. It’s the plain-language version of the formal spec PDD Kit writes as Verus contracts. You might be wondering whether someone now has to read the proof instead of the code. Nobody does, because the coding agent writes the proof and Verus checks every step of it. If Verus accepts the proof, it holds whether or not anyone reads it. The spec is what the proof is held to, so that’s what people review, and this one is short enough to learn to read in a few minutes. Each function gets an ensures block: statements about its result, r, that must hold for every possible input. Verus checks them when you build, and if any clause could fail for even one input, the build fails and Verus points at that clause. Each clause reads as an if-then, and Figure 11 takes apart the clause for the developer’s first requirement. Figure 11. The ensures clause on login_flow for “You only get a token with the right password.” The same account a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. Notice that the same a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. For example, imagine a bug where login checks the password against one account but signs the token for another. Bob logs in with his own, correct password and gets back a token for Alice’s account. Each step looks fine on its own, but this clause catches it, because the password check and the token have to name the same account. That’s the kind of wiring bug a test suite rarely thinks to look for. The spec also has to talk about SQLite, bcrypt and JWTs without running any of them. It does that with uninterpreted functions , names with no body: customer_on_file(email) and admin_on_file(username) for the rows the database holds, bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) for what bcrypt would say, and token_claims(token, secret) for what a token carries. Verus knows nothing about them except what the trusted contracts from Step 4 promise. The proof says “whatever the database holds, login does the right thing with it,” and a trusted contract says “the lookup returns what the database holds.” /// The customers row the database holds for /// exactly this email, if any, when login looks. /// Left abstract: only `Customer::find_by_email`'s /// trusted contract says what it is. pub uninterp spec fn customer_on_file(email: Seq ) -> Option ; ... /// What bcrypt says about `password` against a /// stored `hash`: Some(true) when it is the password /// the hash was made from, Some(false) when it is /// not, None when bcrypt cannot read the hash. /// Left abstract: its meaning is bcrypt's, taken on trust through `check_password`. pub uninterp spec fn bcrypt_verdict(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> Option ; /// The password is the right one for the stored hash, by bcrypt's verdict. pub open spec fn password_matches(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> bool { bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) == Some(true) } On top of those, named_account(email, username) says which account a login names: the customers row for the email when one is sent, otherwise the admins row for the username, otherwise none. It’s written like Rust, but it’s a mathematical definition that never runs and only appears in contracts. Code like this is called ghost code , since the verifier checks it but the compiler erases it from the program. With it, the developer’s two-sentence request ends up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow (Figure 12). /// The account a login names: the customers row for /// the email when one is sent (role "customer"), /// otherwise the admins row for the username (role "admin"), otherwise none. pub open spec fn named_account(email: Option , username: Option ) -> Option { match email { Some(e) => match customer_on_file(e@) { Some(c) => Some(NamedAccount { id: c.id@, password_hash: c.password_hash@, role: customer_role() }), None => None, }, None => match username { Some(u) => match admin_on_file(u@) { Some(a) => Some(NamedAccount { id: a.id@, password_hash: a.password_hash@, role: admin_role() }), None => None, }, None => None, }, } } Figure 12. The two-sentence request and the Both ways decision ended up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow. Four of them keep today’s refusals, so the storefront and the existing API tests keep working. Here’s the whole contract, with its doc comment trimmed. Each clause has the plain-English comment above it that the intent artifact shows the team: /// The whole login, awaited end to end: from the /// request's fields to the token or the HTTP error. /// ... pub async fn login_flow(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, config: &Config, email: Option , username: Option , password: &str) -> (r: Result ) ensures // Neither an email nor a username: 400 with today's message. email is None && username is None ==> (r matches Err(AppError::BadRequest(m)) && m@ == missing_identity_text()), // A token only for the account the login names, with its right // password; it carries that account's id and its table's role. r matches Ok(t) ==> (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.sub@ == a.id && c.role@ == a.role), // The right password for the named account always gets a // token, unless a lookup or signing failure gives 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash)) ==> (r is Ok || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A login naming an account nobody holds gets // 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. ((email is Some || username is Some) && named_account(email, username) is None) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A wrong password for an account whose hash bcrypt // can read gets 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) == Some(false)) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // An account whose stored hash bcrypt cannot read gets 500 and no token. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) is None) ==> r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_)), // The admin role only for an admins row // found by username, with no email sent. (r matches Ok(t) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == admin_role()) ==> (email is None && username matches Some(u) && admin_on_file(u@) is Some), // An email login's token always carries the customer role. (r matches Ok(t) && email is Some) ==> (token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == customer_role()), { unimplemented!() } The trusted boundary shows up in the code too. check_password is one of the functions whose body Verus doesn’t check. Its contract ties it to bcrypt_verdict , an uninterpreted model of bcrypt with no axioms: /// Asks bcrypt whether `password` matches the stored `hash`. /// Trusted, not proved: Verus cannot check bcrypt's hashing, /// so this wrapper's contract is assumed. /// Every password promise of `login_flow` rests on it. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn check_password(password: &str, hash: &str) -> (r: Result ) ensures // bcrypt answers (Ok) exactly when it can read the stored hash. r is Ok <==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) is Some, // Its answer is its verdict: true for the // right password, false for any other. r matches Ok(b) ==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) == Some(b), { bcrypt::verify(password, hash).map_err(|e| e.to_string()) } The doc comment above it says what rests on it: every password promise of login_flow . Every login ends in one of a handful of places, and only one of them has a token (Figure 13). The proof covers all of them at once. Figure 13. Every way a login can end, from the plan. login_flow is async: it awaits a database query. Verus can put contracts on async functions, with one rule worth knowing (Figure 14). requires is checked when the call creates the future. ensures describes the value you get when you aw

Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up. So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in. PODCAST SERIES The AI Revolution in Medicine, Revisited Join Microsoft’s Peter Lee on a journey to discover how AI is impacting healthcare and what it means for the future of medicine. Listen now Opens in a new tab Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical. Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it. How PDD Kit works PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab) , GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document. The workflow has two halves (Figure 1). First, team members review intent in plain language. PDD Kit asks the questions a careful reviewer would ask, explains the relevant code as it goes, and records the answers in an intent artifact , a document that bridges the user’s intent with the formal specification or tests. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it. Figure 1. Proof-Driven Development with PDD Kit. Team members settle intent. Verus and the test suite hold the code to it. Consequently, every result in PDD Kit says which kind of verification it rests on: Formal verification is a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every possible input, checked by a tool called a verifier. For PDD Kit today, that verifier is Verus (opens in new tab) , a proof language for Rust co-developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI-SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison and the Weizmann Institute of Science. Empirical verification checks code by running it and observing what it does. It covers what a proof can’t reach, such as a third-party cryptography library or a user interface. It uses unit and end-to-end tests, terminal automation, browser agents, and computer-use agents for anything a browser can’t drive. A passing test only shows the code worked on the inputs it tried, so PDD Kit labels it as evidence rather than proof. The line between the two is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) : the code that the proof assumes behaves as described. PDD Kit makes that line explicit and asks you to sign off on each piece. The capstone: a full-stack web app To show PDD Kit integrating with existing codebases, we built Pet Store, a full-stack web app written entirely in Rust (opens in new tab) . The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab) . Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust. For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences: Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements: You only get a token with the right password. Only admin accounts get admin tokens. We kept the request rough on purpose. Capturing the intent of the user and turning the user request into something a proof can check is PDD Kit’s job. Step 1: Questions before code PDD Kit’s planning workflow, pdd-plan, reads the code and comes back, before writing anything, with questions in a Decisions tab. When a question depends on how the code works, the card explains that part first: the goal, how the pieces fit, and the exact function involved, so you can answer without opening the source. Figure 2. The first decision card. “Only with the right password” on its own is also met by a login that refuses everyone. Proving both ways rules that out. The question looks pedantic, but it matters. “You only get a token with the right password” rules out the bad case, a wrong password getting a token, and a login that refuses everyone keeps that promise perfectly. “The right password always works” is the half that rules it out. Formally, the first is an implication (token ⇒ right password) and the second is its converse. Together they make an “if and only if.” An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways. Step 2: A human readable intent map As the conversation goes on, PDD Kit keeps a rough work section at the top of the plan current, so a user can keep track of important concepts without having to scroll back through a long chat to find what was agreed. It includes a flowchart of the login being specified, a spec landscape of what will be proved and what will be trusted, and, when a picture helps, a mental model. For login, PDD Kit drew a ticket desk (Figure 3). Figure 3. PDD Kit’s mental model for login. The field you send picks the window, the window picks the table and with it the role, and nothing prints until the password matches. Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent. Figure 4. An intent map entry after the decision: a login gets a token only with the right password for that account, and always with it. The flowchart shows every way the password check can end. The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token. Figure 5. Two readings of the same sentence. They differ in one cell, and that cell changes what the proof has to establish. Step 3: Proving the login function Before anything gets built, PDD Kit asks the team to sign off on the plan as a whole. Its first draft proved the decision at the center of login, picking the table and gating on the password, and kept the handler around it trusted and tested. That’s a sensible default, and it’s what PDD Kit recommended, but the developer wanted more. The handler is where the lookups get awaited and the token gets signed, and that glue is exactly where a refactor can quietly swap two lines. So at intent review the developer chose to give the login handler its own async spec, so the proof covers that glue too instead of trusting it (Figure 6). Figure 6. Proving more of login means trusting more small wrappers. The card says so before the developer chooses. That choice moved almost everything into the proof and left the login handler with nothing to do but unpack the request. A new async function, login_flow , carries the contract from the request’s fields all the way to the token or the HTTP error. PDD Kit then brought the revised plan back for a fresh sign-off, because matching your intent isn’t proof, and it doesn’t approve new trust or a wider scope. Step 4: Where proof stops There are plenty of things you can’t prove about a program, and login runs into most of them: Code the verifier can’t see. bcrypt’s hashing, sqlx’s queries and jsonwebtoken’s signing live in other crates, outside the proof. Facts about the outside world. What SQLite holds right now and what time the clock says are inputs to the program, not something its code can establish. Whether, and how fast, something finishes. The spec says what you get if login answers. A hung query, or a slow one, breaks nothing in it. Anything a person has to judge , like whether an error message helps or a screen makes sense. Whatever nobody wrote down. A proof covers its spec and says nothing about requirements outside it. That’s where empirical verification comes in. PDD Kit spells out the trusted boundary, the part of the TCB this proof leans on. It wraps each trusted piece in a small function with an assumed contract, using Verus’s #[verifier::external_body] or external_fn_specification , asks the developer to accept each one on its own, and writes a test for every assumed clause into the plan. For login, the developer signed off on six pieces: The two lookups, Customer::find_by_email and Admin::find_by_username . Each awaited, successful lookup returns exactly the row its own table holds for that email or username, or none. check_password , a thin wrapper around bcrypt::verify . It errors only on a stored hash bcrypt can’t read, and Ok(true) means exactly the right password. generate_token , which signs exactly the claims it is given under the configured secret and reports a signing failure as a 500. expiry_from_now , which reads the clock and writes an expiry exactly 24 hours later. database_error , which turns a failed lookup into today’s 500 with sqlx’s message. The login handler shell, which unpacks the request and passes its fields to login_flow unchanged. In the spec, a lookup keeps its code where it is and gets a contract from the outside with external_fn_specification : /// Looks up a customer by exact email. /// Trusted, not proved: the SQL query runs in sqlx, which Verus cannot check. /// Every customer promise of `login_flow` rests on it. #[verifier::external_fn_specification] pub async fn ex_customer_find_by_email(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, email: &str) -> (r: Result , sqlx::Error>) ensures // When the query succeeds, it returns the customers row on // file for exactly this email, or None when there is none. r matches Ok(found) ==> found == customer_on_file(email@), { Customer::find_by_email(pool, email).await } The clock is a small wrapper marked #[verifier::external_body] . Verus uses its ensures clause and never reads the body: /// Reads the clock and computes a token's expiry 24 hours ahead. /// Trusted, not proved: chrono's clock is outside the proof. /// It panics if the time is out of range, as today's login does; /// that panic is not promised against. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn expiry_from_now() -> (r: Expiry) ensures // The expiry is exactly 24 hours (86,400 seconds) after the clock reading. r.exp as int == r.now as int + 86_400, { ... } Figure 7 puts the three layers together: what Verus proves, what people accept and tests check, and what nobody is promising. Figure 7. Where the login proof stops. Verus proves the core for every input. People accept the trusted ring and tests check it. The plan lists what nobody is promising. Figure 8 maps what gets proved and what gets trusted. Each trust decision is its own card. It shows the clauses Verus will take on faith, what the developer is accepting, and which promise falls apart if the assumption is wrong (Figure 9). Every assumed clause then gets an empirical check in the plan’s Empirical verification section, written as Given/When/Then scenarios before any test exists (Figure 10). An entry says planned until it has run, and then it records the command’s result and the commit it ran against. Figure 8. What gets proved and what gets trusted in login. Green functions are proved by Verus for every input. Amber pieces are trusted, accepted by the developer, and checked by the planned tests in the plan’s §4.1. Figure 9. A trust card for check_password . Verus takes these two clauses on faith, so a person accepts them and two tests check them. Figure 10. A planned test for the trusted check_password , written before the test exists. The plan labels a passing test as evidence rather than proof. The plan is just as explicit about what nobody is promising: that the login future ever completes, that an out-of-range clock won’t panic, anything about the timing or rate of attempts, and how other endpoints read the role. Step 5: Reading the spec The intent artifact is what the team reviews. It’s the plain-language version of the formal spec PDD Kit writes as Verus contracts. You might be wondering whether someone now has to read the proof instead of the code. Nobody does, because the coding agent writes the proof and Verus checks every step of it. If Verus accepts the proof, it holds whether or not anyone reads it. The spec is what the proof is held to, so that’s what people review, and this one is short enough to learn to read in a few minutes. Each function gets an ensures block: statements about its result, r, that must hold for every possible input. Verus checks them when you build, and if any clause could fail for even one input, the build fails and Verus points at that clause. Each clause reads as an if-then, and Figure 11 takes apart the clause for the developer’s first requirement. Figure 11. The ensures clause on login_flow for “You only get a token with the right password.” The same account a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. Notice that the same a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. For example, imagine a bug where login checks the password against one account but signs the token for another. Bob logs in with his own, correct password and gets back a token for Alice’s account. Each step looks fine on its own, but this clause catches it, because the password check and the token have to name the same account. That’s the kind of wiring bug a test suite rarely thinks to look for. The spec also has to talk about SQLite, bcrypt and JWTs without running any of them. It does that with uninterpreted functions , names with no body: customer_on_file(email) and admin_on_file(username) for the rows the database holds, bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) for what bcrypt would say, and token_claims(token, secret) for what a token carries. Verus knows nothing about them except what the trusted contracts from Step 4 promise. The proof says “whatever the database holds, login does the right thing with it,” and a trusted contract says “the lookup returns what the database holds.” /// The customers row the database holds for /// exactly this email, if any, when login looks. /// Left abstract: only `Customer::find_by_email`'s /// trusted contract says what it is. pub uninterp spec fn customer_on_file(email: Seq ) -> Option ; ... /// What bcrypt says about `password` against a /// stored `hash`: Some(true) when it is the password /// the hash was made from, Some(false) when it is /// not, None when bcrypt cannot read the hash. /// Left abstract: its meaning is bcrypt's, taken on trust through `check_password`. pub uninterp spec fn bcrypt_verdict(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> Option ; /// The password is the right one for the stored hash, by bcrypt's verdict. pub open spec fn password_matches(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> bool { bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) == Some(true) } On top of those, named_account(email, username) says which account a login names: the customers row for the email when one is sent, otherwise the admins row for the username, otherwise none. It’s written like Rust, but it’s a mathematical definition that never runs and only appears in contracts. Code like this is called ghost code , since the verifier checks it but the compiler erases it from the program. With it, the developer’s two-sentence request ends up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow (Figure 12). /// The account a login names: the customers row for /// the email when one is sent (role "customer"), /// otherwise the admins row for the username (role "admin"), otherwise none. pub open spec fn named_account(email: Option , username: Option ) -> Option { match email { Some(e) => match customer_on_file(e@) { Some(c) => Some(NamedAccount { id: c.id@, password_hash: c.password_hash@, role: customer_role() }), None => None, }, None => match username { Some(u) => match admin_on_file(u@) { Some(a) => Some(NamedAccount { id: a.id@, password_hash: a.password_hash@, role: admin_role() }), None => None, }, None => None, }, } } Figure 12. The two-sentence request and the Both ways decision ended up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow. Four of them keep today’s refusals, so the storefront and the existing API tests keep working. Here’s the whole contract, with its doc comment trimmed. Each clause has the plain-English comment above it that the intent artifact shows the team: /// The whole login, awaited end to end: from the /// request's fields to the token or the HTTP error. /// ... pub async fn login_flow(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, config: &Config, email: Option , username: Option , password: &str) -> (r: Result ) ensures // Neither an email nor a username: 400 with today's message. email is None && username is None ==> (r matches Err(AppError::BadRequest(m)) && m@ == missing_identity_text()), // A token only for the account the login names, with its right // password; it carries that account's id and its table's role. r matches Ok(t) ==> (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.sub@ == a.id && c.role@ == a.role), // The right password for the named account always gets a // token, unless a lookup or signing failure gives 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash)) ==> (r is Ok || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A login naming an account nobody holds gets // 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. ((email is Some || username is Some) && named_account(email, username) is None) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A wrong password for an account whose hash bcrypt // can read gets 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) == Some(false)) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // An account whose stored hash bcrypt cannot read gets 500 and no token. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) is None) ==> r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_)), // The admin role only for an admins row // found by username, with no email sent. (r matches Ok(t) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == admin_role()) ==> (email is None && username matches Some(u) && admin_on_file(u@) is Some), // An email login's token always carries the customer role. (r matches Ok(t) && email is Some) ==> (token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == customer_role()), { unimplemented!() } The trusted boundary shows up in the code too. check_password is one of the functions whose body Verus doesn’t check. Its contract ties it to bcrypt_verdict , an uninterpreted model of bcrypt with no axioms: /// Asks bcrypt whether `password` matches the stored `hash`. /// Trusted, not proved: Verus cannot check bcrypt's hashing, /// so this wrapper's contract is assumed. /// Every password promise of `login_flow` rests on it. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn check_password(password: &str, hash: &str) -> (r: Result ) ensures // bcrypt answers (Ok) exactly when it can read the stored hash. r is Ok <==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) is Some, // Its answer is its verdict: true for the // right password, false for any other. r matches Ok(b) ==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) == Some(b), { bcrypt::verify(password, hash).map_err(|e| e.to_string()) } The doc comment above it says what rests on it: every password promise of login_flow . Every login ends in one of a handful of places, and only one of them has a token (Figure 13). The proof covers all of them at once. Figure 13. Every way a login can end, from the plan. login_flow is async: it awaits a database query. Verus can put contracts on async functions, with one rule worth knowing (Figure 14). requires is checked when the call creates the future. ensures describes the value you get when you aw

items.title: High-Level Platform meets in Moldova to strengthen digital connectivity between the EU, the Black Sea region, South-Caucasus and Central Asia
items.summary: Yesterday and today, the first High-Level Connectivity Platform Meeting on Digital takes place in Chișinău, Moldova, jointly hosted by the European Commission and the Moldovan Ministry of Economic Development and Digitalisation. © Oleksii Liskonih The meeting sets the groundwork for stronger digital connectivity between Europe and Centra Asia, via the Black Sea region, the South Caucasus and Türkiye, in the form of an Integrated EU Secure Connectivity Offer. The Platform brings together European technology, expertise, standards and financing to strengthen secure, trusted and resilient digital connectivity. It contributes to the EU's plans to develop the Middle Corridor, which will connect Central Asia across the Caspian Sea to the South Caucasus and directly to the European market, via Türkiye and the Black Sea. The aim is to diversify routes, triple trade flows and slash freight transit times by 2030. The Integrated EU Secure Connectivity Offer is a regional application of the EU Tech

The Platform brings together European technology, expertise, standards and financing to strengthen secure, trusted and resilient digital connectivity. It contributes to the EU's plans to develop the Middle Corridor, which will connect Central Asia across the Caspian Sea to the South Caucasus and directly to the European market, via Türkiye and the Black Sea. The aim is to diversify routes, triple trade flows and slash freight transit times by 2030. The Integrated EU Secure Connectivity Offer is a regional application of the EU Tech Business Offer as outlined in the EU International Digital Strategy , and in line with EU secure connectivity initiatives such as IRIS and policies such as the EU toolbox for 5G security. items.content: Algorithms and theory Google’s mission presents many exciting algorithmic and optimization challenges across different product areas including Search, Ads, Social, and Google Infrastructure. These include optimizing internal systems such as scheduling the machines that power the numerous computations done each day, as well as optimizations that affect core products and users, from online allocation of ads to page-views to automatic management of ad campaigns, and from clustering large-scale graphs to finding best paths in transportation networks. Other than employing new algorithmic ideas to impact millions of users, Google researchers contribute to the state-of-the-art research in these areas by publishing in top conferences and journals. Recent Publications See More Depth-CoT Tradeoffs in Transformers: A Look at Path Following Clayton Sanford Matus Telgarsky Justin D. Li 2027 Preview Preview abstract Modern transformers have been scaled up in size, data, training-time compute, and more recently test-time compute based on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the consequences of trading off these parameters are unknown. We construct explicit tradeoffs between two of these aspects: the number of layers in a transformer and the number of CoT tokens. Our first result is general: with mild assumptions and a single-token prompt, for any integer k, a transformer using soft attention and SwiGLU MLP layers with L layers and n CoT tokens can be converted to a transformer with at most ckL layers and ⌈n/k⌉ CoT tokens, and vice versa, although with an increase to the size of other parameters. We then a multi-token prompt path following task, finding that additional preprocessing from the multi-token prompt changes the depth-CoT relationship in this case. We construct an attention-only network with L layers and 2^(L−2) heads that can traverse 2^(L−1) − 1 edges along a path with a single CoT token, demonstrating at least an exponential relationship between increases in depth and reductions in the number of CoT tokens needed to traverse the entire path. This relationship for the path following task holds empirically as well, as demonstrated by training networks with up to 5 layers, with the tradeoff between depth and the maximum number of edge traversals in a single CoT token exactly matching our theoretical constructions. View details Geo-Contextual AI Concierge: Minimizing Internal Support Friction Through Proactive Knowledge Synthesis Neeraj Choudhary Dónal Doyle Technical Report (2026) Preview Preview abstract In large-scale distributed enterprises, traditional Knowledge Management (KM) systems face a critical failure mode: static documentation cannot keep pace with evolving operational realities and regional nuances. This "knowledge latency" forces employees out of self-service workflows and into costly support ticketing queues. This paper introduces SENTINEL, a geo-contextual AI framework designed to shift enterprise support from reactive retrieval to proactive interception. The architecture employs a novel dual-engine system integrated into an omni-present interface. The first engine utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct pre-emptive, historical case-grounded audits of documentation, generating a "Contextual Density" score that identifies friction zones. The second engine is an autonomous Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) agent that surfaces in-situ via a location-intelligent assistant window, resolving queries in real-time. By functioning as a strategic "defensive barrier" at the point of origin, SENTINEL demonstrates how a proactive AI assistant can drive high-fidelity, in-situ case deflection. View details Rational Transductors Mehryar Mohri ICML 2026 Preview Preview abstract Standard Transformers excel at semantic modeling but struggle with rigid sequential logic and state tracking, fundamentally limited to AC0 complexity without intermediate chain-of- thought. In this work, we introduce Rational Transductors, a dual-stream architecture that augments the Transformer with a linear, matrix-valued recurrence derived from Weighted Finite Automata (WFA). By injecting rational state information into the attention mechanism via a Deep Rational Injection scheme, our framework strictly generalizes the expressive power of Transformers to capture all Regular Languages and NC1-complete problems (such as Parity and Modular Counting) while preserving O(log T) parallel training efficiency. View details Distributional Alignment Games for Answer-Level Fine-Tuning Mehryar Mohri Jon Schneider Yifan Wu ICML 2026 Preview Preview abstract We focus on the problem of \emph{Answer-Level Fine-Tuning} (ALFT), where the goal is to optimize a language model based on the correctness or properties of its final answers, rather than the specific reasoning traces used to produce them. Directly optimizing answer-level objectives is computationally intractable due to the need to marginalize over the vast space of latent reasoning paths. To overcome this, we propose a general game-theoretical framework that lifts the problem to a \emph{Distributional Alignment Game}. We formulate ALFT as a two-player game between a Policy (the generator) and a Target (an auxiliary distribution). We prove that the Nash Equilibrium of this game corresponds exactly to the solution of the original answer-level optimization problem. View details Cardio Load in exercise and everyday life: A modified TRIMP metric for continuously-sensing consumer wearables Justin Phillips Daniel Roggen YongSuk Cho Robert Harle Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise (2026) Preview Preview abstract PURPOSE: To introduce Cardio Load (CL), a metric quantifying cardiovascular work from all activities across the day, and to investigate its distribution by age, gender, and workout profiles. CL adapts the Training Impulse (TRIMP) model by leveraging continuous heart rate and movement data from wearables, enabling minute-level intensity estimation. We also discuss the derivation of weekly target loads, intended to guide fitness maintenance. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 31.2 million hours of wrist-worn wearable data collected over a six-week period. The dataset comprised a 40,000-subject subset (37.9% female) of consenting Google Pixel Watch® users in the United States, aged 18 to 80 years (18-39: 41.8%, 40-59: 43.5%, 60+: 14.6%). Measured data included minute-interval heart rate averages, resting and maximum heart rates, minute-interval averaged accelerometer log energy, and manually-logged or auto-detected activity types. Cardio Load scores and target loads were calculated daily for each subject and compared across age and gender. We also compared the proportions of CL gained during workouts and incidental daily activities for these groups. RESULTS: Overall, the study population's mean ± SD weekly CL scores were 221 ± 156 (female) and 259 ± 169 (male). Median weekly Cardio Load (CL) values exhibited consistency for individuals between 30 and 75 years of age. When analyzed in five-year age groups, the coefficient of variation (CV%) of median weekly CL values within this age range was less than 4.5%, with younger and older subjects demonstrating higher and lower median CL, respectively. The median proportion of CL accumulated during structured workouts versus incidental daily activity was 41.0% (female) and 49.0% (male) for all subjects, though this varied considerably with average weekly workout duration. CV% of weekly target load and daily target load over 6 weeks was 23.6% and 35.2% respectively. CONCLUSION: Cardio Load provides a continuous quantification of activity load from wearables, acknowledging both structured workouts and everydayincidental activity. CL is equitably rewarded for age ranges spanning 30-75 years. Weekly target loads were found to have little measurement variability and be more consistent and, consequently, more practical for planning training and physical activity than daily targets. View details Marginalized Bundle Adjustment: Multi-View Camera Pose from Monocular Depth Estimates Shengjie Zhu Ahmed Abdelkader Mark Matthews Xiaoming Liu Vincent Chu International Conference on 3D Vision (2026) Preview Preview abstract Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a classical 3D vision task for recovering camera parameters and scene geometry from multi-view images. Recent advances in deep learning enable accurate monocular depth estimation (MDE) that infers structure from a single image without depending on camera motion. But integrating MDE into SfM remains challenging. Unlike classical triangulated sparse pointclouds, MDE produces dense depthmaps with significantly higher error variance. Inspired by modern RANSAC estimators, we propose a Marginalized Bundle Adjustment (MBA) to accommodate MDE error variance with its density. With MBA, we show that MDE depthmaps are sufficiently accurate to support SoTA or competitive results in Structure-from-Motion and camera relocalization. Our benchmark demonstrates consistent remarkable results from two-view, few-frames small multiview, to thousands-frames large multiview system. Our method highlights the significant potential of MDE on multi-view 3D vision tasks.
