To overcome this, we propose a general game-theoretical framework that lifts the problem to a \emph{Distributional Alignment Game}. We formulate ALFT as a two-player game between a Policy (the generator) and a Target (an auxiliary distribution). We prove that the Nash Equilibrium of this game corresponds exactly to the solution of the original answer-level optimization problem. View details Cardio Load in exercise and everyday life: A modified TRIMP metric for continuously-sensing consumer wearables Justin Phillips Daniel Roggen YongSuk Cho Robert Harle Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise (2026) Preview Preview abstract PURPOSE: To introduce Cardio Load (CL), a metric quantifying cardiovascular work from all activities across the day, and to investigate its distribution by age, gender, and workout profiles. CL adapts the Training Impulse (TRIMP) model by leveraging continuous heart rate and movement data from wearables, enabling minute-level intensity estimation. We also discuss the derivation of weekly target loads, intended to guide fitness maintenance. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 31.2 million hours of wrist-worn wearable data collected over a six-week period. The dataset comprised a 40,000-subject subset (37.9% female) of consenting Google Pixel Watch® users in the United States, aged 18 to 80 years (18-39: 41.8%, 40-59: 43.5%, 60+: 14.6%). Measured data included minute-interval heart rate averages, resting and maximum heart rates, minute-interval averaged accelerometer log energy, and manually-logged or auto-detected activity types. Cardio Load scores and target loads were calculated daily for each subject and compared across age and gender. We also compared the proportions of CL gained during workouts and incidental daily activities for these groups. RESULTS: Overall, the study population's mean ± SD weekly CL scores were 221 ± 156 (female) and 259 ± 169 (male). Median weekly Cardio Load (CL) values exhibited consistency for individuals between 30 and 75 years of age. When analyzed in five-year age groups, the coefficient of variation (CV%) of median weekly CL values within this age range was less than 4.5%, with younger and older subjects demonstrating higher and lower median CL, respectively. The median proportion of CL accumulated during structured workouts versus incidental daily activity was 41.0% (female) and 49.0% (male) for all subjects, though this varied considerably with average weekly workout duration. CV% of weekly target load and daily target load over 6 weeks was 23.6% and 35.2% respectively. CONCLUSION: Cardio Load provides a continuous quantification of activity load from wearables, acknowledging both structured workouts and everydayincidental activity. CL is equitably rewarded for age ranges spanning 30-75 years. Weekly target loads were found to have little measurement variability and be more consistent and, consequently, more practical for planning training and physical activity than daily targets. View details Marginalized Bundle Adjustment: Multi-View Camera Pose from Monocular Depth Estimates Shengjie Zhu Ahmed Abdelkader Mark Matthews Xiaoming Liu Vincent Chu International Conference on 3D Vision (2026) Preview Preview abstract Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a classical 3D vision task for recovering camera parameters and scene geometry from multi-view images. Recent advances in deep learning enable accurate monocular depth estimation (MDE) that infers structure from a single image without depending on camera motion. But integrating MDE into SfM remains challenging. Unlike classical triangulated sparse pointclouds, MDE produces dense depthmaps with significantly higher error variance. Inspired by modern RANSAC estimators, we propose a Marginalized Bundle Adjustment (MBA) to accommodate MDE error variance with its density. With MBA, we show that MDE depthmaps are sufficiently accurate to support SoTA or competitive results in Structure-from-Motion and camera relocalization. Our benchmark demonstrates consistent remarkable results from two-view, few-frames small multiview, to thousands-frames large multiview system. Our method highlights the significant potential of MDE on multi-view 3D vision tasks. items.content: The European Commission launched a consultation to update its election guidelines under the Digital Services Act (DSA), addressing the rapid evolution of technologies, particularly generative Artificial Intelligence (AI), and the growing sophistication of manipulation risks. GettyImages © bizoo_n The election guidelines , published in 2024, offer guidance to Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) and Very Large Online Search Engines (VLOSEs) on assessing and mitigating systemic risks for electoral processes. Article 35 of the DSA requires platforms to assess and mitigate systemic risks to election integrity while safeguarding fundamental rights, including freedom of expression and information. The proposed update builds on two years of experience gathered under the DSA and the Code of Conduct on Disinformation . As part of the update, the Commission proposes measures for VLOPs and VLOSEs to better deter information manipulation risks, make recommender systems safer, and adapt to the evolving AI landscape. The updated guidelines also aim to enhance protections for political candidates. The consultation invites the submission of relevant experience and expertise by 23 November 2026. Last update 10 November 2026 Print as PDF

items.title: Commission preliminarily finds TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed in breach of Digital Services Act for harmful ‘rabbit holes’ effect
items.summary: The European Commission has preliminarily found TikTok in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) for the so-called ‘rabbit hole effect’ of its recommender system. TikTok's ‘For You' feed shows users a continuous stream of personalised videos, even when those are related to mental health struggles and body image. The more a user interacts with a certain type of content, the more TikTok's ‘For You' feed algorithm recommends similar content. This design can be harmful when such endless and repeated exposure involves, for example, content about sadness, isolation or body image. These ‘rabbit holes' can have a detrimental impact on users' mental health, especially that of vulnerable adults and minors. These preliminary findings focus on both risk assessment and mitigation measures. items.content: Featured projects TL;DR PyTorch models now run in the web browser on the GPU through ExecuTorch, with no conversion to another framework’s format. You export with torch.export to an ExecuTorch .pte file, and the same file runs in any WebGPU browser via ExecuTorch’s new WebGPU backend . It works across a broad range of models: LLMs (e.g. Llama 3.2, Qwen3, Gemma 3), vision-language (e.g. SmolVLM), segmentation, depth, object detection, super-resolution and speech-to-text (e.g. Whisper). Everything runs locally in the tab, and no data leaves the device. Try it in the ExecuTorch WebGPU Playground . On the same machine, WebGPU is 4–7× faster than ExecuTorch’s CPU path (Webassembly + XNNPACK) on prefill and 2–10× faster on decode. Why the Browser? The web is the largest deployment surface with billions of users on Chrome, Firefox and Safari. Browser inference ensures privacy by keeping users’ prompts, model inputs, and outputs on the user’s device rather than the server. This reduces network latency, enables offline use-cases, and lowers server-side inference costs. With the ExecuTorch WebGPU backend, PyTorch models get a native path to GPU-accelerated inference in WebGPU-enabled browsers on desktop, laptop and mobile. WebGPU, the modern successor to WebGL, provides native compute shaders, shared memory, storage buffers, and barriers, making it viable for high-performance ML inference directly in the browser. Today, running a PyTorch model in the browser usually means first converting it to another framework’s format, such as GGUF, ONNX or TFLite. The ExecuTorch WebGPU backend lets PyTorch models reach the browser without leaving the PyTorch toolchain. Backend Design [Figure 1: ExecuTorch WebGPU backend design: a PyTorch model is exported once to a .pte file and runs in any WebGPU browser through the ExecuTorch Wasm runtime] Three principles guided the WebGPU backend’s design: Architecture, export, and dynamic runtime. Models export through ExecuTorch’s torch.export() and WebGPUPartitioner and run via WGSL compute shaders. At runtime, the WebGPU runtime allocates GPU buffers and dispatches compute shaders into command buffers. Dynamic shapes are handled via allocate-at-max buffers with per-dispatch workgroup recalculation to enable batched prefill, and the runtime routes shapes to specialized WGSL kernels at runtime. Same artifact across multiple devices and browsers. One model (.pte file) runs in WebGPU browsers such as Chrome and Safari, natively on Metal (macOS), Vulkan (Linux/Android) and D3D12 (Windows), translating WGSL to Metal Shading Language, SPIR-V or HLSL depending on the platform. For browser deployment, the dynamic C++ runtime compiles to Webassembly via Emscripten and emdawnwebgpu bridges its WebGPU API calls to any browser’s WebGPU JavaScript API. Zero friction for the end user. With WebGPU, models run in the browser sandbox with no native installation, backend server, and no data leaving the device. For developers, deployment is a .pte file served over CDN on a web page. Pipeline compilation, memory management, and dispatch scheduling are all handled through the WebGPU backend, with all data staying in GPU device memory within the browser tab. Performance We benchmarked ExecuTorch WebGPU against ExecuTorch’s own Webassembly (wasm) CPU backend (XNNPACK, multi-threaded) on the same machine, using quantized Llama 3.2 1B and Qwen3-0.6B in Google Chrome on Apple M1 Pro. Each data point is the median of 5 runs after 3 warmups, across 128 to 8K tokens of context, with identical token IDs for both backends. Both are timed with wall-clock time, since GPU timestamps aren’t available for CPU execution. WebGPU uses 4-bit groupwise weights (group size 64) with fp32 activations; the CPU uses XNNPACK’s 4-bit weights with 8-bit dynamic activations. [Figure 2: ExecuTorch WebGPU is 4–7× faster than ExecuTorch Wasm (XNNPACK) on prefill and 2–10× faster on decode, measured in Chrome on Apple M1 Pro] Models in Practice We’ve validated the WebGPU backend across models with very different architectures, demonstrating that the operator coverage generalizes beyond autoregressive text generation: LLM Inference Llama 3.2 1B (4-bit quantized) Qwen2.5-0.5B (4-bit quantized) Qwen3-0.6B (4-bit quantized) Gemma 3 1B Vision-Language Understanding SmolVLM : image question answering and captioning Vision Depth Anything V2 : monocular depth estimation SAM 2 (SAM 2.1 Hiera Tiny) : promptable image segmentation D-FINE : object detection Real-ESRGAN : super-resolution Background Removal (MODNet) : foreground segmentation Voice Whisper (base) : speech-to-text Phonon-31M-EN : text-to-speech On-Device Training LoRA and DiReFT fine-tuning for Llama 3.2 1B, Qwen2.5 0.5B and Qwen3 0.6B, aimed at personalized assistants and domain adaptation on-device [Figure 3: ExecuTorch WebGPU demonstration] Try it: ExecuTorch WebGPU Playground The ExecuTorch WebGPU Playground runs many of the models above, all on the same WebAssembly + WebGPU runtime. All the prompts, photos, camera frames and audio never leave your device. Each model’s Hugging Face repo includes the .pte files, a model card, and the exact export recipe. What’s Next The backend is still in early development. We’ll keep making the backend faster and more stable, and expand operator, data type, and model coverage. Contributions / Feedback ExecuTorch is open source, and we’d love your contributions to the WebGPU backend. If something breaks or a model you care about isn’t supported, open an issue or reach us on the ExecuTorch Discord . Contributions are welcome too, whether that’s new operators, new models or performance improvements. Learn more at ExecuTorch Documentation | ExecuTorch repo | WebGPU Backend

For browser deployment, the dynamic C++ runtime compiles to Webassembly via Emscripten and emdawnwebgpu bridges its WebGPU API calls to any browser’s WebGPU JavaScript API. Zero friction for the end user. With WebGPU, models run in the browser sandbox with no native installation, backend server, and no data leaving the device. For developers, deployment is a .pte file served over CDN on a web page. Pipeline compilation, memory management, and dispatch scheduling are all handled through the WebGPU backend, with all data staying in GPU device memory within the browser tab. Performance We benchmarked ExecuTorch WebGPU against ExecuTorch’s own Webassembly (wasm) CPU backend (XNNPACK, multi-threaded) on the same machine, using quantized Llama 3.2 1B and Qwen3-0.6B in Google Chrome on Apple M1 Pro. Each data point is the median of 5 runs after 3 warmups, across 128 to 8K tokens of context, with identical token IDs for both backends. Both are timed with wall-clock time, since GPU timestamps aren’t available for CPU execution. WebGPU uses 4-bit groupwise weights (group size 64) with fp32 activations; the CPU uses XNNPACK’s 4-bit weights with 8-bit dynamic activations. [Figure 2: ExecuTorch WebGPU is 4–7× faster than ExecuTorch Wasm (XNNPACK) on prefill and 2–10× faster on decode, measured in Chrome on Apple M1 Pro] Models in Practice We’ve validated the WebGPU backend across models with very different architectures, demonstrating that the operator coverage generalizes beyond autoregressive text generation: LLM Inference Llama 3.2 1B (4-bit quantized) Qwen2.5-0.5B (4-bit quantized) Qwen3-0.6B (4-bit quantized) Gemma 3 1B Vision-Language Understanding SmolVLM : image question answering and captioning Vision Depth Anything V2 : monocular depth estimation SAM 2 (SAM 2.1 Hiera Tiny) : promptable image segmentation D-FINE : object detection Real-ESRGAN : super-resolution Background Removal (MODNet) : foreground segmentation Voice Whisper (base) : speech-to-text Phonon-31M-EN : text-to-speech On-Device Training LoRA and DiReFT fine-tuning for Llama 3.2 1B, Qwen2.5 0.5B and Qwen3 0.6B, aimed at personalized assistants and domain adaptation on-device [Figure 3: ExecuTorch WebGPU demonstration] Try it: ExecuTorch WebGPU Playground The ExecuTorch WebGPU Playground runs many of the models above, all on the same WebAssembly + WebGPU runtime. All the prompts, photos, camera frames and audio never leave your device. Each model’s Hugging Face repo includes the .pte files, a model card, and the exact export recipe. What’s Next The backend is still in early development. We’ll keep making the backend faster and more stable, and expand operator, data type, and model coverage. Contributions / Feedback ExecuTorch is open source, and we’d love your contributions to the WebGPU backend. If something breaks or a model you care about isn’t supported, open an issue or reach us on the ExecuTorch Discord . Contributions are welcome too, whether that’s new operators, new models or performance improvements. Learn more at ExecuTorch Documentation | ExecuTorch repo | WebGPU Backend

At the center is a megakernel: all 62 layers of a decode or verify step run as one Pallas program, and every weight load, KV read and cross-device transfer is pipelined behind compute. The rest of the work falls into three groups: faster decode steps (collective folding, a max-free attention loop that pipelines its KV chunks, an expert loop that keeps register spills off its common path, and DFlash2 speculative decoding), more KV cache per chip (sequence-on-lane KV layout in the megakernel, and L2 HiCache on TPU with session-aware eviction), and faster prefill (a fused MoE kernel and sequence parallelism). Decode speed. The megakernel halves the time per output token for one or two concurrent requests, where it helps the most; the gain narrows as concurrency grows. Its verify step runs within 1.5–1.7× of the time it takes just to stream its weights from HBM. AgentX. On the 1M-context version of SemiAnalysis’s agentic-coding benchmark, our curve runs from 433 output tokens/s per request at 6,101 tokens/s per chip to 25,906 tokens/s per chip at 95 tokens/s per request (Figure 1). Results Figure 1. InferenceX AgentX, 1M-context trace set: tokens per dollar against p90 interactivity. TPU v7: one host, four chips, FP8 compute with NVFP4 expert weights. GB200 (FP4) is shown as a baseline from InferenceX’s published results as of 2026-11-02. Costs are InferenceX’s external owning costs: $1.21 per TPU v7 chip-hour and $1.86 per GB200 GPU-hour. AgentX is built from 393 opt-in Claude Code sessions. It replays their request lengths, prefix sharing between turns, tool pauses and subagent structure, with synthetic tokens in place of the original content. We run its 1M-context trace set, as the GB200 baseline does, where prompts reach about 990K tokens; models with shorter context windows run a version capped at 256K. Throughput counts input and output tokens. Every TPU point in Figure 1 finishes requests within 47 s at p90. Background The model Muse Spark Open is Meta’s open-weights mixture-of-experts (MoE) [1] model, with 816B parameters in total and about 42B active per token. 62 decoder layers, all of them MoE. Each layer routes every token to 8 of 256 experts. Hybrid attention. 46 layers use sliding-window attention [2] over the last 2,048 tokens; the other 16 attend over the full context, up to 1M tokens. Attention has 128 query heads and 16 KV heads, each 64 wide. NVFP4 experts. Expert weights are 4-bit, with one scale per 16 values, a microscaling format [3]. The hardware One TPU v7 (Ironwood) host has four chips. Each chip packs two chiplets, each with one TensorCore and its own HBM, and frameworks expose each chiplet as a device, so a host has 8 devices. We shard the model 8 ways with tensor parallelism [4], one shard per device. Figure 2. One TPU v7 chip, simplified from the architecture diagram in Google Cloud’s TPU7x documentation . The numbers are Google’s published figures. Each device is a single-threaded processor: one program runs at a time, so speed comes from keeping the matrix units fed and overlapping memory transfers with compute inside that program. These are the units that matter in this post, as described in Google Cloud’s TPU7x documentation and JAX’s Pallas TPU guide : Scalar unit. One per device, with its own small scalar memory (SMEM). It runs the control flow: loops, branches and address math. MXU, the matrix unit. Two per device. They do the matmuls; the chip’s peak is 2,307 TFLOPs in bf16 and 4,614 in fp8. At small batch they mostly wait for weights to arrive from HBM. Vector unit (VPU). Elementwise work such as norms, softmax exponentials and format conversions. On recent TPUs it computes on 2D vector registers of 8 × 128 32-bit values, 8 sublanes by 128 lanes, so a data layout that leaves lanes empty wastes both vector work and memory (section 7). A cross-lane unit (XLU) next to it does transposes and permutes. VMEM. On-chip SRAM next to the MXUs and the vector unit, with much higher bandwidth than HBM. Kernels stage their tiles here, so its size bounds how much a kernel can keep in flight. DMA engines. They move data between HBM, VMEM and other devices in the background: a kernel starts a copy and waits for it later, while it computes. The megakernel’s pipelining (section 2) is built on them. HBM. 192 GiB per chip at 7.37 TB/s, 96 GiB of it on each device. Die-to-die link. It joins the two devices of a chip; Google documents it as six times faster than a 1D ICI link. Section 8’s pair exchange leans on it. ICI. Six links per chip at 200 GB/s each, counting both directions, for 1,200 GB/s per chip. The four chips of a host talk to each other over it; slices of 64 chips or more form 3D tori. Host. Each chip connects to the host’s CPUs over PCIe Gen5 ×16. A 4-chip host has 960 GB of DRAM, which L2 HiCache uses as a second cache tier (section 7). SparseCores. Four per chip. This work does not use them. The TorchTPU post has a longer primer. The software The server is SGLang-TorchTPU : SGLang’s [5] scheduler, KV cache and model code in PyTorch, with Pallas kernels on the hot paths. We decode with speculative decoding [6, 7]: a small draft model guesses the next few tokens, and the full model checks them all in one forward pass, the verify step . Each (request, position) pair in a verify step is a row , so two requests verifying 8 tokens each make a 16-row step. 1. A megakernel At small batch, generating a token does little math per weight, so the step is as fast as HBM can stream the weights, as long as nothing interrupts the stream. A decode or verify step should therefore be one uninterrupted stream of weights from HBM into the MXU. Our previous path (“native” below) ran each layer as several kernels plus collectives, and every boundary stopped the stream. The megakernel runs all 62 layers of a step as one Pallas program per device, so the next weights are always in flight. Whole-step megakernels have been built for GPUs [8, 9] and, on TPU v7, for Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 [10]. Ours runs inside SGLang’s serving path, on its paged KV cache, for the decode and DFlash2 verify steps of many requests at once. The native path was already built from fused Pallas blocks, yet its verify step took 2.9× the time needed to stream its weights. Profiling our first one-kernel prototype showed why: at batch 1 the matmuls and attention cost almost nothing, while collectives cost about 45 µs per layer. Nothing overlaps across a program boundary, so the step was bound by overhead, not by bandwidth. Figure 3. One step. Inside the megakernel every layer runs the same flow (white); the shaded boxes are data movement the kernel issues itself. For each step, every device runs one pallas_call that covers all 62 layers and the final norm. SGLang still runs the embedding, the draft model, a small KV-write kernel, the LM head and sampling around it. Figure 4. Time per verify step, both paths with DFlash2 speculative decoding (GSM8K, measured on an earlier Muse Spark checkpoint). The floor is the time to stream that step’s distinct experts and dense weights from HBM. Per output token, the megakernel is 1.94× faster than the native path for a single request (1.95 ms against 3.78 ms) and 1.85× for two concurrent requests. The next sections show what made one program this fast. 2. Pipelining everything inside the megakernel A step is mostly data movement: weights, KV cache and partial sums between devices. Once the whole step is one program, the kernel can schedule every transfer so that it lands just before the compute that needs it [11], including across layer boundaries [10]. Figure 5 sketches one layer. Figure 5. One layer of a step, schematic. Each DMA stream runs ahead of, or alongside, the compute that consumes it. Weights arrive before they are needed A ring for dense weights. Attention, o-proj and router weights stream through a ring of tiles that prefetches across layer boundaries. About ten tiles in flight sustain 3.34 TB/s per device, while a single DMA stream reaches only 1.13 TB/s. Experts as soon as routing finishes. The router’s choice is known only mid-layer, so the kernel requests each chosen expert’s weights the moment routing ends, with three experts in flight. The next layer during the expert loop. Refills for the next layer’s attention weights are held until the expert loop runs, so they never compete with the expert weights the current layer is waiting for. Collectives leave as soon as their data exists Tensor parallelism exchanges partial sums between the 8 devices several times per layer. Instead of a separate collective after each matmul, the kernel writes partial results straight into the owning device’s memory with remote DMAs issued from inside the kernel; a small round costs about 3 µs. Streamed o-proj. Each o-proj output tile leaves for its owner as soon as it is computed, while the next tile is still being multiplied. Pipelined KV writes Each step writes its new K and V rows into the cache. In our fp8 sequence-on-lane cache (section 7), a token is one lane column of a 256-token page, so writing a token means reading the whole page block into VMEM, merging the new columns, and writing the page back. This runs as a small kernel right after the megakernel, because XLA copies the aliased operands of any kernel that issues remote DMA. It used to do every page in turn: read, wait, merge, write, wait, for each request and each of 62 layers. Figure 6. Schematic. The pipelined kernel issues all of a layer’s page reads at once, merges each page as it lands, and starts its write; the next layer’s reads start immediately on a second VMEM bank. The new kernel loads all layers’ new rows once, then keeps two VMEM banks: layer l reads into one while layer l−1’s writes drain from the other, and a bank is reused only after the writes of two layers earlier have landed. The write cost per step fell from 810 to 155 µs at 16 rows and from 2,286 to 336 µs at 64 rows, with bit-identical results. 3. Collective folding Because each layer is split across 8 devices, a device often has to collect the others’ results before it can continue. After the MoE and after attention, each device holds one slice of the layer’s output along the hidden dimension, and must all-gather the other seven slices before the next matvec can run. Collective folding lets that matvec start on the slices as they arrive instead of waiting for the whole gather, as decomposed collective matmuls do [12], here across the RMS norm that sits between the two. Figure 7. Schematic. The folded matvec multiplies each gathered slice as soon as it lands, starting with the device’s own, and applies the per-row normalization at the end. What makes this possible is where Muse Spark normalizes. The next layer’s attention input is an RMS norm [13] of the residual stream α·x + β·s·f, where x is the residual this device already holds, f is the gathered MoE output and s is f’s own norm factor. The two norm factors, s and the final r, are each one scalar per row. Scalars per row commute with the matmul, so the projection splits into a part the device can compute right away and a part that adds up slice by slice: Here g is the norm’s gain vector, f_d is the slice from device d, and W_d is the matching block of weight rows. The kernel stacks the local part and the arriving slice into one product per block, consumes the slices in a fixed peer order, and reorders the weight ring so that W’s blocks stream in the same order. Once the last slice is in, it computes s and r and scales the result. The kernel folds two all-gathers per layer this way: the MoE output into the next layer’s qkv projection, and the attention output into the pooler and router. The residual stream itself is unchanged; only the point where the matmul input is rounded to bf16 moves, so results are not bit-identical, and our accuracy checks cover it. 4. Enabling better pipelining in attention At long context, attention is the largest part of a step. The kernel walks the KV cache chunk by chunk, and the key bottleneck was the running max of online softmax [14]: it chained every chunk to the one before, so chunks could not be pipelined. The running max chains every chunk Online softmax, as used by FlashAttention [15], keeps the maximum score seen so far. Each new chunk computes its scores, updates that maximum, exponentiates against it, and rescales everything accumulated so far whenever the maximum grows. So each chunk is a serial chain (wait for its DMA, QK, max, exp, sum, P·V, rescale) that cannot start its exponentials until the previous chunk’s maximum is known. In a microbenchmark this chain costs about 0.17 µs per chunk, whether the chunk is fp8 or bf16. Muse Spark makes the max unnecessary Muse Spark normalizes q and k (QK-norm [16, 17]) with an RMS norm that has no learned weight, and gives q a fixed gain. No attention score can exceed 43.8 in magnitude, far from where exp overflows in f32. The running max exists only to prevent that overflow, so the kernel drops it, along with the rescale. It checks the bound from the model’s constants when it is built. FlashDecoding++ [18] breaks the same chain on GPUs with a unified max value and a recomputation path for the rare overflow; here the bound is exact, so the kernel needs no fallback. Figure 8. Schematic. With a running max, each chunk’s chain waits on the previous chunk. Without it, chunks are independent and their stages overlap. Independent chunks pipeline Without the max, chunks no longer depend on each other. The kernel issues all DMA waits at the top of each loop iteration, splits the chunks across several independent softmax streams that merge at the end, as Flash-Decoding does across the KV sequence [19], and software-pipelines the loop [11]: it scores the next chunks while it multiplies the previous chunks’ probabilities by V. Three smaller changes shorten each chain further: Chunk size by layer type. Global layers read the cache in long chunks of 1,024 to 2,048 tokens, so a 100K context needs far fewer chains. Sliding-window layers use 512-token chunks, since their window spans only a few. fp8 keys straight into the MXU. Widening each fp8 chunk to bf16 on the vector unit cost more vector work than the MXU work it fed. Mixed bf16 × fp8 dots are exact, so the keys now go in as fp8. The attention scale in the queries. Muse Spark’s attention scale is 1/8, a power of two, so multiplying the queries once instead of every score is exact. Figure 9. Microbenchmark at production shapes. The memory floor is the time to read the KV bytes. In the microbenchmark, longer chunks with independent streams cut attention time 2.4×, and dropping the running max took it to 3.9×. In the server, the pipelined loop raised per-request decode speed by 18% for two requests at 500K context. 5. Keeping register pressure off the common path A processor computes on values held in its registers, a small, fixed set of storage slots next to the arithmetic units. When code needs more live values than the registers hold, the compiler spills some of them to memory and loads them back later [20], and those extra stores and loads cost time on every pass through the code. In a loop with several branches, the compiler has to fit the live values of all branches into the same registers, so one heavy branch can make every pass through the loop spill, even when that branch never runs. The megakernel’s expert loop had exactly this problem. A step loops over the experts its rows were routed to. For each one, the kernel waits for the expert’s weights and runs a path chosen by how many rows the expert serves: a few-row path, with small variants for one to eight rows, and a dequantize-then-multiply path for busier experts. As the batch grows, a step visits more experts, but most of them still serve only one or two rows, so the light path is the one that matters. One heavy branch slows the light path The 8-row variant keeps large f32 accumulators that do not fit in the vector registers even on their own. Because it shared one loop body with the one- and two-row variants, the common path spilled registers to memory and loaded them back on every expert: about 0.37 µs per expert, against roughly 1.2 µs to stream that expert’s weights. That overhead had nothing to do with the work the light path itself did. Two loops instead of one The fix keeps the heavy code out of the light path’s loop. The kernel sorts a step’s experts by row count and runs two loops: one for experts with at most four rows, and one for the rest. Each loop body now holds only its own variants, so the few-row loop carries 61–64% fewer spill instructions. Every expert still takes the same path as before, so the output is bit-identical. Figure 10. Schematic. In one shared loop body, every few-row expert is followed by a spill and refill, and the loop falls behind its weight stream. In their own loop, few-row experts keep pace with the weights. In a kernel test with random routing, decode steps with many requests got 13–19% faster, and the expert loop now keeps pace with its weight stream. 6. Speculative decoding with DFlash2 Without speculation, every output token costs one full pass over the active weights. DFlash [21] drafts a whole block of tokens in one forward pass of a small model; we use Muse Spark’s DFlash2 draft model. Figure 11. One speculative step. The draft model reads hidden states captured from the full model. The token strip is an illustration. The draft attends bidirectionally within its block and proposes all of the block’s tokens at once. The full model checks the whole block in one megakernel step and keeps the longest prefix of drafts that matches its own choices, plus one token of its own. This suits TPU well: MXU time grows with the number of row and output tiles, not with multiply-adds, and a block’s few rows fit in the same row tile as one token, so verifying a block costs little more than verifying one token. Measured on GSM8K with real acceptance, DFlash2 cut the megakernel’s time per output token for a single request from 3.93 to 1.95 ms, 2.0×. 7. More context per device: KV layout and L2 HiCache On agent traffic, KV capacity is throughput: every prefix that falls out of the cache comes back as a 100K-token re-prefill. After the weights, each device has only about 20 GiB left for KV, split between a full-attention pool for the 16 global layers and a sliding-window pool for the other 46. fp8 KV in a sequence-on-lane layout Each device holds 2 of the 16 KV heads, each 64 values wide: half of a vector register’s 128 lanes. A token-major cache packs a head’s K and V side by side to fill the lanes. That works in bf16, but fp8 [22] packs four values per 32-bit word down the sublanes, so a K-and-V pair is padded to four slots and switching to fp8 alone saves nothing. KV bytes per token, per layer, per device bf16 fp8 Token-major, K and V packed per head 512 B 512 B Sequence-on-lane 512 B 256 B The sequence-on-lane layout puts a page’s tokens along the 128 lanes and the head dimension down the sublanes, so each word holds four fp8 values of one token and nothing is padded. It halves both the KV memory and the KV bytes each step reads. Google engineers added this layout to SGLang-TorchTPU’s ragged paged attention kernel ( #344 ), which serves prefill here, and the TorchTPU post describes it for Qwen 3.5. We rewrote the megakernel’s attention reads and its KV writes for it. The draft model’s KV in the sliding-window pool The draft model only attends to the last 2,048 tokens, but the server allocated its KV for the full context, almost a third of all KV memory per cached token. Serving it from the sliding-window pool lets the same HBM hold 38% more tokens. L2 HiCache on TPU We enabled SGLang’s hierarchical cache (HiCache) [23] on TPU, with host DRAM as an L2 behind every HBM pool: full-attention, sliding-window and draft. When HBM evicts a session’s prefix during a tool pause, its pages stay in host memory and are copied back on the next turn instead of being recomputed, as in multi-turn KV caching systems such as CachedAttention [24]. Making it work alongside speculative decoding and the overlap scheduler needed a new synchronization fence. On agent traffic, the L2 cache raised throughput by up to 77%. Session-aware eviction Agent traffic brought a second problem: the cache did not know which old prefixes would be needed again. An agent session is a tree of conversations: a main agent can sit idle for a quarter of an hour while its sub-agents run, then come back with its whole context. To plain LRU eviction, that idle conversation looks like the coldest data in the cache, so it goes first, and its next turn recomputes a long prefix. A hybrid model makes the loss worse: reusing a prefix needs both its full-attention KV and the sliding-window KV of its last 2,048 tokens, so losing only the small window makes the large full-attention KV useless. On this trace, prefill computed about 1.2× the tokens that the best possible cache would. Figure 12. Schematic. A main agent idles while its sub-agents run. Plain LRU evicts its KV first; session-aware eviction keeps it in host memory until everything else has gone. SGLang’s session-aware radix cache [5] ( sgl-project/sglang#29173 ) gives the cache that knowledge. Requests from the same conversation share a session id, and KV that a live session will reuse is evicted only after everything else. We adapted it to agent traffic: the session id comes from the per-conversation id the client already sends, and the protection applies only in host memory, so HBM stays plain LRU for the requests that are running while host memory holds the idle conversations. In the highest-throughput run of Figure 1, prefill now computes within 1–5% of what the best possible cache would. 8. Prefill: a fused MoE kernel and fair batching Before a request can start decoding, the server runs its new prompt tokens through the model in chunks of 4,096 tokens [25, 26]: the prefill. A chunk has enough rows to keep the matrix unit busy, so unlike decode, prefill time goes to compute and to moving results between devices. On agent traffic a single turn can bring hundreds of thousands of new tokens, so prefill speed decides how long requests wait before their first token. In the MoE layers of prefill, every device computes a partial result for every (token, expert) pair, and each token’s owner must add up 8 of them. Moving those partials, one small write at a time, cost more than the matrix math. The fused MoE kernel and the pair exchange Experts are sharded with tensor parallelism: each device holds 1/8 of every expert. Each device therefore runs every (token, expert) row of a prefill chunk against its slice, producing a full-width partial per row; Muse Spark normalizes each expert’s output before the weighted sum, so a row’s 8 partials must all be added up before its owner can apply the norm and combine experts. The kernel streams one expert’s weights while the next prefetches, runs gate/up, SwiGLU [27] and down, and writes each finished row straight into its owner’s HBM, overlapping later tiles. Figure 13. The two devices on a chip share a die-to-die link, which Google documents as six times faster than a 1D ICI link to another chip. Each row’s write took about 50 ns of scalar work on the same unit that issues the matmuls, so writes serialized with compute. The pair exchange uses the chip’s topology instead. Each device sends its whole tile to its sibling on the same chip over the fast on-chip link, and the pair’s sum then goes to each remote owner once, as one DMA per contiguous run of rows. Cross-chip bytes halve, each owner adds 5 blocks instead of 8, and the MoE kernel went from 3,247 to 2,368 µs per layer. Smaller changes trimmed the rest o

Each device is a single-threaded processor: one program runs at a time, so speed comes from keeping the matrix units fed and overlapping memory transfers with compute inside that program. These are the units that matter in this post, as described in Google Cloud’s TPU7x documentation and JAX’s Pallas TPU guide : Scalar unit. One per device, with its own small scalar memory (SMEM). It runs the control flow: loops, branches and address math. MXU, the matrix unit. Two per device. They do the matmuls; the chip’s peak is 2,307 TFLOPs in bf16 and 4,614 in fp8. At small batch they mostly wait for weights to arrive from HBM. Vector unit (VPU). Elementwise work such as norms, softmax exponentials and format conversions. On recent TPUs it computes on 2D vector registers of 8 × 128 32-bit values, 8 sublanes by 128 lanes, so a data layout that leaves lanes empty wastes both vector work and memory (section 7). A cross-lane unit (XLU) next to it does transposes and permutes. VMEM. On-chip SRAM next to the MXUs and the vector unit, with much higher bandwidth than HBM. Kernels stage their tiles here, so its size bounds how much a kernel can keep in flight. DMA engines. They move data between HBM, VMEM and other devices in the background: a kernel starts a copy and waits for it later, while it computes. The megakernel’s pipelining (section 2) is built on them. HBM. 192 GiB per chip at 7.37 TB/s, 96 GiB of it on each device. Die-to-die link. It joins the two devices of a chip; Google documents it as six times faster than a 1D ICI link. Section 8’s pair exchange leans on it. ICI. Six links per chip at 200 GB/s each, counting both directions, for 1,200 GB/s per chip. The four chips of a host talk to each other over it; slices of 64 chips or more form 3D tori. Host. Each chip connects to the host’s CPUs over PCIe Gen5 ×16. A 4-chip host has 960 GB of DRAM, which L2 HiCache uses as a second cache tier (section 7). SparseCores. Four per chip. This work does not use them. The TorchTPU post has a longer primer. The software The server is SGLang-TorchTPU : SGLang’s [5] scheduler, KV cache and model code in PyTorch, with Pallas kernels on the hot paths. We decode with speculative decoding [6, 7]: a small draft model guesses the next few tokens, and the full model checks them all in one forward pass, the verify step . Each (request, position) pair in a verify step is a row , so two requests verifying 8 tokens each make a 16-row step. 1. A megakernel At small batch, generating a token does little math per weight, so the step is as fast as HBM can stream the weights, as long as nothing interrupts the stream. A decode or verify step should therefore be one uninterrupted stream of weights from HBM into the MXU. Our previous path (“native” below) ran each layer as several kernels plus collectives, and every boundary stopped the stream. The megakernel runs all 62 layers of a step as one Pallas program per device, so the next weights are always in flight. Whole-step megakernels have been built for GPUs [8, 9] and, on TPU v7, for Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 [10]. Ours runs inside SGLang’s serving path, on its paged KV cache, for the decode and DFlash2 verify steps of many requests at once. The native path was already built from fused Pallas blocks, yet its verify step took 2.9× the time needed to stream its weights. Profiling our first one-kernel prototype showed why: at batch 1 the matmuls and attention cost almost nothing, while collectives cost about 45 µs per layer. Nothing overlaps across a program boundary, so the step was bound by overhead, not by bandwidth. Figure 3. One step. Inside the megakernel every layer runs the same flow (white); the shaded boxes are data movement the kernel issues itself. For each step, every device runs one pallas_call that covers all 62 layers and the final norm. SGLang still runs the embedding, the draft model, a small KV-write kernel, the LM head and sampling around it. Figure 4. Time per verify step, both paths with DFlash2 speculative decoding (GSM8K, measured on an earlier Muse Spark checkpoint). The floor is the time to stream that step’s distinct experts and dense weights from HBM. Per output token, the megakernel is 1.94× faster than the native path for a single request (1.95 ms against 3.78 ms) and 1.85× for two concurrent requests. The next sections show what made one program this fast. 2. Pipelining everything inside the megakernel A step is mostly data movement: weights, KV cache and partial sums between devices. Once the whole step is one program, the kernel can schedule every transfer so that it lands just before the compute that needs it [11], including across layer boundaries [10]. Figure 5 sketches one layer. Figure 5. One layer of a step, schematic. Each DMA stream runs ahead of, or alongside, the compute that consumes it. Weights arrive before they are needed A ring for dense weights. Attention, o-proj and router weights stream through a ring of tiles that prefetches across layer boundaries. About ten tiles in flight sustain 3.34 TB/s per device, while a single DMA stream reaches only 1.13 TB/s. Experts as soon as routing finishes. The router’s choice is known only mid-layer, so the kernel requests each chosen expert’s weights the moment routing ends, with three experts in flight. The next layer during the expert loop. Refills for the next layer’s attention weights are held until the expert loop runs, so they never compete with the expert weights the current layer is waiting for. Collectives leave as soon as their data exists Tensor parallelism exchanges partial sums between the 8 devices several times per layer. Instead of a separate collective after each matmul, the kernel writes partial results straight into the owning device’s memory with remote DMAs issued from inside the kernel; a small round costs about 3 µs. Streamed o-proj. Each o-proj output tile leaves for its owner as soon as it is computed, while the next tile is still being multiplied. Pipelined KV writes Each step writes its new K and V rows into the cache. In our fp8 sequence-on-lane cache (section 7), a token is one lane column of a 256-token page, so writing a token means reading the whole page block into VMEM, merging the new columns, and writing the page back. This runs as a small kernel right after the megakernel, because XLA copies the aliased operands of any kernel that issues remote DMA. It used to do every page in turn: read, wait, merge, write, wait, for each request and each of 62 layers. Figure 6. Schematic. The pipelined kernel issues all of a layer’s page reads at once, merges each page as it lands, and starts its write; the next layer’s reads start immediately on a second VMEM bank. The new kernel loads all layers’ new rows once, then keeps two VMEM banks: layer l reads into one while layer l−1’s writes drain from the other, and a bank is reused only after the writes of two layers earlier have landed. The write cost per step fell from 810 to 155 µs at 16 rows and from 2,286 to 336 µs at 64 rows, with bit-identical results. 3. Collective folding Because each layer is split across 8 devices, a device often has to collect the others’ results before it can continue. After the MoE and after attention, each device holds one slice of the layer’s output along the hidden dimension, and must all-gather the other seven slices before the next matvec can run. Collective folding lets that matvec start on the slices as they arrive instead of waiting for the whole gather, as decomposed collective matmuls do [12], here across the RMS norm that sits between the two. Figure 7. Schematic. The folded matvec multiplies each gathered slice as soon as it lands, starting with the device’s own, and applies the per-row normalization at the end. What makes this possible is where Muse Spark normalizes. The next layer’s attention input is an RMS norm [13] of the residual stream α·x + β·s·f, where x is the residual this device already holds, f is the gathered MoE output and s is f’s own norm factor. The two norm factors, s and the final r, are each one scalar per row. Scalars per row commute with the matmul, so the projection splits into a part the device can compute right away and a part that adds up slice by slice: Here g is the norm’s gain vector, f_d is the slice from device d, and W_d is the matching block of weight rows. The kernel stacks the local part and the arriving slice into one product per block, consumes the slices in a fixed peer order, and reorders the weight ring so that W’s blocks stream in the same order. Once the last slice is in, it computes s and r and scales the result. The kernel folds two all-gathers per layer this way: the MoE output into the next layer’s qkv projection, and the attention output into the pooler and router. The residual stream itself is unchanged; only the point where the matmul input is rounded to bf16 moves, so results are not bit-identical, and our accuracy checks cover it. 4. Enabling better pipelining in attention At long context, attention is the largest part of a step. The kernel walks the KV cache chunk by chunk, and the key bottleneck was the running max of online softmax [14]: it chained every chunk to the one before, so chunks could not be pipelined. The running max chains every chunk Online softmax, as used by FlashAttention [15], keeps the maximum score seen so far. Each new chunk computes its scores, updates that maximum, exponentiates against it, and rescales everything accumulated so far whenever the maximum grows. So each chunk is a serial chain (wait for its DMA, QK, max, exp, sum, P·V, rescale) that cannot start its exponentials until the previous chunk’s maximum is known. In a microbenchmark this chain costs about 0.17 µs per chunk, whether the chunk is fp8 or bf16. Muse Spark makes the max unnecessary Muse Spark normalizes q and k (QK-norm [16, 17]) with an RMS norm that has no learned weight, and gives q a fixed gain. No attention score can exceed 43.8 in magnitude, far from where exp overflows in f32. The running max exists only to prevent that overflow, so the kernel drops it, along with the rescale. It checks the bound from the model’s constants when it is built. FlashDecoding++ [18] breaks the same chain on GPUs with a unified max value and a recomputation path for the rare overflow; here the bound is exact, so the kernel needs no fallback. Figure 8. Schematic. With a running max, each chunk’s chain waits on the previous chunk. Without it, chunks are independent and their stages overlap. Independent chunks pipeline Without the max, chunks no longer depend on each other. The kernel issues all DMA waits at the top of each loop iteration, splits the chunks across several independent softmax streams that merge at the end, as Flash-Decoding does across the KV sequence [19], and software-pipelines the loop [11]: it scores the next chunks while it multiplies the previous chunks’ probabilities by V. Three smaller changes shorten each chain further: Chunk size by layer type. Global layers read the cache in long chunks of 1,024 to 2,048 tokens, so a 100K context needs far fewer chains. Sliding-window layers use 512-token chunks, since their window spans only a few. fp8 keys straight into the MXU. Widening each fp8 chunk to bf16 on the vector unit cost more vector work than the MXU work it fed. Mixed bf16 × fp8 dots are exact, so the keys now go in as fp8. The attention scale in the queries. Muse Spark’s attention scale is 1/8, a power of two, so multiplying the queries once instead of every score is exact. Figure 9. Microbenchmark at production shapes. The memory floor is the time to read the KV bytes. In the microbenchmark, longer chunks with independent streams cut attention time 2.4×, and dropping the running max took it to 3.9×. In the server, the pipelined loop raised per-request decode speed by 18% for two requests at 500K context. 5. Keeping register pressure off the common path A processor computes on values held in its registers, a small, fixed set of storage slots next to the arithmetic units. When code needs more live values than the registers hold, the compiler spills some of them to memory and loads them back later [20], and those extra stores and loads cost time on every pass through the code. In a loop with several branches, the compiler has to fit the live values of all branches into the same registers, so one heavy branch can make every pass through the loop spill, even when that branch never runs. The megakernel’s expert loop had exactly this problem. A step loops over the experts its rows were routed to. For each one, the kernel waits for the expert’s weights and runs a path chosen by how many rows the expert serves: a few-row path, with small variants for one to eight rows, and a dequantize-then-multiply path for busier experts. As the batch grows, a step visits more experts, but most of them still serve only one or two rows, so the light path is the one that matters. One heavy branch slows the light path The 8-row variant keeps large f32 accumulators that do not fit in the vector registers even on their own. Because it shared one loop body with the one- and two-row variants, the common path spilled registers to memory and loaded them back on every expert: about 0.37 µs per expert, against roughly 1.2 µs to stream that expert’s weights. That overhead had nothing to do with the work the light path itself did. Two loops instead of one The fix keeps the heavy code out of the light path’s loop. The kernel sorts a step’s experts by row count and runs two loops: one for experts with at most four rows, and one for the rest. Each loop body now holds only its own variants, so the few-row loop carries 61–64% fewer spill instructions. Every expert still takes the same path as before, so the output is bit-identical. Figure 10. Schematic. In one shared loop body, every few-row expert is followed by a spill and refill, and the loop falls behind its weight stream. In their own loop, few-row experts keep pace with the weights. In a kernel test with random routing, decode steps with many requests got 13–19% faster, and the expert loop now keeps pace with its weight stream. 6. Speculative decoding with DFlash2 Without speculation, every output token costs one full pass over the active weights. DFlash [21] drafts a whole block of tokens in one forward pass of a small model; we use Muse Spark’s DFlash2 draft model. Figure 11. One speculative step. The draft model reads hidden states captured from the full model. The token strip is an illustration. The draft attends bidirectionally within its block and proposes all of the block’s tokens at once. The full model checks the whole block in one megakernel step and keeps the longest prefix of drafts that matches its own choices, plus one token of its own. This suits TPU well: MXU time grows with the number of row and output tiles, not with multiply-adds, and a block’s few rows fit in the same row tile as one token, so verifying a block costs little more than verifying one token. Measured on GSM8K with real acceptance, DFlash2 cut the megakernel’s time per output token for a single request from 3.93 to 1.95 ms, 2.0×. 7. More context per device: KV layout and L2 HiCache On agent traffic, KV capacity is throughput: every prefix that falls out of the cache comes back as a 100K-token re-prefill. After the weights, each device has only about 20 GiB left for KV, split between a full-attention pool for the 16 global layers and a sliding-window pool for the other 46. fp8 KV in a sequence-on-lane layout Each device holds 2 of the 16 KV heads, each 64 values wide: half of a vector register’s 128 lanes. A token-major cache packs a head’s K and V side by side to fill the lanes. That works in bf16, but fp8 [22] packs four values per 32-bit word down the sublanes, so a K-and-V pair is padded to four slots and switching to fp8 alone saves nothing. KV bytes per token, per layer, per device bf16 fp8 Token-major, K and V packed per head 512 B 512 B Sequence-on-lane 512 B 256 B The sequence-on-lane layout puts a page’s tokens along the 128 lanes and the head dimension down the sublanes, so each word holds four fp8 values of one token and nothing is padded. It halves both the KV memory and the KV bytes each step reads. Google engineers added this layout to SGLang-TorchTPU’s ragged paged attention kernel ( #344 ), which serves prefill here, and the TorchTPU post describes it for Qwen 3.5. We rewrote the megakernel’s attention reads and its KV writes for it. The draft model’s KV in the sliding-window pool The draft model only attends to the last 2,048 tokens, but the server allocated its KV for the full context, almost a third of all KV memory per cached token. Serving it from the sliding-window pool lets the same HBM hold 38% more tokens. L2 HiCache on TPU We enabled SGLang’s hierarchical cache (HiCache) [23] on TPU, with host DRAM as an L2 behind every HBM pool: full-attention, sliding-window and draft. When HBM evicts a session’s prefix during a tool pause, its pages stay in host memory and are copied back on the next turn instead of being recomputed, as in multi-turn KV caching systems such as CachedAttention [24]. Making it work alongside speculative decoding and the overlap scheduler needed a new synchronization fence. On agent traffic, the L2 cache raised throughput by up to 77%. Session-aware eviction Agent traffic brought a second problem: the cache did not know which old prefixes would be needed again. An agent session is a tree of conversations: a main agent can sit idle for a quarter of an hour while its sub-agents run, then come back with its whole context. To plain LRU eviction, that idle conversation looks like the coldest data in the cache, so it goes first, and its next turn recomputes a long prefix. A hybrid model makes the loss worse: reusing a prefix needs both its full-attention KV and the sliding-window KV of its last 2,048 tokens, so losing only the small window makes the large full-attention KV useless. On this trace, prefill computed about 1.2× the tokens that the best possible cache would. Figure 12. Schematic. A main agent idles while its sub-agents run. Plain LRU evicts its KV first; session-aware eviction keeps it in host memory until everything else has gone. SGLang’s session-aware radix cache [5] ( sgl-project/sglang#29173 ) gives the cache that knowledge. Requests from the same conversation share a session id, and KV that a live session will reuse is evicted only after everything else. We adapted it to agent traffic: the session id comes from the per-conversation id the client already sends, and the protection applies only in host memory, so HBM stays plain LRU for the requests that are running while host memory holds the idle conversations. In the highest-throughput run of Figure 1, prefill now computes within 1–5% of what the best possible cache would. 8. Prefill: a fused MoE kernel and fair batching Before a request can start decoding, the server runs its new prompt tokens through the model in chunks of 4,096 tokens [25, 26]: the prefill. A chunk has enough rows to keep the matrix unit busy, so unlike decode, prefill time goes to compute and to moving results between devices. On agent traffic a single turn can bring hundreds of thousands of new tokens, so prefill speed decides how long requests wait before their first token. In the MoE layers of prefill, every device computes a partial result for every (token, expert) pair, and each token’s owner must add up 8 of them. Moving those partials, one small write at a time, cost more than the matrix math. The fused MoE kernel and the pair exchange Experts are sharded with tensor parallelism: each device holds 1/8 of every expert. Each device therefore runs every (token, expert) row of a prefill chunk against its slice, producing a full-width partial per row; Muse Spark normalizes each expert’s output before the weighted sum, so a row’s 8 partials must all be added up before its owner can apply the norm and combine experts. The kernel streams one expert’s weights while the next prefetches, runs gate/up, SwiGLU [27] and down, and writes each finished row straight into its owner’s HBM, overlapping later tiles. Figure 13. The two devices on a chip share a die-to-die link, which Google documents as six times faster than a 1D ICI link to another chip. Each row’s write took about 50 ns of scalar work on the same unit that issues the matmuls, so writes serialized with compute. The pair exchange uses the chip’s topology instead. Each device sends its whole tile to its sibling on the same chip over the fast on-chip link, and the pair’s sum then goes to each remote owner once, as one DMA per contiguous run of rows. Cross-chip bytes halve, each owner adds 5 blocks instead of 8, and the MoE kernel went from 3,247 to 2,368 µs per layer. Smaller changes trimmed the rest o

items.title: Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar
items.summary:
Zero-knowledge proofs can verify computing results without rerunning workloads or exposing sensitive data. Magnetar helps bring them into the mainstream with support for standard programming languages, major speed gains, and quantum-resistant security.

The post Proof-based general-purpose computing with Magnetar appeared first on Microsoft Research.

items.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. Microsoft Research StorY OptiMind: When the system meets the floor A three‑month pilot in a Midwestern bottling plant shows what happens when AI moves beyond chat and into decision-making, where constraints shift, stakes are real, and answers must hold. Learn more Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project. Opens in a new tab Related publications An O(1) Bound for the KLS Constant Meet the authors Xinzhi Zhang Senior Researcher Learn more Research Areas Artificial intelligence Mathematics

They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. Microsoft Research StorY OptiMind: When the system meets the floor A three‑month pilot in a Midwestern bottling plant shows what happens when AI moves beyond chat and into decision-making, where constraints shift, stakes are real, and answers must hold. Learn more Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project.
