items.raw_text: Back to Articles Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3 Team Article Published October 27, 2026 Upvote 104 +98 Leonie Monigatti iamleonie Follow LiquidAI Jimmy T.H. Smith jimmysmith1919 Follow LiquidAI Anthony Maltsev amaltsev Follow LiquidAI Maxime Labonne mlabonne Follow LiquidAI Brandon Brandon3967 Follow LiquidAI Samuel Stevens samuelstevens Follow LiquidAI Ryan Shubert shubeydoo Follow LiquidAI Tianshu Yu tianshu-yu Follow LiquidAI Sina s-jse Follow LiquidAI Tim Seyde tseyde Follow LiquidAI Rouzbeh Amin Tafreshi rouzbehat78 Follow LiquidAI Alexander Amini alexanderamini Follow LiquidAI Saniya Karwa saniyakarwa Follow LiquidAI Marc Harkonen haerski Follow LiquidAI Anna Piunova orech Follow LiquidAI Calder Katyal CalderKat Follow LiquidAI Ishwarya Ananthabhotla ianant93 Follow LiquidAI Farris Atif farris-liquid Follow LiquidAI Tarek Dakhran tdakhran Follow LiquidAI Paul Pak paulpak58 Follow LiquidAI xx tugot17 Follow LiquidAI Mihir Bafna mihirbafna Follow LiquidAI Kyle Bruce Wheeler m3m0ryh0l3 Follow LiquidAI Aditya Tadimeti adityatadimeti Follow LiquidAI Alfred Eng alfredeng Follow LiquidAI Karthik Macherla karthikrmacherla Follow LiquidAI Khoi Nguyen KTLK Follow LiquidAI Aldo Gael Carranza agcarranza Follow LiquidAI Aurelien Lac Aurelien-Lac Follow LiquidAI Tyler Murray undfined Follow LiquidAI Raahul Vignesh Raahul26 Follow LiquidAI Song Duong sduong Follow LiquidAI Ramin Hasani raminmh Follow LiquidAI Mathias Lechner mlech26l Follow LiquidAI Akhilesh Deepak Gotmare akhileshdeepakgotmare Follow LiquidAI Fernando Fernandes Neto fernandofernandes Follow LiquidAI Jiahui Wang WWWjiahui Follow LiquidAI Yuri Khrustalev ykhrustalev Follow LiquidAI Alay Shah alay2shah Follow LiquidAI Simon Lee yungisimon Follow LiquidAI Mayank Agarwal mayankagarwal Follow LiquidAI Zetian Li zetianli Follow LiquidAI changyi yang changyiyang Follow LiquidAI Sinoué GAD GAD-cell Follow LiquidAI nathan ranchin nathanrchn Follow LiquidAI Sergei Tilga tilgasergey Follow LiquidAI LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs. LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family: More capability per parameter: a new tri-hybrid architecture and training recipe allow LFM3-1.7B to outperform LFM2.5-2.6B while using 35% fewer parameters. Every modality on one backbone: six 2B-class models (text, vision, audio, omni, and decision) trained from LFM3-1.7B-Base, including our first omni model and video input for our vision model. Built for the edge: the text model fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit precision, new in-house vision and audio encoders speed up processing, and the text model’s 256K context window lets agents run on-device. Made to be specialized: every model fine-tunes on a single GPU, so you can adapt it to your data, terminology, and deployment environment. How we built a more expressive backbone LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU. LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes: Tri-hybrid layer mix: 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention (SWA) layers with a 256-token window, and 6 global attention layers. The convolutions use a kernel size of 7, up from 3 in LFM2. Head-wise gated attention: a sigmoid gate scales each head's output, so a head can switch off when it has nothing to add. This can help suppress activation outliers that hurt quantization. Partial RoPE: global attention layers rotate only the highest-frequency half of each head, so the other half matches on content regardless of distance. SWA layers keep full RoPE. Sandwich norm: each block normalizes both its input and its output to keep activations well-scaled. The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B . The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens. One backbone for six models Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device. Model Input Output Built on LFM3-1.7B Text Text LFM3-1.7B-Base LFM3-VL-2B Text, images, video Text LFM3 backbone + vision encoder LFM3-Audio-2B Text, audio Text, speech LFM3 backbone + audio encoder, audio decoder, and LiquidCodec LFM3-Omni-2B Text, images, video, audio Text, speech LFM3 backbone + vision and audio encoders and audio decoder d1-2B Text, images, video Calibrated answers LFM3-VL-2B d1-omni-2B Text, images, video, audio Calibrated answers LFM3-Omni-2B The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders: Vision encoder: it combines convolution and attention and uses 3x less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models. Our 164M-parameter encoder matches Qwen3.5-2B's vision encoder in accuracy while requiring 2.2x fewer FLOPs (both measured with the same LFM2.5-230M language backbone). For video, it embeds each pair of sampled frames into one temporal slice, halving the temporal sequence length. Audio encoder and LiquidCodec: the audio encoder mixes sliding-window attention and short convolutions and is fully causal, so the model can prefill while you speak, with time to first token as low as 50 ms. LiquidCodec, our new audio tokenizer, turns generated tokens into speech at about 87x real time on a single CPU thread on Apple M4 Max and supports streaming decoding. How to use the LFM3 models Each model runs in transformers . The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports. LFM3-1.7B Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card . To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers : pip install -U transformers Then load and run the model: from transformers import pipeline generator = pipeline( "text-generation" , model= "LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B" , trust_remote_code= True , ) messages = [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is C. elegans?" }] output = generator( messages, do_sample= True , temperature= 0.1 , top_k= 50 , repetition_penalty= 1.1 , max_new_tokens= 2048 , ) print (output[ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][- 1 ][ "content" ]) For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide . LFM3-VL-2B Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card . To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.21.0" torch torchvision pillow Then load and run the model: import torch from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B" model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map= "auto" , trust_remote_code= True ) processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "url" : "https://placecats.com/300/200" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Describe this image." }, ], } ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, do_sample= True , temperature= 0.1 , top_k= 50 , repetition_penalty= 1.1 , max_new_tokens= 16384 , # generate() needs an explicit limit; reasoning can be long ) generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] :] print (processor.batch_decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens= True )[ 0 ]) See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp. LFM3-Audio-2B Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card . To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch accelerate librosa soundfile Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub: import torch import soundfile as sf from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B" device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32 model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code= True ). eval () processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device). eval () Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech: conversation = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "Respond with interleaved text and audio." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : [{ "type" : "audio" , "audio" : "question.wav" }]}, { "role" : "assistant" , "content" : "<|mixed_start|>" }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, continue_final_message= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(device) with torch.no_grad(): outputs = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 1024 , audio_temperature= 1.0 , audio_top_k= 128 , audio_repetition_penalty= 1.1 , audio_repetition_window= 4096 , return_dict_in_generate= True , ) text = processor.decode( outputs.sequences[ 0 , inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:], skip_special_tokens= True , ) waveform = codec.decode( outputs.audio_codes[: 1 , :, :outputs.audio_lengths[ 0 ]] ).audio_values[ 0 ] # 24 kHz print (text) sf.write( "reply.wav" , waveform. float ().cpu().numpy(), 24_000 ) See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling. LFM3-Omni-2B Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card . To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch torchvision torchcodec accelerate pillow librosa soundfile import torch import soundfile as sf from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Omni-2B" device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32 model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code= True ). eval () processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code= True ) codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device). eval () Then ask a question about a photo by voice: conversation = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "Answer questions about the provided image. Base every answer only on what can be seen. Respond with text." , }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : "photo.jpg" }, { "type" : "audio" , "audio" : "question.wav" }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(device) with torch.no_grad(): outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 1024 , generation_mode= "text" ) print (processor.decode( outputs.sequences[ 0 , inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:outputs.sequence_lengths[ 0 ]], skip_special_tokens= True , )) See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling. d1-2B and d1-omni-2B Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B . Between the two d1 models: d1-2B : choose it for text, pictures, and video. It replaces d1-3B with a third fewer parameters and scores higher on all four of our decision suites, for example, 75.5 against 64.0 on ImajevBench. d1-omni-2B : choose it when your inputs include audio. If you ask by voice instead of in writing, it keeps nearly all of its accuracy. To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies: pip install "transformers>=5.19" torch torchvision pillow Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass: import torch from transformers import AutoModel device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu" dtype = torch.float32 if device == "cpu" else torch.bfloat16 model = AutoModel.from_pretrained( "LiquidAI/d1-2B" , trust_remote_code= True , dtype=dtype).to(device) # Several named questions over one state, answered in one pass questions = { "refund" : { "type" : "noul" , "instructions" : "Is the customer asking for a refund?" }, # yes/no: P(yes) "team" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Charges, refunds, invoices" , "shipping" : "Delivery and parcels" , "technical" : "App or site faults" }}, "topics" : { "type" : "choice" , "multiple" : True , "instructions" : "Which topics does the message raise?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and charges" , "delivery" : "Shipping and parcels" , "login" : "Signing in to the account" }}, "urgency" : { "type" : "score" , "instructions" : "How urgent is this ticket?" , "criteria" : [ "low" , "medium" , "high" ]}, } out = model.system_one( "I was charged twice and my parcel never arrived. Please refund one charge." , questions) a = out[ "answers" ] urgency = a[ "urgency" ][ "legend" ][ str ( int (a[ "urgency" ][ "score" ]))] print ( round (a[ "refund" ][ "noul" ], 2 ), a[ "team" ][ "choice" ], a[ "topics" ][ "choices" ], urgency) # 1.0 billing ['billing', 'delivery'] medium For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions. Fine-tune LFM3 for your task LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud. Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation. Model Method Task Notebook LFM3-1.7B SFT Extract structured JSON from messy documents Open in Colab LFM3-1.7B DPO Answer from retrieved documents, or decline Open in Colab LFM3-1.7B GRPO Call the right tools in a 108-tool phone app Open in Colab LFM3-1.7B CPT Learn a new language (Turkish) from raw text Open in Colab LFM3-VL-2B SFT Read receipt photos into JSON Open in Colab LFM3-VL-2B GRPO Transcribe images of equations to LaTeX Open in Colab LFM3-Audio-2B SFT Map spoken smart-home commands to function calls Open in Colab LFM3-Audio-2B SFT Teach the model a new voice Open in Colab LFM3-Omni-2B SFT Map spoken smart-home commands to function calls Open in Colab LFM3-Omni-2B SFT Answer spoken questions about medical images Open in Colab Example: teaching LFM3 to act We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation . The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware. Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video . Get Started with LFM3 All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today: Download: the LFM3 collection on Hugging Face, including LFM3-1.7B-Base for your own post-training. Fine-tune: adapt LFM3 to your task with our fine-tuning notebooks . Use in your harness: follow our guide on how to run a local agent, like OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and Pi. We can't wait to see what you build. Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood. Updated Granite Speech ASR model — multilingual speech-to-text across 10 languages with native punctuation and capitalization, so transcripts are ready for downstream models without a formatting pass. Updated Decision adapter in granitelib-core — featuring improved overall performance on the Jev Decision Index test set. While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy. This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon. Until then, test out our latest models , and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo. items.summary: Back to Articles Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language Enterprise Article Published November 3, 2026 Upvote 20 +14 Praveen Venkateswaran praveenv Follow ibm-research Anupama Murthi anupamamurthi Follow ibm-research Hamid Adebayo harmedox Follow ibm-research Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all. Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all. Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other. Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language , and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it. Why decks are hard for small models A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at. It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from. It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent. There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them. Build it like a human: a designer and a coder Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter: The designer reads the plan and writes a structured JSON brief: the palette, the type system, and for each slide its layout, its exact content and a short design rationale. The coder takes one slide's spec from the brief and writes the pptxgenjs JavaScript that draws it, preceded by its reasoning. Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster. We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×. Synthesizing decks and their reasoning There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides. Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example: "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance." The coder reasons about geometry: "The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart." The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example. The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest. What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions. Steering a deck in plain English Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives , short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]] : ## Rollout plan - March: pilot with two teams - May: security review complete - July: rollout to all of engineering - September: company-wide launch - November: first adoption review [[make this a timeline]] The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead. The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase. Category Example directive Layout [[make this a timeline]] Tone [[be candid, no spin]] Audience [[this is for the board]] Order [[lead with the ask]] Leaving out [[no pricing]] Emphasis [[highlight the headline number]] Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive. Building a check-and-repair harness Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first. Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned. First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code. The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse. Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right). To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average. Evaluation We evaluate on PresentBench , which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper. Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean. Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model. PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close. What's next The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training. We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling ) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining. What we learned Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts: Put the reasoning in the data. Training on why a choice was made, including what was rejected, teaches more than the choice alone. Fix the examples before adding a rule. When the teacher got something wrong, our first instinct was to add a rule to its prompt, and that rarely helped. The teacher copied its reference decks far more than it followed instructions, so fixing the reference was what actually changed its output. Make repairs safe by default. A fix that's kept only when it measurably helps can run on every output. Build the checker first. It's what makes the data trustworthy and the outputs safe to ship. items.content: Back to Articles Transformers Model Integration Contracts Published November 3, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 17 +11 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months. When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it. Why bugs reach main Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels. The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main. Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study , the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB. This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU. Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine. Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main. Introducing Model Integration Contracts transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts: a fixture : the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned a usage path : a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the model, such as generating text or running a training step baselines : the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a human The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines. A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic . For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt: inputs = tokenizer( "The capital of France is" , return_tensors= "pt" ) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 4 , do_sample= False ) new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:] print (tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens= True )) It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md . A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later. On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes. The UMT5 regression We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28 . Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20. One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint. We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup. The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details. How models are shrunk The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear. The recipe now has four steps: Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds, including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers. Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible. We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the ModelTester in test_modeling_<model>.py already picks a small config by hand, so we take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name. Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte. Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test. Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds. Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR. We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail. The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style. Building MICs with agents Our CLI, tmic , creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review. To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model : pip install "transformers-mic[runtime]" "hf-doc-builder @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/doc-builder.git" hf auth login tmic run org/model --local-only --fixtures-only --no-history --bill-to '' It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account ( --bill-to '' ). The CLI docs cover the individual steps. We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space . Random vs Overfit With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path. So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study , the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24. That gives us two ways to build the weights: Start with random weights and a fixed seed. Overfit on a few examples, like "The capital of France is" => "Paris". The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed. So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both. Open questions As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet: How many real bugs does it catch on PRs, not just in replays? How often does it send us chasing false alarms? How much work do baseline reviews take? We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss. Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for. Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs. Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space , try the tmic workflow , and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract. items.raw_text: Back to Articles Transformers Model Integration Contracts Published November 3, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 17 +11 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months. When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it. Why bugs reach main Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels. The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main. Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study , the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB. This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU. Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine. Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main. Introducing Model Integration Contracts transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts: a fixture : the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned a usage path : a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the model, such as generating text or running a training step baselines : the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a human The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines. A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic . For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt: inputs = tokenizer( "The capital of France is" , return_tensors= "pt" ) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 4 , do_sample= False ) new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:] print (tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens= True )) It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md . A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later. On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes. The UMT5 regression We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28 . Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20. One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint. We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup. The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details. How models are shrunk The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear. The recipe now has four steps: Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds, including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers. Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible. We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the ModelTester in test_modeling_<model>.py already picks a small config by hand, so we take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name. Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte. Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test. Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds. Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR. We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail. The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style. Building MICs with agents Our CLI, tmic , creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review. To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model : pip install "transformers-mic[runtime]" "hf-doc-builder @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/doc-builder.git" hf auth login tmic run org/model --local-only --fixtures-only --no-history --bill-to '' It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account ( --bill-to '' ). The CLI docs cover the individual steps. We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space . Random vs Overfit With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path. So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study , the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24. That gives us two ways to build the weights: Start with random weights and a fixed seed. Overfit on a few examples, like "The capital of France is" => "Paris". The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed. So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both. Open questions As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet: How many real bugs does it catch on PRs, not just in replays? How often does it send us chasing false alarms? How much work do baseline reviews take? We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss. Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for. Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs. Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space , try the tmic workflow , and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract. items.content: Back to Articles A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks. Published November 5, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 38 +32 Olesia Krizhevich olesiagradium Follow gradium Laurent Mazare lmz Follow gradium Eric Bezzam bezzam Follow Eustache Le Bihan eustlb Follow Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you. We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard. Why a voice should live on your device Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate. Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both. We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design. Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages. What we released Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio . Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes. It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now . Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license. Demos and first projects The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page. The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one. Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it. Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face. How Phonon did on the Hugging Face Open TTS Leaderboard The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub , the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility ( word error rate of the outputs ), speed ( inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio ), and naturalness ( UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean ). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most. On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish , and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size. Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio. Inference We built a new inference framework, ptts , specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®). Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile , e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself. It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs. Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer , held by the processor next to the text tokenizer: from transformers import AutoProcessor, GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration model_id = "gradium/phonon-31m-en" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map= "auto" ) model = GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map= "auto" ) print ( f" {model.num_parameters():,} " ) # 30,788,354 print ( f" {processor.audio_tokenizer.num_parameters():,} " ) # 10,305,313 A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices . from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download from safetensors.torch import load_file path = hf_hub_download( "gradium/phonon-voices" , "voices/LMDIYE0Oa377Qh6Z.safetensors" ) voice = load_file(path)[ "speaker_wavs" ][ 0 ].T # (num_frames, 512) The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs: conversation = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [{ "type" : "audio" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Hello from Phonon." }]} ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, tokenize= True , return_dict= True , add_generation_prompt= True , processor_kwargs={ "audio_prompt_latents" : [voice]}, ).to(model.device) # prompt: <|audio_prompt|> × num_frames, "Hello from Phonon.", <|audio_bos|> generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio: outputs = model.generate(**inputs) # audio_latents: (batch_size, num_frames, 32) audio = processor.decode(outputs.audio_latents, outputs.audio_latents_mask) processor.save_audio(audio, "phonon.wav" ) See the docs 🤗 for more! What's next Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio . Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device. We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need. Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks. Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build. Models mentioned in this article 3 Datasets mentioned in this article 1 Spaces mentioned in this article 3 More Articles from our Blog audio speech leaderboard Egyptian and Nigerian English join the Open ASR Leaderboard 10 November 6, 2026 audio speech leaderboard Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning 81 September 30, 2026 Community frederik-nlp 1 day ago Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win. One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.
