We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text. Consider a customer support system receiving the following message: "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today." The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers. llama cli -hf ggml-org/gemma-4-e4b-it-GGUF:Q4_0 > We have the following customer support ticket, "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today." , which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. Give the answers in JSON. [Start thinking] ... [end thinking] ```json { "team_to_handle" : "Billing" , "urgency" : "High" , "request_refund" : true } But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text ? from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "department" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and refunds" , "technical" : "Bugs and technical issues" , "sales" : "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, } } ) # { # 'department': { # 'type': 'choice', # 'choice': 'billing', # 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975, # 'probabilities': { # 'billing': 0.9982666969299316, # 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616, # 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412 # } # } # } This is the key idea behind decision models . What are decision models? A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands. TypeSafe AI introduced Jev , describing it as a System One model . The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2). The community has converged to the term decision model , because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". ( A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models ) For a decision model, the fundamental interface is: State + Questions + Allowed Answers → Decisions + Probabilities Why not use LLMs for everything? We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks. However, there are a few problems with this approach. LLMs are not guaranteed to follow the requested schema: Even with explicit instructions, a model might produce invalid JSON, introduce unexpected keys, or return an answer outside the allowed choices. Constrained decoding helps, but does not eliminate the computational overhead: Libraries such as Outlines and XGrammar can enforce grammars or JSON schemas by restricting which tokens the model is allowed to generate at each step. This ensures the output follows the supported structural constraints, but introduces additional work. Why generate an entire response: LLMs are designed for open-ended generation, but when our application only needs to choose between predefined answers, autoregressive decoding can be unnecessary work. How are decision models different from classification models? Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification. Traditional classification Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments: Billing Technical support Sales A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution. The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head . If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model. Zero-shot classification Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time. For example: from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline( "zero-shot-classification" , model= "facebook/bart-large-mnli" , ) classifier( "My payment was deducted twice." , candidate_labels=[ "billing" , "technical support" , "sales" ], ) # {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.', # 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support'], # 'scores': [0.8466812372207642, 0.0962134450674057, 0.05710534751415253]} Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs. from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline( "zero-shot-classification" , model= "facebook/bart-large-mnli" , ) classifier( "My payment was deducted twice." , candidate_labels=[ "billing" , "technical support" , "sales" , "legal" ], ) # {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.', # 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support', 'legal'], # 'scores': [0.8185835480690002, 0.09302053600549698, 0.05521026626229286, 0.03318570926785469]} One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis. This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is. Where decision models differ Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul). More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions . Consider these three approaches: Property Classification Zero-shot classification Decision model Probability over choices Yes Yes Yes Labels defined at inference No Yes Yes Multiple typed questions No No Yes Ordered scoring and yes/no decisions Task-specific Possible with adaptation Native primitives The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions. The decision model interface A decision model request has the following two components: state questions State The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models. For example: { "customer_message" : "I was charged twice. Please refund me today." , "subscription" : "pro" , "previous_tickets" : 2 } Questions and their primitives Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions: Choice: Select one of several possible answers. Score: Evaluate something on an ordered scale. Noul: Answer a yes/no question probabilistically. Let's go over them one by one. Choice: A probability distribution over options Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification. Suppose we ask: Which department should handle this customer request? The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales. from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "department" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and refunds" , "technical" : "Bugs and technical issues" , "sales" : "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, } } ) # { # 'department': { # 'type': 'choice', # 'choice': 'billing', # 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975, # 'probabilities': { # 'billing': 0.9982666969299316, # 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616, # 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412 # } # } # } The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits ($z_1,\ldots,z_K$), (with K classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax: p i = exp ⁡ ( z i / T ) ∑ j = 1 K exp ⁡ ( z j ) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} p i ​ = ∑ j = 1 K ​ exp ( z j ​ ) exp ( z i ​ / T ) ​ Here, (K) is the number of choices. Consider this illustrative distribution: Choice Probability Billing 0.998 Technical support 0.001 Sales 0.001 The probabilities sum to one: ∑ i = 1 K p i = 1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i = 1 ∑ K ​ p i ​ = 1. The model chooses the option with the largest probability: y ^ = arg ⁡ max ⁡ i p i \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y ^ ​ = ar g i max ​ p i ​ In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives. Score: The expectation of an ordered distribution Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale? Consider the question: How urgent is this customer request? We define three levels: 0: Low urgency 1: Medium urgency 2: High urgency from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "urgency" : { "type" : "score" , "instructions" : "How urgent is the request?" , "criteria" : [ "low" , "medium" , "high" ] }, } } ) # { # 'urgency': { # 'type': 'score', # 'score': 1.7053890228271484, # 'legend': { # '0': 'low', # '1': 'medium', # '2': 'high' # }, # 'confidence': 0.5580834252759814, # 'probabilities': { # '0': 0.014908230863511562, # '1': 0.26479458808898926, # '2': 0.7202972173690796 # } # } # } The model again produces a probability distribution: Level Probability 0 — Low 0.10 1 — Medium 0.26 2 — High 0.72 Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index . For a random variable (X) representing the level, the expectation is: E [ X ] = ∑ i = 0 K − 1 i p i \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E [ X ] = i = 0 ∑ K − 1 ​ i p i ​ For our example: E [ X ] = 0 ( 0.10 ) + 1 ( 0.26 ) + 2 ( 0.72 ) = 1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.10)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E [ X ] = 0 ( 0.10 ) + 1 ( 0.26 ) + 2 ( 0.72 ) = 1.7 The reported score is therefore 1.7 . This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7. Noul: A Bernoulli decision The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question. For example: Is the customer requesting a refund? from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "refund" : { "type" : "noul" , "instructions" : "Is the customer requesting a refund?" } } } ) # { # 'refund': { # 'type': 'noul', # 'noul': 0.9947046637535095 # } # } Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli). Let (Y) represent a binary outcome: Y ∼ Bernoulli ⁡ ( p ) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y ∼ Bernoulli ( p ) where P ( Y = 1 ) = p , P ( Y = 0 ) = 1 − p . P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P ( Y = 1 ) = p , P ( Y = 0 ) = 1 − p . If the model returns: { "type" : "noul" , "noul" : 0.92 } it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No. The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it. Confidence: How certain is the model? So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score. The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that. For a Choice with (K) options, the confidence is: p max ⁡ − 1 K 1 − 1 K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1 − K 1 ​ p m a x ​ − K 1 ​ ​ where ($p_{\max}$) is the largest predicted probability. The intuition here is: A uniform distribution has confidence 0. ($p_{\max} = \frac{1}{K}$). This means the model estimates that all choices are equally likely. A distribution concentrated entirely on one option has confidence 1. ($p_{\max} = 1$) The larger the winning probability relative to a uniform distribution, the higher the confidence. In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.80: C = 3 ( 0.99 ) − 1 2 = 0.98 C=\frac{3(0.99)-1}{2}=0.98 C = 2 3 ( 0.99 ) − 1 ​ = 0.98 Notice that the winning probability is 0.99, but the reported confidence is 0.98. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558. Decision models in the Hugging Face ecosystem Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations. Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation . A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once: inference engines like llama.cpp can serve any decision model through the same API the Hub can package and surface them consistently and training tools can target shared primitives instead of individual architectures The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces. 1. Serving with Transformers Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline , AutoModelForDecision , and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models. from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) print (decide) # DecisionPipeline: {'model': 'JevForDecision', 'dtype': 'bfloat16', 'device': 'cuda', 'input_modalities': 'text'} One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so: from transformers import AutoModelForDecision, DecisionConfig model_id = "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" config = DecisionConfig.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForDecision.from_pretrained(model_id) Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint . We can start a local server using the serving dependencies: pip install "transformers[serving]" transformers serve Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request: curl http : //localhost:8000/v1/systemone \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' { "model" : "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" , "state" : "I was charged twice. Please refund me today." , "questions" : { "department" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and refunds" , "technical" : "Bugs and technical issues" , "sales" : "Pricing and subscriptions" } } , "urgency" : { "type" : "score" , "instructions" : "How urgent is the request?" , "criteria" : [ "low" , "medium" , "high" ] } , "refund" : { "type" : "noul" , "instructions" : "Is the customer requesting a refund?" } } } ' The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities. { "model" : "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" , "answers" :{ "department" :{ "type" : "choice" , "choice" : "billing" , "confidence" :0.9974000453948975, "probabilities" :{ "billing" :0.9982666969299316, "technical" :0.0010246571619063616, "sales" :0.0007087149424478412 } }, "urgency" :{ "type" : "score" , "score" :1.7525686174631119, "legend" :{ "0" : "low" , "1" : "medium" , "2" : "high" }, "confidence" :0.6288529792800546, "probabilities" :{ "0" :0.014000383205711842, "1" :0.2194305807352066, "2" :0.7665690183639526 } }, "refund" :{ "type" : "noul" , "noul" :0.9953224062919617 } }, "usage" :{ "input_tokens" :148, "output_tokens" :0} } An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model. 2. Serving with llama.cpp llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API. For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub: llama serve -hf ggml-org/Kev-4B-GGUF The default server runs on port 9931. We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone . With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request. The useful property is interface compatibility. curl http://localhost: 9931 /v1/systemone \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "ggml-org/Kev-4B-GGUF", "state": "I was charged twice. Please refund me today.", "questions": { "department": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "criteria": { "billing": "Payments and refunds", "technical": "Bugs and technical issues", "sales": "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, "urgency": { "type": "score", "instructions": "How urgent is the request?", "criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"] }, "refund": { "type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the customer requesting a refund?" } } }' 3. Discovering models on the Hugging Face Hub Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture. For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones. 4. Training decision models using Hugging Face tooling Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API. Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter: each example is a decision request (a state plus questions ) paired with the gold answer. model.decision_config.prepare_inputs turns the request into model inputs, the same way it does at inference time. the model returns one logit per option, so a choice question is trained with a plain cross-entropy loss over the options. import os; os.environ[ "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES" ]= "2" import torch import torch.nn.functional as F from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForDecision, Trainer, TrainingArguments checkpoint = "autotrust/JEV-9B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint) model = AutoModelForDecision.from_pretrained(checkpoint) examples = [ ( "I was charged twice. Please refund me." , "refund" ), ( "My package has not arrived." , "shipping" ), ( "The application crashes when I open it." , "technical" ), ( "I want my money back." , "refund" ), ( "Where is my delivery?" , "shipping" ), ( "I cannot log into my account." , "technical" ), ] options = { "refund" : "Billing issues and refunds" , "shipping" : "Orders and deliveries" , "technical" : "Software and account issues" , } def preprocess ( text, label ): request = { "state" : text, "questions" : { "category" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Classify the support request." , "criteria" : options, } }, } (inputs, questions), = model.decision_config.prepare_inputs( request, tokenizer ) inputs[ "marks" ] = inputs[ "marks" ].unsqueeze( 0 ) inputs[ "num_options" ] = torch.tensor([[ len (questions[ 0 ].options)]]) inputs[ "question_type_ids" ] = torch.tensor([[ 1 ]]) # choice inputs[ "labels" ] = torch.tensor( [questions[ 0 ].options.index(label)] ) return inputs dataset = [preprocess(text, label) for text, label in examples] class DecisionTrainer ( Trainer ): def compute_loss ( self, model, inputs, return_outputs= False , **kwargs ): inputs = inputs.copy() labels = inputs.pop( "labels" ) logits = model(**inputs) logits = logits.unsqueeze( 0 ) # [3] -> [1, 3] loss = F.cross_entropy(logits. float (), labels) return (loss, logits) if return_outputs else loss trainer = DecisionTrainer( model=model, args=TrainingArguments( output_dir= "./decision-toy" , max_steps= 30 , per_device_train_batch_size= 1 , learning_rate= 1e-3 , logging_steps= 5 , save_strategy= "no" , report_to= "none" , remove_unused_columns= False , ), train_dataset=dataset, data_collator= lambda batch: batch[ 0 ], ) trainer.train() First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL ( huggingface/trl#8040 ), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open. If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head. Final thoughts Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software . Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs. from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline( "zero-shot-classification" , model= "facebook/bart-large-mnli" , ) classifier( "My payment was deducted twice." , candidate_labels=[ "billing" , "technical support" , "sales" , "legal" ], ) # {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.', # 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support', 'legal'], # 'scores': [0.8185835480690002, 0.09302053600549698, 0.05521026626229286, 0.03318570926785469]} One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis. This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is. Where decision models differ Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul). More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions . Consider these three approaches: Property Classification Zero-shot classification Decision model Probability over choices Yes Yes Yes Labels defined at inference No Yes Yes Multiple typed questions No No Yes Ordered scoring and yes/no decisions Task-specific Possible with adaptation Native primitives The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions. The decision model interface A decision model request has the following two components: state questions State The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models. For example: { "customer_message" : "I was charged twice. Please refund me today." , "subscription" : "pro" , "previous_tickets" : 2 } Questions and their primitives Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions: Choice: Select one of several possible answers. Score: Evaluate something on an ordered scale. Noul: Answer a yes/no question probabilistically. Let's go over them one by one. Choice: A probability distribution over options Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification. Suppose we ask: Which department should handle this customer request? The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales. from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "department" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and refunds" , "technical" : "Bugs and technical issues" , "sales" : "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, } } ) # { # 'department': { # 'type': 'choice', # 'choice': 'billing', # 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975, # 'probabilities': { # 'billing': 0.9982666969299316, # 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616, # 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412 # } # } # } The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits ($z_1,\ldots,z_K$), (with K classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax: p i = exp ⁡ ( z i / T ) ∑ j = 1 K exp ⁡ ( z j ) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} p i ​ = ∑ j = 1 K ​ exp ( z j ​ ) exp ( z i ​ / T ) ​ Here, (K) is the number of choices. Consider this illustrative distribution: Choice Probability Billing 0.998 Technical support 0.001 Sales 0.001 The probabilities sum to one: ∑ i = 1 K p i = 1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i = 1 ∑ K ​ p i ​ = 1. The model chooses the option with the largest probability: y ^ = arg ⁡ max ⁡ i p i \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y ^ ​ = ar g i max ​ p i ​ In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives. Score: The expectation of an ordered distribution Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale? Consider the question: How urgent is this customer request? We define three levels: 0: Low urgency 1: Medium urgency 2: High urgency from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "urgency" : { "type" : "score" , "instructions" : "How urgent is the request?" , "criteria" : [ "low" , "medium" , "high" ] }, } } ) # { # 'urgency': { # 'type': 'score', # 'score': 1.7053890228271484, # 'legend': { # '0': 'low', # '1': 'medium', # '2': 'high' # }, # 'confidence': 0.5580834252759814, # 'probabilities': { # '0': 0.014908230863511562, # '1': 0.26479458808898926, # '2': 0.7202972173690796 # } # } # } The model again produces a probability distribution: Level Probability 0 — Low 0.10 1 — Medium 0.26 2 — High 0.72 Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index . For a random variable (X) representing the level, the expectation is: E [ X ] = ∑ i = 0 K − 1 i p i \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E [ X ] = i = 0 ∑ K − 1 ​ i p i ​ For our example: E [ X ] = 0 ( 0.10 ) + 1 ( 0.26 ) + 2 ( 0.72 ) = 1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.10)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E [ X ] = 0 ( 0.10 ) + 1 ( 0.26 ) + 2 ( 0.72 ) = 1.7 The reported score is therefore 1.7 . This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7. Noul: A Bernoulli decision The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question. For example: Is the customer requesting a refund? from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) decision = decide( { "state" : "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund." , "questions" : { "refund" : { "type" : "noul" , "instructions" : "Is the customer requesting a refund?" } } } ) # { # 'refund': { # 'type': 'noul', # 'noul': 0.9947046637535095 # } # } Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli). Let (Y) represent a binary outcome: Y ∼ Bernoulli ⁡ ( p ) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y ∼ Bernoulli ( p ) where P ( Y = 1 ) = p , P ( Y = 0 ) = 1 − p . P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P ( Y = 1 ) = p , P ( Y = 0 ) = 1 − p . If the model returns: { "type" : "noul" , "noul" : 0.92 } it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No. The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it. Confidence: How certain is the model? So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score. The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that. For a Choice with (K) options, the confidence is: p max ⁡ − 1 K 1 − 1 K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1 − K 1 ​ p m a x ​ − K 1 ​ ​ where ($p_{\max}$) is the largest predicted probability. The intuition here is: A uniform distribution has confidence 0. ($p_{\max} = \frac{1}{K}$). This means the model estimates that all choices are equally likely. A distribution concentrated entirely on one option has confidence 1. ($p_{\max} = 1$) The larger the winning probability relative to a uniform distribution, the higher the confidence. In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.80: C = 3 ( 0.99 ) − 1 2 = 0.98 C=\frac{3(0.99)-1}{2}=0.98 C = 2 3 ( 0.99 ) − 1 ​ = 0.98 Notice that the winning probability is 0.99, but the reported confidence is 0.98. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558. Decision models in the Hugging Face ecosystem Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations. Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation . A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once: inference engines like llama.cpp can serve any decision model through the same API the Hub can package and surface them consistently and training tools can target shared primitives instead of individual architectures The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces. 1. Serving with Transformers Transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline , AutoModelForDecision , and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models. from transformers import pipeline decide = pipeline( "decision" , model= "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" ) print (decide) # DecisionPipeline: {'model': 'JevForDecision', 'dtype': 'bfloat16', 'device': 'cuda', 'input_modalities': 'text'} One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so: from transformers import AutoModelForDecision, DecisionConfig model_id = "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" config = DecisionConfig.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForDecision.from_pretrained(model_id) Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint . We can start a local server using the serving dependencies: pip install "transformers[serving]" transformers serve Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request: curl http : //localhost:8000/v1/systemone \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d ' { "model" : "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" , "state" : "I was charged twice. Please refund me today." , "questions" : { "department" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Payments and refunds" , "technical" : "Bugs and technical issues" , "sales" : "Pricing and subscriptions" } } , "urgency" : { "type" : "score" , "instructions" : "How urgent is the request?" , "criteria" : [ "low" , "medium" , "high" ] } , "refund" : { "type" : "noul" , "instructions" : "Is the customer requesting a refund?" } } } ' The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities. { "model" : "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide" , "answers" :{ "department" :{ "type" : "choice" , "choice" : "billing" , "confidence" :0.9974000453948975, "probabilities" :{ "billing" :0.9982666969299316, "technical" :0.0010246571619063616, "sales" :0.0007087149424478412 } }, "urgency" :{ "type" : "score" , "score" :1.7525686174631119, "legend" :{ "0" : "low" , "1" : "medium" , "2" : "high" }, "confidence" :0.6288529792800546, "probabilities" :{ "0" :0.014000383205711842, "1" :0.2194305807352066, "2" :0.7665690183639526 } }, "refund" :{ "type" : "noul" , "noul" :0.9953224062919617 } }, "usage" :{ "input_tokens" :148, "output_tokens" :0} } An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model. 2. Serving with llama.cpp llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API. For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub: llama serve -hf ggml-org/Kev-4B-GGUF The default server runs on port 9931. We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone . With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request. The useful property is interface compatibility. curl http://localhost: 9931 /v1/systemone \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "ggml-org/Kev-4B-GGUF", "state": "I was charged twice. Please refund me today.", "questions": { "department": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?", "criteria": { "billing": "Payments and refunds", "technical": "Bugs and technical issues", "sales": "Pricing and subscriptions" } }, "urgency": { "type": "score", "instructions": "How urgent is the request?", "criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"] }, "refund": { "type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the customer requesting a refund?" } } }' 3. Discovering models on the Hugging Face Hub Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture. For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones. 4. Training decision models using Hugging Face tooling Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API. Below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter: each example is a decision request (a state plus questions ) paired with the gold answer. model.decision_config.prepare_inputs turns the request into model inputs, the same way it does at inference time. the model returns one logit per option, so a choice question is trained with a plain cross-entropy loss over the options. import os; os.environ[ "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES" ]= "2" import torch import torch.nn.functional as F from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForDecision, Trainer, TrainingArguments checkpoint = "autotrust/JEV-9B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint) model = AutoModelForDecision.from_pretrained(checkpoint) examples = [ ( "I was charged twice. Please refund me." , "refund" ), ( "My package has not arrived." , "shipping" ), ( "The application crashes when I open it." , "technical" ), ( "I want my money back." , "refund" ), ( "Where is my delivery?" , "shipping" ), ( "I cannot log into my account." , "technical" ), ] options = { "refund" : "Billing issues and refunds" , "shipping" : "Orders and deliveries" , "technical" : "Software and account issues" , } def preprocess ( text, label ): request = { "state" : text, "questions" : { "category" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Classify the support request." , "criteria" : options, } }, } (inputs, questions), = model.decision_config.prepare_inputs( request, tokenizer ) inputs[ "marks" ] = inputs[ "marks" ].unsqueeze( 0 ) inputs[ "num_options" ] = torch.tensor([[ len (questions[ 0 ].options)]]) inputs[ "question_type_ids" ] = torch.tensor([[ 1 ]]) # choice inputs[ "labels" ] = torch.tensor( [questions[ 0 ].options.index(label)] ) return inputs dataset = [preprocess(text, label) for text, label in examples] class DecisionTrainer ( Trainer ): def compute_loss ( self, model, inputs, return_outputs= False , **kwargs ): inputs = inputs.copy() labels = inputs.pop( "labels" ) logits = model(**inputs) logits = logits.unsqueeze( 0 ) # [3] -> [1, 3] loss = F.cross_entropy(logits. float (), labels) return (loss, logits) if return_outputs else loss trainer = DecisionTrainer( model=model, args=TrainingArguments( output_dir= "./decision-toy" , max_steps= 30 , per_device_train_batch_size= 1 , learning_rate= 1e-3 , logging_steps= 5 , save_strategy= "no" , report_to= "none" , remove_unused_columns= False , ), train_dataset=dataset, data_collator= lambda batch: batch[ 0 ], ) trainer.train() First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL ( huggingface/trl#8040 ), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open. If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head. Final thoughts Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software . Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions. A common data-centric solution is to enforce balanced subgroup proportions, but full balance can be costly, infeasible, and not always necessary. In this work, we study whether balanced training data is the unique optimal configuration for robust subpopulation generalization. We extend a Gaussian feature-model framework to theoretically characterize the performance landscape across general training subgroup distributions. We show that multiple configurations, including substantially imbalanced ones, can perform comparably to the balanced one. We further derive gradient-based directions for adjusting subgroup proportions to improve adjusted accuracy and worst-group accuracy more efficiently. These findings suggest that strategically allocating data offers a more flexible and principled path to robust performance than simple balancing. The code is available at this https URL . items.content: Guiding Data Allocation for Robust Subpopulation Generalization Zhaoying Pan,Yipei Wang,Shenyu Lu Xiaoqian WangElmore Family School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Purdue University Email: {pan433, wang4865, lu876, joywang}@purdue.edu Abstract Machine learning models often achieve high average accuracy in the training data while performing poorly on test data due to subpopulation shift. A common data-centric solution is to enforce balanced subgroup proportions, but full balance can be costly, infeasible, and not always necessary. In this work, we study whether balanced training data is the unique optimal configuration for robust subpopulation generalization. We extend a Gaussian feature-model framework to theoretically characterize the performance landscape across general training subgroup distributions. We show that multiple configurations, including substantially imbalanced ones, can perform comparably to the balanced one. We further derive gradient-based directions for adjusting subgroup proportions to improve adjusted accuracy and worst-group accuracy more efficiently. These findings suggest that strategically allocating data offers a more flexible and principled path to robust performance than simple balancing. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/subpop-data-allocation . † † footnotetext: Corresponding author. 1 Introduction Machine learning models trained on data with imbalanced subgroup distributions often achieve high overall test performance but suffer from performance disparities in subgroups Geirhos et al. (2020) ; Koh et al. (2021) ; Quiñonero-Candela et al. (2022) or favor the majority groups He and Garcia (2009) ; Johnson and Khoshgoftaar (2019) ; Zhang et al. (2023) . This challenge has been widely studied under topics such as spurious correlation Arjovsky et al. (2019) ; Sagawa et al. (2020b) ; Geirhos et al. (2020) , fairness Hardt et al. (2016) ; Kearns et al. (2018) ; Mehrabi et al. (2021) , and class imbalance Krawczyk (2016) ; Lin et al. (2017) ; Cui et al. (2019) in machine learning, where the goal is to ensure robust generalization across subgroups or to improve the performance on the worst-performing group. One common framework to encompass the above studies is the subpopulation shift Koh et al. (2021) ; Yang et al. (2023) , which refers to discrepancies between the subgroup proportions in the training and test data. In many cases, the evaluation focuses on the worst-group performance Sagawa et al. (2020a) or the overall performance on balanced test data Yang et al. (2023) , where models trained and evaluated on data with subpopulation shifts are likely to fail Koh et al. (2021) . (a) Optimal Accuracy. (b) Projection of Group Sizes to Coordinates in 3-simplex. (c) Estimated Directions. Figure 1 : (a) Test accuracy varies over diverse training data configurations and many match or exceed the performance of the balanced configuration. (b) Data configurations visualized by projecting group sizes onto a 3-simplex, including the configurations for the balanced (center), the highly skewed (vertex), and a random configuration (unique coordinate). (c) Visualization of directions estimated according to the gradients (Grad) and balancing (Bal) towards the center. A widely acknowledged strategy to ensure generalization against subpopulation shifts is to use fully balanced data to allow the models to be trained sufficiently on each subgroup to avoid potential bias towards specific groups Sagawa et al. (2020a) ; Idrissi et al. (2022) ; Deng et al. (2023) . However, collecting fully balanced data is often prohibitively expensive or infeasible in real-world settings Koh et al. (2021) . Many real-world datasets are inherently imbalanced Koh et al. (2021) . The Waterbirds dataset Sagawa et al. (2020a) , designed to classify bird species, exhibits a strong correlation between the bird species and backgrounds ( e .g. waterbirds appear more often in water backgrounds rather than land). Or in skin cancer diagnosis, benign cases greatly predominate over the malignant ones among all data Codella et al. (2019) ; Wu et al. (2023) . Therefore, attempting to balance the datasets might require significant efforts and costs. Motivated by the challenges of balancing subgroups, we ask a fundamental question ( Optimality ): Is fully balanced data the only optimal configuration of training data for robust generalization under subpopulation shifts? We show the accuracy obtained from diverse configurations with variants of Waterbirds in Figure 1 (a), where we find that many configurations for the training subgroup distribution can achieve test accuracy comparable to or even exceeding that of perfectly balanced training data. Building on this fact, we ask whether it is always most efficient to improve the data towards full balance, or whether there exists a shortcut that does not necessarily lead to balance, as the question of Divergence . Prior work Wang and Wang (2024) contributed theoretical solutions to the test accuracy when models are trained on data with spurious correlation. Following the framework proposed by Wang and Wang (2024) , we examine the test accuracy and use the derivative of the theoretical test accuracy, which characterizes the direction that yields the greatest performance improvement. Considering the direction towards balanced subgroups as an oracle direction, we compare their similarity and find that many training configurations yield a different derived direction. This observation reveals that the derived directions might offer new paths other than balancing direction towards robust performance and suggests the potential of strategically adjusting the data distribution for better robustness ( Efficiency ). In practice, this can guide data collection with principled allocation strategies to ensure the robustness of downstream model training. To validate our findings, we conducted a series of controlled experiments on synthetic and standard datasets, covering images and text. We varied the training data configurations systematically to compare the directions by measuring performance gains obtained along different directions, which shows the advantage of the derived directions on specific configurations and validates the Divergence question. Secondly, for those training configurations where directions differ, we conducted experiments that allocate data gradually along various directions, to demonstrate the potential application to dataset collection, which corresponds to the answer to Efficiency. Lastly, we confirm the Optimality by showing the existence of multiple configurations that achieve comparable optimal performance across datasets. Collectively, our empirical analysis demonstrates that our theoretical insights consistently apply to practical settings. Moreover, we demonstrate the potential applications of our method by integrating the allocation with resampling and last-layer retraining methods. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: 1. We characterize the performance landscape by extending a prior Gaussian modeling framework and identify imbalanced configurations that perform comparably to balance. 2. We derive principled directions for adjusting subgroup configurations to improve robustness more efficiently than enforcing full balance. 3. We empirically validate our theoretical insights and show the potential in data allocation with extensive experiments. 2 Related Work Subpopulation Shifts Subpopulation shift refers to changes in subgroup proportions between training and test distributions. The WILDS benchmark Koh et al. (2021) introduced real-world datasets for evaluating robustness under distribution shifts, categorizing them into domain shift and subpopulation shift. Yang et al. Yang et al. (2023) further formalized this setting by unifying related benchmarks and methods under a common framework. A large body of work in subpopulation shifts has sought to improve robustness through model-side interventions, including group-robust training Sagawa et al. (2020a) ; Duchi and Namkoong (2021) , feature regularization Zhang et al. (2022) ; Wang and Wang (2024) ; Lu et al. (2024) ; Wen et al. (2025) , etc. These methods primarily address subpopulation shift by modifying the learning algorithm or training objective. In contrast, our work focuses on the data side of subpopulation robustness: we study how the subgroup proportions in the training data affect downstream performance and utilize it to improve the robustness. Subgroup Allocation. Closer to our work, prior studies have examined subgroup allocation itself and shown that balancing is not universally optimal. Rolf et al. (2021) studies subgroup allocation through empirical scaling laws to show that the allocation optimizing a given objective does not need to be balanced and proposes that subgroup composition is a key determinant of performance. Schrouff et al. (2024) provides an analysis of causal conditions on when balancing succeeds or fails as a fairness intervention. Alloula et al. (2025) examines when subgroup balance matters in subgroup allocation, and proposes a sensitivity explanation based on latent separation. Claucich et al. (2025) argues that the effect of subgroup allocation depends on subgroup separation in pretrained latent representations, offering a representation-level explanation for balancing failure. Our work is most closely related to Rolf et al. (2021) ; Alloula et al. (2025) in the setup of analyzing performance for data allocation. Unlike the pilot-training sweeps of Rolf et al. (2021) , which rely on extensive empirical exploration, our approach determines the allocation direction analytically from estimated feature separability at negligible cost. Gaussian Data Modeling Recent studies Montanari et al. (2019) ; Mei and Montanari (2021) have employed Gaussian data modeling or linear approximations for theoretical derivations to understand phenomena such as benign overfitting and double descent. Although Gaussian data modeling is idealized, these works showed that the derived key insights generalize beyond Gaussian assumptions. Similar Gaussian modeling has also been utilized in the analysis of distribution shifts, such as spurious correlation Nagarajan et al. (2021) ; Wang and Wang (2024) , class imbalance Liu et al. (2022) , or out-of-distribution detection Ming et al. (2022) ; Yao et al. (2022) . Our analysis builds directly on Wang and Wang (2024) , whose symmetric spurious-correlation setting is a special case of the more general subgroup configuration. We extend this framework to characterize the allocation landscape and analyze how performance changes as subgroup proportions vary independently. Balance-based Robustness Methods. Subgroup balance is commonly used in robustness methods such as resampling and last-layer retraining. Resampling methods over-sample minority groups or under-sample majority groups to construct a balanced training distribution, providing a simple and effective baseline for group robustness Idrissi et al. (2022) . Last-layer retraining methods instead fit or reweight a classifier on a held-out subset, which is often balanced or constructed using limited group annotations Kirichenko et al. (2023) ; Izmailov et al. (2022) ; LaBonte et al. (2023) ; Qiu et al. (2023) . Group-robust sample reweighting further learns per-example weights with influence functions and observes that exact group balance can be suboptimal Qiao et al. (2025) . Our allocation guidance complements both families, that Grad replaces balance as the target subgroup distribution for resampling or stage-two retraining. 3 Subpopulation Robustness across Configurations 3.1 Data Modeling Following prior theoretical studies of spurious correlation and subpopulation shifts ( Sagawa et al., 2020b ; Yao et al., 2022 ; Idrissi et al., 2022 ; Ming et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Wang and Wang, 2024 ) , we consider binary classification over a dataset 𝒟 = 𝒳 × 𝒴 {\mathcal{D}}={\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}} , where 𝒳 {\mathcal{X}} is the input space and 𝒴 = { − 1 , 1 } {\mathcal{Y}}=\{-1,1\} is the label space. Each example 𝒙 ∈ 𝒳 {\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}} has a label y ∈ { − 1 , 1 } y\in\{-1,1\} and is associated with N N binary attributes 𝒂 = ( a 1 , … , a N ) ∈ 𝒜 = { ± 1 } N {\bm{a}}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{N})\in{\mathcal{A}}=\{\pm 1\}^{N} . Without loss of generality, we let a 1 a_{1} be the invariant attribute, which is always aligned with the label, i.e., a 1 ≡ y a_{1}\equiv y . The remaining attributes a 2 , … , a N a_{2},\ldots,a_{N} may be correlated with the label. Our Gaussian feature model and subsequent Bayesian-performance analysis build on Wang and Wang (2024) . Although the notation of an invariant attribute is motivated by spurious correlation Wang and Wang (2024) , we extend this scope to model different forms of subpopulation shift through the training subgroup configuration. We provide a detailed comparison with related work in Appendix E . Feature Modeling. We represent each input 𝒙 {\bm{x}} by a feature vector 𝒛 = ( 𝒛 1 , … , 𝒛 N ) ∈ 𝒵 {\bm{z}}=({\bm{z}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{z}}_{N})\in{\mathcal{Z}} , where each component 𝒛 n {\bm{z}}_{n} corresponds to attribute a n a_{n} . Thus, each subgroup corresponds to one component in a Gaussian mixture over the feature space. We measure the separability of the n n -th attribute by the Mahalanobis distance m n = 𝝁 n ⊤ ​ Σ n − 1 ​ 𝝁 n m_{n}={\bm{\mu}}_{n}^{\top}\Sigma_{n}^{-1}{\bm{\mu}}_{n} . A larger m n m_{n} indicates that the corresponding attribute is easier to classify from the feature representation. Subpopulation modeling. Subpopulation shift is modeled through changes in the subgroup proportions between training and test data. The N N binary attributes define 2 N 2^{N} subgroups. We denote the training proportion of subgroup 𝒂 {\bm{a}} by r 𝒂 r_{\bm{a}} , with r 𝒂 ≥ 0 r_{\bm{a}}\geq 0 and ∑ 𝒂 ∈ 𝒜 r 𝒂 = 1 \sum_{{\bm{a}}\in{\mathcal{A}}}r_{\bm{a}}=1 . For simplicity, we study models trained under arbitrary subgroup configurations { r 𝒂 } 𝒂 ∈ 𝒜 \{r_{\bm{a}}\}_{{\bm{a}}\in{\mathcal{A}}} and evaluate them on balanced test data throughout the analysis. For theoretical derivation, it is useful to reparameterize the subgroup proportions r 𝒂 r_{\bm{a}} using independent variables. Let β = ℙ ⁡ ( Y = 1 ) , α sign ⁡ ( y ) ( n ) = ℙ ⁡ ( a n = y ∣ Y = y ) \beta={\mathbb{P}}(Y=1),\quad\alpha_{\sign(y)}^{(n)}={\mathbb{P}}(a_{n}=y\mid Y=y) denote the positive-label proportion and the probability that attribute a n a_{n} is aligned with the label within examples of label y y . 𝜶 {\bm{\alpha}} further denotes all the attribute-label alignment probabilities. Since a 1 a_{1} is the invariant attribute, we have α + ( 1 ) = α − ( 1 ) = 1 \alpha_{+}^{(1)}=\alpha_{-}^{(1)}=1 . This parameterization represents the 2 N 2^{N} subgroup proportions using 2 ​ N − 1 2N-1 free variables, which allows a tractable subsequent theoretical analysis. 3.2 Analysis Given a linear classifier y ^ = sign ⁡ ( 𝒘 ⊤ ​ 𝒛 + b ) \hat{y}=\mathrm{sign}({\bm{w}}^{\top}{\bm{z}}+b) , we first characterize its accuracy on each subgroup. The training distribution is specified by the feature parameters ( 𝝁 , Σ ) ({\bm{\mu}},\Sigma) and the subgroup-configuration parameters ( 𝜶 , β ) ({\bm{\alpha}},\beta) . These parameters determine the Bayesian optimal linear classifier, which we then evaluate on balanced test data. The following lemma extends the symmetric group-accuracy expression of Wang and Wang (2024) to arbitrary subgroup configurations. Lemma 1. (Bayesian Group Accuracy) For a subgroup specified by attributes 𝐚 ∈ { ± 1 } N {\bm{a}}\in\{\pm 1\}^{N} , the group accuracy of a linear classifier ( 𝐰 , b ) ({\bm{w}},b) is A ​ c ​ c 𝒂 ​ ( 𝒘 , b ) = 1 2 ​ ( 1 + erf ⁡ ( 𝝁 𝒂 ⊤ ​ 𝒘 + a 1 ​ b 2 ​ 𝒘 ⊤ ​ Σ ​ 𝒘 ) ) \displaystyle Acc_{{\bm{a}}}({\bm{w}},b)=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\operatorname{erf}\left(\frac{{\bm{\mu}}_{\bm{a}}^{\top}{\bm{w}}+a_{1}b}{\sqrt{2{\bm{w}}^{\top}\Sigma{\bm{w}}}}\right)\right) (1) where 𝛍 𝐚 = [ a 1 ​ 𝛍 1 ⊤ , … , a N ​ 𝛍 N ⊤ ] ⊤ {\bm{\mu}}_{\bm{a}}=[a_{1}{\bm{\mu}}_{1}^{\top},\ldots,a_{N}{\bm{\mu}}_{N}^{\top}]^{\top} is the subgroup mean. Following Wang and Wang (2024) , we obtain the Bayesian optimal linear classifier by maximizing the overall accuracy on the training distribution. Under the Gaussian feature model, the optimal classifier is aligned with the feature directions: 𝒘 n ∗ = η n ​ Σ n − 1 ​ 𝝁 n {\bm{w}}_{n}^{*}=\eta_{n}\Sigma_{n}^{-1}{\bm{\mu}}_{n} , where each η n ∈ ℝ \eta_{n}\in{\mathbb{R}} is a scalar coefficient for the n n -th feature component. The coefficients η 1 , … , η N \eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{N} and the bias b b are determined by the training statistics ( 𝝁 , Σ , 𝜶 , β ) ({\bm{\mu}},\Sigma,{\bm{\alpha}},\beta) through the optimality conditions of the training accuracy. We provide the full derivation and the resulting equation system in the appendix. Once ( 𝒘 ∗ , b ∗ ) ({\bm{w}}^{*},b^{*}) is solved, Lemma 1 gives the theoretical test accuracy of the classifier on each subgroup. The key implication is that the test performance can be solved and expressed as a function of the training subgroup configuration. items.raw_text: Guiding Data Allocation for Robust Subpopulation Generalization Zhaoying Pan,Yipei Wang,Shenyu Lu Xiaoqian WangElmore Family School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Purdue University Email: {pan433, wang4865, lu876, joywang}@purdue.edu Abstract Machine learning models often achieve high average accuracy in the training data while performing poorly on test data due to subpopulation shift. A common data-centric solution is to enforce balanced subgroup proportions, but full balance can be costly, infeasible, and not always necessary. In this work, we study whether balanced training data is the unique optimal configuration for robust subpopulation generalization. We extend a Gaussian feature-model framework to theoretically characterize the performance landscape across general training subgroup distributions. We show that multiple configurations, including substantially imbalanced ones, can perform comparably to the balanced one. We further derive gradient-based directions for adjusting subgroup proportions to improve adjusted accuracy and worst-group accuracy more efficiently. These findings suggest that strategically allocating data offers a more flexible and principled path to robust performance than simple balancing. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/subpop-data-allocation . † † footnotetext: Corresponding author. 1 Introduction Machine learning models trained on data with imbalanced subgroup distributions often achieve high overall test performance but suffer from performance disparities in subgroups Geirhos et al. (2020) ; Koh et al. (2021) ; Quiñonero-Candela et al. (2022) or favor the majority groups He and Garcia (2009) ; Johnson and Khoshgoftaar (2019) ; Zhang et al. (2023) . This challenge has been widely studied under topics such as spurious correlation Arjovsky et al. (2019) ; Sagawa et al. (2020b) ; Geirhos et al. (2020) , fairness Hardt et al. (2016) ; Kearns et al. (2018) ; Mehrabi et al. (2021) , and class imbalance Krawczyk (2016) ; Lin et al. (2017) ; Cui et al. (2019) in machine learning, where the goal is to ensure robust generalization across subgroups or to improve the performance on the worst-performing group. One common framework to encompass the above studies is the subpopulation shift Koh et al. (2021) ; Yang et al. (2023) , which refers to discrepancies between the subgroup proportions in the training and test data. In many cases, the evaluation focuses on the worst-group performance Sagawa et al. (2020a) or the overall performance on balanced test data Yang et al. (2023) , where models trained and evaluated on data with subpopulation shifts are likely to fail Koh et al. (2021) . (a) Optimal Accuracy. (b) Projection of Group Sizes to Coordinates in 3-simplex. (c) Estimated Directions. Figure 1 : (a) Test accuracy varies over diverse training data configurations and many match or exceed the performance of the balanced configuration. (b) Data configurations visualized by projecting group sizes onto a 3-simplex, including the configurations for the balanced (center), the highly skewed (vertex), and a random configuration (unique coordinate). (c) Visualization of directions estimated according to the gradients (Grad) and balancing (Bal) towards the center. A widely acknowledged strategy to ensure generalization against subpopulation shifts is to use fully balanced data to allow the models to be trained sufficiently on each subgroup to avoid potential bias towards specific groups Sagawa et al. (2020a) ; Idrissi et al. (2022) ; Deng et al. (2023) . However, collecting fully balanced data is often prohibitively expensive or infeasible in real-world settings Koh et al. (2021) . Many real-world datasets are inherently imbalanced Koh et al. (2021) . The Waterbirds dataset Sagawa et al. (2020a) , designed to classify bird species, exhibits a strong correlation between the bird species and backgrounds ( e .g. waterbirds appear more often in water backgrounds rather than land). Or in skin cancer diagnosis, benign cases greatly predominate over the malignant ones among all data Codella et al. (2019) ; Wu et al. (2023) . Therefore, attempting to balance the datasets might require significant efforts and costs. Motivated by the challenges of balancing subgroups, we ask a fundamental question ( Optimality ): Is fully balanced data the only optimal configuration of training data for robust generalization under subpopulation shifts? We show the accuracy obtained from diverse configurations with variants of Waterbirds in Figure 1 (a), where we find that many configurations for the training subgroup distribution can achieve test accuracy comparable to or even exceeding that of perfectly balanced training data. Building on this fact, we ask whether it is always most efficient to improve the data towards full balance, or whether there exists a shortcut that does not necessarily lead to balance, as the question of Divergence . Prior work Wang and Wang (2024) contributed theoretical solutions to the test accuracy when models are trained on data with spurious correlation. Following the framework proposed by Wang and Wang (2024) , we examine the test accuracy and use the derivative of the theoretical test accuracy, which characterizes the direction that yields the greatest performance improvement. Considering the direction towards balanced subgroups as an oracle direction, we compare their similarity and find that many training configurations yield a different derived direction. This observation reveals that the derived directions might offer new paths other than balancing direction towards robust performance and suggests the potential of strategically adjusting the data distribution for better robustness ( Efficiency ). In practice, this can guide data collection with principled allocation strategies to ensure the robustness of downstream model training. To validate our findings, we conducted a series of controlled experiments on synthetic and standard datasets, covering images and text. We varied the training data configurations systematically to compare the directions by measuring performance gains obtained along different directions, which shows the advantage of the derived directions on specific configurations and validates the Divergence question. Secondly, for those training configurations where directions differ, we conducted experiments that allocate data gradually along various directions, to demonstrate the potential application to dataset collection, which corresponds to the answer to Efficiency. Lastly, we confirm the Optimality by showing the existence of multiple configurations that achieve comparable optimal performance across datasets. Collectively, our empirical analysis demonstrates that our theoretical insights consistently apply to practical settings. Moreover, we demonstrate the potential applications of our method by integrating the allocation with resampling and last-layer retraining methods. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: 1. We characterize the performance landscape by extending a prior Gaussian modeling framework and identify imbalanced configurations that perform comparably to balance. 2. We derive principled directions for adjusting subgroup configurations to improve robustness more efficiently than enforcing full balance. 3. We empirically validate our theoretical insights and show the potential in data allocation with extensive experiments. 2 Related Work Subpopulation Shifts Subpopulation shift refers to changes in subgroup proportions between training and test distributions. The WILDS benchmark Koh et al. (2021) introduced real-world datasets for evaluating robustness under distribution shifts, categorizing them into domain shift and subpopulation shift. Yang et al. Yang et al. (2023) further formalized this setting by unifying related benchmarks and methods under a common framework. A large body of work in subpopulation shifts has sought to improve robustness through model-side interventions, including group-robust training Sagawa et al. (2020a) ; Duchi and Namkoong (2021) , feature regularization Zhang et al. (2022) ; Wang and Wang (2024) ; Lu et al. (2024) ; Wen et al. (2025) , etc. These methods primarily address subpopulation shift by modifying the learning algorithm or training objective. In contrast, our work focuses on the data side of subpopulation robustness: we study how the subgroup proportions in the training data affect downstream performance and utilize it to improve the robustness. Subgroup Allocation. Closer to our work, prior studies have examined subgroup allocation itself and shown that balancing is not universally optimal. Rolf et al. (2021) studies subgroup allocation through empirical scaling laws to show that the allocation optimizing a given objective does not need to be balanced and proposes that subgroup composition is a key determinant of performance. Schrouff et al. (2024) provides an analysis of causal conditions on when balancing succeeds or fails as a fairness intervention. Alloula et al. (2025) examines when subgroup balance matters in subgroup allocation, and proposes a sensitivity explanation based on latent separation. Claucich et al. (2025) argues that the effect of subgroup allocation depends on subgroup separation in pretrained latent representations, offering a representation-level explanation for balancing failure. Our work is most closely related to Rolf et al. (2021) ; Alloula et al. (2025) in the setup of analyzing performance for data allocation. Unlike the pilot-training sweeps of Rolf et al. (2021) , which rely on extensive empirical exploration, our approach determines the allocation direction analytically from estimated feature separability at negligible cost. Gaussian Data Modeling Recent studies Montanari et al. (2019) ; Mei and Montanari (2021) have employed Gaussian data modeling or linear approximations for theoretical derivations to understand phenomena such as benign overfitting and double descent. Although Gaussian data modeling is idealized, these works showed that the derived key insights generalize beyond Gaussian assumptions. Similar Gaussian modeling has also been utilized in the analysis of distribution shifts, such as spurious correlation Nagarajan et al. (2021) ; Wang and Wang (2024) , class imbalance Liu et al. (2022) , or out-of-distribution detection Ming et al. (2022) ; Yao et al. (2022) . Our analysis builds directly on Wang and Wang (2024) , whose symmetric spurious-correlation setting is a special case of the more general subgroup configuration. We extend this framework to characterize the allocation landscape and analyze how performance changes as subgroup proportions vary independently. Balance-based Robustness Methods. Subgroup balance is commonly used in robustness methods such as resampling and last-layer retraining. Resampling methods over-sample minority groups or under-sample majority groups to construct a balanced training distribution, providing a simple and effective baseline for group robustness Idrissi et al. (2022) . Last-layer retraining methods instead fit or reweight a classifier on a held-out subset, which is often balanced or constructed using limited group annotations Kirichenko et al. (2023) ; Izmailov et al. (2022) ; LaBonte et al. (2023) ; Qiu et al. (2023) . Group-robust sample reweighting further learns per-example weights with influence functions and observes that exact group balance can be suboptimal Qiao et al. (2025) . items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.12880 (cs) [Submitted on 9 Nov 2026] Title: Kolmogorov-Chapman Maps: Trajectory-Free Learning for Simulating Molecular Dynamics Authors: Majdi Hassan , Marta Skreta , Dominique Beaini , Kirill Neklyudov View a PDF of the paper titled Kolmogorov-Chapman Maps: Trajectory-Free Learning for Simulating Molecular Dynamics, by Majdi Hassan and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Stochastic differential equations (SDEs) describe stochastic processes across a wide range of scientific domains, including physics, biology, and finance. Although individual numerical integration steps are inexpensive, observing meaningful events or transitions can require millions of sequential steps, resulting in substantial wall-clock simulation time and poor hardware utilization. Deep learning offers an alternative by amortizing many integration steps into a single neural network forward pass, potentially enabling much faster simulation. However, existing supervised approaches typically require long simulated trajectory data, which restricts their applicability. In this work, we introduce Kolmogorov-Chapman Maps (KC-Maps), a method for learning the transition kernel of an SDE that relies only on the trajectory-free marginal samples together with the known drift and diffusion coefficients. Given an initial time and state of a process, KC-Maps models its distribution integrated to any given time, corresponding to the weak solution of the SDE. To recover the correct dynamics, KC-Maps satisfies two key properties: (i) it satisfies the boundary conditions, which we incorporate directly into the neural network architecture, and (ii) it respects the Kolmogorov--Chapman equation, which provides an efficient training objective. We empirically demonstrate that KC-Maps learns to integrate the dynamics of peptide molecular systems and outperforms classical molecular dynamics in terms of GPU-hours. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.12878 (cs) [Submitted on 9 Nov 2026] Title: Adaptive Quantization Preserves Fast Rates for TD Learning over Rate-Limited Channels Authors: Sreejeet Maity , Aritra Mitra View a PDF of the paper titled Adaptive Quantization Preserves Fast Rates for TD Learning over Rate-Limited Channels, by Sreejeet Maity and 1 other authors View PDF Abstract: Motivated by reinforcement learning subject to communication constraints, we study a policy evaluation problem with linear function approximation over a rate-limited channel. In our setup, an agent interacting with an unknown environment (modeled as a Markov Decision Process) transmits quantized estimates of a temporal-difference (TD) learning update direction to a server over a finite-capacity channel. Our goal is to investigate to what extent one can preserve the statistical convergence rates achievable when the channel has infinite capacity. To that end, we propose a new algorithm called Batched Adaptively Quantized TD (BAQ-TD), which uses batching to reduce the variance of the transmitted information, and adaptive quantization to encode innovations. We prove a high-probability finite-time error bound for BAQ-TD, and show that, above a certain finite channel capacity, BAQ-TD preserves the convergence rate of unquantized TD up to logarithmic factors. Specifically, for a $d$-dimensional value function parameter, we establish that transmitting a total of $\mathcal{O}(d \log(T))$ bits over a horizon of length $T$ suffices to achieve the order-optimal rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/T)$, marking an exponential improvement in communication-complexity over prior work. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.12871 (cs) [Submitted on 9 Nov 2026] Title: Vendi Anomaly Scores for Efficient and Accurate Anomaly Detection Authors: Amey Pasarkar , Adji Bousso Dieng View a PDF of the paper titled Vendi Anomaly Scores for Efficient and Accurate Anomaly Detection, by Amey Pasarkar and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Anomaly detection (AD) is a critical for trustworthy machine learning and scientific discovery. Existing methods typically define anomalies through local density, isolation heuristics, or distance from a fitted distribution, making them sensitive to neighborhood scale, partitioning choices, or restrictive distributional assumptions. In this work, we introduce a new paradigm by formulating anomaly detection from a diversity perspective. We propose the $\textit{Vendi Anomaly Score}$ (VAS), which detects anomalies by quantifying how much a sample changes the diversity of the dataset, as measured by the Vendi score, when removed. VAS captures both local redundancy and global data structure without relying on density estimation or partitioning heuristics. Moreover, VAS requires no hyperparameter tuning, instead adapting automatically to the spectral structure of the data. VAS is non-parametric and scales linearly with dataset size. Across 148 benchmark embedding datasets derived from 10 source datasets and 4 embedding architectures, VAS achieves state-of-the-art AD performance. We further validate VAS on large-scale ImageNet experiments, where it remains robust as both contamination rate and dataset scale increase.
