items.content: Vendi Anomaly Scores for Efficient and Accurate Anomaly Detection Amey P. Pasarkar ∗,‡ Adji Bousso Dieng †,‡ * Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics, Princeton University † Department of Computer Science, Princeton University ‡ Vertaix Abstract Anomaly detection (AD) is a critical for trustworthy machine learning and scientific discovery. Existing methods typically define anomalies through local density, isolation heuristics, or distance from a fitted distribution, making them sensitive to neighborhood scale, partitioning choices, or restrictive distributional assumptions. In this work, we introduce a new paradigm by formulating anomaly detection from a diversity perspective. We propose the Vendi Anomaly Score (VAS), which detects anomalies by quantifying how much a sample changes the diversity of the dataset, as measured by the Vendi score, when removed. VAS captures both local redundancy and global data structure without relying on density estimation or partitioning heuristics. Moreover, VAS requires no hyperparameter tuning, instead adapting automatically to the spectral structure of the data. VAS is non-parametric and scales linearly with dataset size. Across 148 benchmark embedding datasets derived from 10 source datasets and 4 embedding architectures, VAS achieves state-of-the-art AD performance. We further validate VAS on large-scale ImageNet experiments, where it remains robust as both contamination rate and dataset scale increase. Code to reproduce our results is openly available at https://github.com/vertaix/vendi-anomaly-scores . 1 Introduction Anomaly detection (AD) is essential for analyzing and curating machine learning datasets and for discovery ( Chandola et al., 2009 ; Campolongo et al., 2025 ) . In particular, by identifying samples that are corrupted, mislabeled, out-of-distribution, or otherwise irrelevant, AD helps maintain data quality and improve model reliability ( Ahmed et al., 2017 ; Nassif et al., 2021 ) . Since modern datasets are increasingly inspected through learned embeddings that encode semantic relationships, effective data curation requires AD methods that operate directly in these embedding spaces ( Pang et al., 2021 ; Reiss et al., 2021 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) . AD algorithms are commonly categorized by the supervision available during training. Supervised methods fit detectors using labeled mixtures of normal and anomalous samples ( Ma et al., 2016 ; Vargaftik et al., 2021 ) , while semi-supervised methods assume access to clean data and identify deviations from this reference set ( Dai et al., 2024 ) . Unsupervised AD instead fits directly to the dataset being analyzed, making it especially attractive for modern data curation. As datasets increasingly span diverse modalities, it is often impractical to collect data on anomalies or to construct clean reference sets for every domain, making unsupervised detectors appealing. Unsupervised AD methods typically define anomalies through isolation ( Liu et al., 2008 ) , local density ( Breunig et al., 2000 ) , or distance from a fitted distribution ( Rippel et al., 2021 ) . Isolation-based methods score points by how easily they can be separated from the rest of the data, with classical examples including isolation forests (iForest) ( Liu et al., 2008 ) , extended isolation forests (EIF) ( Hariri et al., 2019 ) , and robust random cut forests (RRCF) ( Guha et al., 2016 ) , as well as geometric variants such as the hypersphere ensembles of INNE ( Bandaragoda et al., 2014 ) and ADERH ( Durani et al., 2025 ) . Other approaches use local neighborhood structure, including k k -nearest neighbor scoring ( Bergman et al., 2020 ) and local outlier factor (LOF) ( Breunig et al., 2000 ) , or fitted feature-space distributions ( Rippel et al., 2021 ) . These methods are often effective, but their performance depends on certain implicit assumptions: isolation methods seek points that are easy to separate based on some heuristic, local methods depend on a chosen neighborhood scale, and distributional methods rely on the adequacy of the fitted density model. On the other hand, deep unsupervised detectors can learn more flexible notions of abnormality ( Xu et al., 2023a ; Xu et al., 2023b ; Goodge et al., 2022 ) , but they require training a model for each dataset, which adds computational cost and other deployment-related challenges. How can we develop AD methods that retain the efficiency of classical detectors while making fewer assumptions about the geometry of embedding data? Contribution. In this paper, we answer this question and make several contributions and findings that we summarize below. • We introduce a new paradigm for AD based on diversity. We propose the Vendi Anomaly Score (VAS), which builds on the Vendi Scores (VS), a family of similarity-based diversity metrics ( Friedman and Dieng, 2022 ; Pasarkar and Dieng, 2023 ) , and defines anomaly through changes in the eigenvalue spectrum of the embedding similarity matrix (Figure 1 ). • We make VAS practical and easy to deploy. We derive an efficient approximation to the exact leave-one-out score, allowing VAS to scale to large embedding datasets. With a simple heuristic, our method also automatically adjusts to different data geometries, eliminating the need for neighborhood selection, fitting clusters, or estimating parametric densities. • We demonstrate the effectiveness of VAS across diverse embedding datasets and large-scale contamination experiments. On ADBENCH image and text benchmarks ( Han et al., 2022 ) , spanning 148 148 total datasets, VAS outperforms all other baselines. We also evaluate VAS on controlled ImageNet experiments with up to 100 ​ k 100\mathrm{k} samples ( Deng et al., 2009 ) , showing that VAS is especially effective for detecting contaminating subpopulations at scale. Figure 1: Overview of VAS. Left: A multimodal dataset contaminated with an anomaly. Right: Removing a rare anomalous point induces a larger change in the eigenvalue spectrum than removing a normal sample. VAS detects these shifts by estimating the change in Vendi Score, derived from the Rényi entropy of order q q of the spectrum (Eq. 1 ). 2 Related Work Our work relates to three lines of research, which we describe below. Unsupervised anomaly detection. Existing unsupervised AD methods typically identify anomalies based on criteria such as separability, local density, or reconstruction error. Partitioning-based methods isolate anomalies by recursively subdividing the feature space. Isolation Forest (iForest) ( Liu et al., 2008 ) and its variants, such as Extended Isolation Forest ( Hariri et al., 2019 ) , identify anomalies as points that can be separated with fewer splits. While effective in low-dimensional or tabular settings, these methods rely on partitions of the feature space, which can struggle to capture complex geometry in high-dimensional embedding spaces. A second class of methods estimates local data density. Techniques such as Local Outlier Factor (LOF) ( Breunig et al., 2000 ) and deep nearest neighbors (DN2) ( Bergman et al., 2020 ) identify anomalies as points that lie in low-density regions relative to their neighbors. However, these approaches require constructing neighborhoods of fixed size, making them sensitive to scale and limiting their ability to adapt to heterogeneous or multimodal data distributions. Ensemble-based methods combine multiple weak signals to improve robustness. For example, Lightweight on-line Detector of Anomalies (LODA) ( Pevnỳ, 2016 ) aggregates anomaly scores from random low-dimensional projections, while ADERH leverages ensembles of random hyperspheres to estimate density and support ( Durani et al., 2025 ) . ADERH provides the strongest results to date for AD on tabular data, although it requires the strong assumption that normal data can be bounded within hyperspheres, which may not be true for embedding data. Recent work has also turned to deep learning to improve AD in complex data. Many of these methods aim to construct representation spaces where anomalies are more easily separated. For example, Deep Isolation Forest ( Xu et al., 2023a ) learns a non-linear transformation of the data that IForest can leverage. LUNAR ( Goodge et al., 2022 ) unifies local outlier methods such as LOF through a graph neural network message-passing framework, introducing learnability into neighborhood-based AD. Similarly, DeepSVDD ( Ruff et al., 2018 ) learns to project normal data within a hypersphere and anomalous data outside of it. RCA ( Liu et al., 2021 ) and RDP ( Wang et al., 2019 ) use collaboration between multiple models to generate a new space where anomalies are more separable. SLAD ( Xu et al., 2023b ) and DTE ( Livernoche et al., 2024 ) both measure how far a sample deviates from normal data. SLAD learns to predict self-supervised “scale” relationships within each sample and identifies anomalies via inconsistencies in these predictions, while DTE leverages diffusion models to estimate deviation from the normal data manifold. Out-of-distribution detection. Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is closely related to semi-supervised AD: both settings assume access to in-distribution data and aim to identify samples that deviate from it. In OOD detection, however, the goal is typically to determine whether a test input falls outside the training distribution of a particular predictive model. As a result, many OOD methods are designed around signals produced by that model, including prediction confidence ( Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016 ) , energy-based scores ( Liu et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) , feature-space statistics such as Mahalanobis distance ( Lee et al., 2018 ; Mueller and Hein, 2025 ) , or other properties of the learned representation ( Fang et al., 2025 ; Bergman et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2022 ) . Standardized benchmarks such as OpenOOD ( Yang et al., 2022 ) evaluate these methods in model-centric settings where the detector is built around a classifier trained on a specified in-distribution dataset. In contrast, we study unsupervised AD. Here, the goal is to identify anomalous samples within the dataset being analyzed, using embeddings produced by a model trained independently on that dataset. We do not assume labels, a clean reference set, prediction logits, or model-specific confidence scores. Our method instead operates directly on the similarity structure of the embedding dataset. Measuring rarity with the Vendi Scores. Friedman and Dieng (2022) introduced the Vendi Score (VS) as a similarity-based diversity measure. It has since been used to evaluate diversity in a wide variety of domains ( Stein et al., 2023 ; Neshat et al., 2025 ; Zamzmi et al., 2025 ; DenAdel et al., 2025 ; Nielsen et al., 2025 ; Barceló et al., 2024 ; Tom et al., ) . Recent methods have explored how the Vendi Scores can be used to identify rare or novel samples in various settings. In active search, Nguyen and Dieng (2024) measure incremental changes to quality-weighted extensions of the VS, showing that changes in the VS can be used to guide the selection of diverse and informative samples in experimental design settings. Similarly, Askari Hemmat et al. (2024) leverage incremental changes to the VS to guide image generation toward underrepresented regions of the output space. The VS has also been used for OOD detection: the Vendi Novelty Scores (VNS) detect OOD samples by measuring how much a test sample increases the diversity of a reference dataset by class-conditional novelty estimates derived from a trained classifier ( Pasarkar and Dieng, 2026 ) . VNS relies on incremental changes to diversity, but it is designed for inference-time OOD detection relative to a fixed training distribution and leverages model-dependent signals. 3 Method We review the Vendi Scores (VS), and introduce our method for leveraging them in unsupervised AD. The Vendi Scores. Let 𝑿 ∈ ℝ N × D \boldsymbol{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} denote a dataset of N N samples. Given a positive semidefinite kernel k ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) k(\cdot,\cdot) , we construct the similarity matrix 𝑲 ∈ ℝ N × N \boldsymbol{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} with entries K i ​ j = k ⁡ ( x i , x j ) K_{ij}=k(x_{i},x_{j}) . The VS ( Friedman and Dieng, 2022 ) measures the diversity of 𝑿 \boldsymbol{X} via the entropy of the eigenvalues of 𝑲 \boldsymbol{K} , normalized such that Tr ​ ( 𝑲 ) = 1 \text{Tr}(\boldsymbol{K})=1 . This definition can be generalized using the Rényi entropy ( Pasarkar and Dieng, 2023 ) . Let λ i ​ ( 𝑲 ) \lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{K}) denote the i i th eigenvalue of 𝑲 \boldsymbol{K} and q ≥ 0 q\geq 0 be the order of the VS. The order- q q is defined as VS q ​ ( 𝑲 ) = exp ⁡ ( 1 1 − q ​ log ​ ∑ i = 1 N λ i ​ ( 𝑲 ) q ) . \text{VS}_{q}(\boldsymbol{K})=\exp\left(\frac{1}{1-q}\log\sum_{i=1}^{N}\lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{K})^{q}\right). (1) This simplifies to the exponential Shannon Entropy when q = 1 q=1 . The parameter q q controls sensitivity to different parts of the spectrum: smaller values emphasize the tail, while larger values emphasize the leading eigenmodes ( Pasarkar and Dieng, 2023 ) . Computing VS q \mathrm{VS}_{q} naively requires the eigendecomposition of the N × N N\times N matrix 𝑲 \boldsymbol{K} , which requires O ⁡ ( N 3 ) O(N^{3}) complexity. However, as Friedman and Dieng (2022) note, when working with ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized features and using a cosine kernel, the VS can be computed more efficiently. We therefore can compute the spectrum using X T ​ X / N X^{T}X/N , reducing the computational cost to O ⁡ ( D 2 ​ N + D 3 ) O(D^{2}N+D^{3}) , which is considerably more efficient in the common ML setting where the number of samples greatly exceeds the feature dimension ( N ≫ D N\gg D ). Fast estimation of diversity influence for anomaly detection. We consider a dataset of N N samples represented by D D -dimensional embeddings 𝑿 ∈ ℝ N × D \boldsymbol{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} , obtained from a pretrained model. The goal of unsupervised AD is to identify which samples are anomalous relative to the rest of the dataset. We aim to learn a scoring function s : { 1 , … , N } → ℝ s:\{1,\dots,N\}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} that assigns a real-valued anomaly score to each sample based on its embedding. Higher scores correspond to more anomalous points. Only the induced ordering matters: any transformation of s ⁡ ( i ) s(i) that preserves the ordering yields an equivalent solution. We define anomaly scores based on the change in dataset diversity when a sample is removed. Assume ℓ 2 \ell_{2} normalized features and let ρ = 1 N ​ 𝑿 ⊤ ​ 𝑿 ∈ ℝ D × D \rho=\frac{1}{N}\boldsymbol{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D} denote the feature covariance matrix corresponding to the cosine kernel. For a sample x i ∈ ℝ D x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} , let 𝑿 − i \boldsymbol{X}_{-i} denote the dataset with x i x_{i} removed, and define ρ − i = 1 N − 1 ​ 𝑿 − i ⊤ ​ 𝑿 − i = 𝑿 ⊤ ​ 𝑿 − x i ​ x i ⊤ N − 1 \rho_{-i}=\frac{1}{N-1}\boldsymbol{X}_{-i}^{\top}\boldsymbol{X}_{-i}=\frac{\boldsymbol{X}^{\top}\boldsymbol{X}-x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}}{N-1} . We then define the anomaly score as, Δ ⁡ ( x i ) = log ⁡ VS q ​ ( ρ ) − log ⁡ VS q ​ ( ρ − i ) . \displaystyle\Delta(x_{i})=\log\mathrm{VS}_{q}(\rho)-\log\mathrm{VS}_{q}(\rho_{-i}). Intuitively, samples that contribute uniquely to the structure of the dataset will induce a larger decrease in diversity when removed, yielding larger values of Δ ⁡ ( x i ) \Delta(x_{i}) , as shown in Figure 1 . However, computing Δ ⁡ ( x i ) \Delta(x_{i}) naively for all N N samples requires O ⁡ ( N ​ D 3 ) O(ND^{3}) time, which is prohibitive for high-dimensional datasets. Moreover, this formulation requires recomputing the spectrum of ρ − i \rho_{-i} after removing each sample, preventing efficient vectorization and limiting the ability to leverage batched GPU computation. (2) We empirically demonstrate the accuracy of the approximation used in VAS in Section 4.1 . VAS can also be interpreted as a spectral quadratic anomaly score, connecting it to classical methods such as Mahalanobis distance and PCA reconstruction error. While these methods use predefined rules for weighting different directions of variation, VAS derives its weighting from each sample’s influence on dataset diversity, with the relative importance of different directions controlled by the Vendi Score order q q . VAS introduces a single hyperparameter: the order q q of the Vendi Score. Previous methods leveraging the Vendi Scores often fix a single value of q q across experiments ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Pasarkar and Dieng, 2026 ) or track the VS across a range of q values to draw diversity profiles ( Dieng and Pasarkar, 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . However, in unsupervised AD, the optimal choice of q q can vary significantly depending on the geometry of the embedding space, and we are not afforded a validation set to tune hyperparameters. Therefore, we design a simple, data-dependent heuristic that adapts q q automatically across datasets. The parameter q q controls how strongly the Vendi Score emphasizes the tail of the eigenvalue spectrum. The importance of this tail varies across datasets. In embedding spaces where the data is highly concentrated, such as BERT embeddings of text, most variance is captured by the leading eigenmode, resulting in a large principal eigenvalue λ 1 \lambda_{1} of the trace-normalized similarity matrix. In this regime, AD requires amplifying the contribution of the spectral tail, which is achieved by using smaller values of q q . In contrast, in more isotropic embedding spaces, such as image representations spanning diverse visual features, the variance is more evenly distributed, leading to a smaller λ 1 \lambda_{1} . In these settings, less emphasis on the tail is needed, and larger values of q q are appropriate. To capture this behavior without manual tuning, we define q q as a function of the principal eigenvalue: q = max ⁡ ( 2 ​ ( 1 − λ 1 ) , 0.1 ) . \displaystyle q=\max\big(2(1-\lambda_{1}),\,0.1\big). The lower bound of 0.1 0.1 is introduced for numerical stability when evaluating ρ q − 1 \rho^{q-1} for small q q . This heuristic assigns smaller values of q q to concentrated datasets and larger values to more dispersed ones, adapting automatically to the spectral structure of the data. Interpreting VAS. Let ρ c = 𝔼 x ∼ P c ​ [ x ​ x ⊤ ] \rho_{c}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P_{c}}[xx^{\top}] . Using G q G_{q} as defined in Proposition 3.1 , for any x ∈ U c x\in U_{c} and q ≠ 1 q\neq 1 , x ⊤ ​ G q ​ x = q ( 1 − q ) ​ Tr ⁡ ( ρ q ) ​ π c q − 1 ​ x ⊤ ​ ρ c q − 1 ​ x . x^{\top}G_{q}x=\frac{q}{(1-q)\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^{q})}\pi_{c}^{q-1}x^{\top}\rho_{c}^{q-1}x. Consequently, the expected VAS score of a sample from component c c is 𝔼 x ∼ P c ​ [ x ⊤ ​ G q ​ x ] = q ( 1 − q ) ​ Tr ⁡ ( ρ q ) ​ ( π c VS q ​ ( ρ c ) ) q − 1 . \mathbb{E}_{x\sim P_{c}}[x^{\top}G_{q}x]=\frac{q}{(1-q)\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^{q})}\left(\frac{\pi_{c}}{\mathrm{VS}_{q}(\rho_{c})}\right)^{q-1}. The proof is provided in Appendix C . Proposition 3.2 shows that the expected VAS score for samples from component c c depends on the ratio π c / VS q ​ ( ρ c ) \pi_{c}/\mathrm{VS}_{q}(\rho_{c}) . Here, π c \pi_{c} is the component mass, while VS q ​ ( ρ c ) \mathrm{VS}_{q}(\rho_{c}) is the component’s effective spectral dimension. Thus, VAS is sensitive to how much probability mass a component has relative to its internal diversity. Components that are small but spectrally diffuse can receive high anomaly scores, even if their samples are not isolated from one another. This component-level sensitivity emerges without explicitly identifying components or forming local neighborhoods; it arises implicitly from the spectrum of the full dataset. Since modern datasets are increasingly inspected through learned embeddings that encode semantic relationships, effective data curation requires AD methods that operate directly in these embedding spaces ( Pang et al., 2021 ; Reiss et al., 2021 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) . AD algorithms are commonly categorized by the supervision available during training. Supervised methods fit detectors using labeled mixtures of normal and anomalous samples ( Ma et al., 2016 ; Vargaftik et al., 2021 ) , while semi-supervised methods assume access to clean data and identify deviations from this reference set ( Dai et al., 2024 ) . Unsupervised AD instead fits directly to the dataset being analyzed, making it especially attractive for modern data curation. As datasets increasingly span diverse modalities, it is often impractical to collect data on anomalies or to construct clean reference sets for every domain, making unsupervised detectors appealing. Unsupervised AD methods typically define anomalies through isolation ( Liu et al., 2008 ) , local density ( Breunig et al., 2000 ) , or distance from a fitted distribution ( Rippel et al., 2021 ) . Isolation-based methods score points by how easily they can be separated from the rest of the data, with classical examples including isolation forests (iForest) ( Liu et al., 2008 ) , extended isolation forests (EIF) ( Hariri et al., 2019 ) , and robust random cut forests (RRCF) ( Guha et al., 2016 ) , as well as geometric variants such as the hypersphere ensembles of INNE ( Bandaragoda et al., 2014 ) and ADERH ( Durani et al., 2025 ) . Other approaches use local neighborhood structure, including k k -nearest neighbor scoring ( Bergman et al., 2020 ) and local outlier factor (LOF) ( Breunig et al., 2000 ) , or fitted feature-space distributions ( Rippel et al., 2021 ) . These methods are often effective, but their performance depends on certain implicit assumptions: isolation methods seek points that are easy to separate based on some heuristic, local methods depend on a chosen neighborhood scale, and distributional methods rely on the adequacy of the fitted density model. On the other hand, deep unsupervised detectors can learn more flexible notions of abnormality ( Xu et al., 2023a ; Xu et al., 2023b ; Goodge et al., 2022 ) , but they require training a model for each dataset, which adds computational cost and other deployment-related challenges. How can we develop AD methods that retain the efficiency of classical detectors while making fewer assumptions about the geometry of embedding data? Contribution. In this paper, we answer this question and make several contributions and findings that we summarize below. • We introduce a new paradigm for AD based on diversity. We propose the Vendi Anomaly Score (VAS), which builds on the Vendi Scores (VS), a family of similarity-based diversity metrics ( Friedman and Dieng, 2022 ; Pasarkar and Dieng, 2023 ) , and defines anomaly through changes in the eigenvalue spectrum of the embedding similarity matrix (Figure 1 ). • We make VAS practical and easy to deploy. We derive an efficient approximation to the exact leave-one-out score, allowing VAS to scale to large embedding datasets. With a simple heuristic, our method also automatically adjusts to different data geometries, eliminating the need for neighborhood selection, fitting clusters, or estimating parametric densities. • We demonstrate the effectiveness of VAS across diverse embedding datasets and large-scale contamination experiments. On ADBENCH image and text benchmarks ( Han et al., 2022 ) , spanning 148 148 total datasets, VAS outperforms all other baselines. We also evaluate VAS on controlled ImageNet experiments with up to 100 ​ k 100\mathrm{k} samples ( Deng et al., 2009 ) , showing that VAS is especially effective for detecting contaminating subpopulations at scale. Figure 1: Overview of VAS. Left: A multimodal dataset contaminated with an anomaly. Right: Removing a rare anomalous point induces a larger change in the eigenvalue spectrum than removing a normal sample. VAS detects these shifts by estimating the change in Vendi Score, derived from the Rényi entropy of order q q of the spectrum (Eq. 1 ). 2 Related Work Our work relates to three lines of research, which we describe below. Unsupervised anomaly detection. Existing unsupervised AD methods typically identify anomalies based on criteria such as separability, local density, or reconstruction error. Partitioning-based methods isolate anomalies by recursively subdividing the feature space. Isolation Forest (iForest) ( Liu et al., 2008 ) and its variants, such as Extended Isolation Forest ( Hariri et al., 2019 ) , identify anomalies as points that can be separated with fewer splits. While effective in low-dimensional or tabular settings, these methods rely on partitions of the feature space, which can struggle to capture complex geometry in high-dimensional embedding spaces. A second class of methods estimates local data density. Techniques such as Local Outlier Factor (LOF) ( Breunig et al., 2000 ) and deep nearest neighbors (DN2) ( Bergman et al., 2020 ) identify anomalies as points that lie in low-density regions relative to their neighbors. However, these approaches require constructing neighborhoods of fixed size, making them sensitive to scale and limiting their ability to adapt to heterogeneous or multimodal data distributions. Ensemble-based methods combine multiple weak signals to improve robustness. For example, Lightweight on-line Detector of Anomalies (LODA) ( Pevnỳ, 2016 ) aggregates anomaly scores from random low-dimensional projections, while ADERH leverages ensembles of random hyperspheres to estimate density and support ( Durani et al., 2025 ) . ADERH provides the strongest results to date for AD on tabular data, although it requires the strong assumption that normal data can be bounded within hyperspheres, which may not be true for embedding data. Recent work has also turned to deep learning to improve AD in complex data. Many of these methods aim to construct representation spaces where anomalies are more easily separated. For example, Deep Isolation Forest ( Xu et al., 2023a ) learns a non-linear transformation of the data that IForest can leverage. LUNAR ( Goodge et al., 2022 ) unifies local outlier methods such as LOF through a graph neural network message-passing framework, introducing learnability into neighborhood-based AD. Similarly, DeepSVDD ( Ruff et al., 2018 ) learns to project normal data within a hypersphere and anomalous data outside of it. RCA ( Liu et al., 2021 ) and RDP ( Wang et al., 2019 ) use collaboration between multiple models to generate a new space where anomalies are more separable. SLAD ( Xu et al., 2023b ) and DTE ( Livernoche et al., 2024 ) both measure how far a sample deviates from normal data. SLAD learns to predict self-supervised “scale” relationships within each sample and identifies anomalies via inconsistencies in these predictions, while DTE leverages diffusion models to estimate deviation from the normal data manifold. Out-of-distribution detection. Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is closely related to semi-supervised AD: both settings assume access to in-distribution data and aim to identify samples that deviate from it. In OOD detection, however, the goal is typically to determine whether a test input falls outside the training distribution of a particular predictive model. As a result, many OOD methods are designed around signals produced by that model, including prediction confidence ( Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016 ) , energy-based scores ( Liu et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) , feature-space statistics such as Mahalanobis distance ( Lee et al., 2018 ; Mueller and Hein, 2025 ) , or other properties of the learned representation ( Fang et al., 2025 ; Bergman et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2022 ) . Standardized benchmarks such as OpenOOD ( Yang et al., 2022 ) evaluate these methods in model-centric settings where the detector is built around a classifier trained on a specified in-distribution dataset. In contrast, we study unsupervised AD. Here, the goal is to identify anomalous samples within the dataset being analyzed, using embeddings produced by a model trained independently on that dataset. We do not assume labels, a clean reference set, prediction logits, or model-specific confidence scores. Our method instead operates directly on the similarity structure of the embedding dataset. Measuring rarity with the Vendi Scores. Friedman and Dieng (2022) introduced the Vendi Score (VS) as a similarity-based diversity measure. It has since been used to evaluate diversity in a wide variety of domains ( Stein et al., 2023 ; Neshat et al., 2025 ; Zamzmi et al., 2025 ; DenAdel et al., 2025 ; Nielsen et al., 2025 ; Barceló et al., 2024 ; Tom et al., ) . Recent methods have explored how the Vendi Scores can be used to identify rare or novel samples in various settings. In active search, Nguyen and Dieng (2024) measure incremental changes to quality-weighted extensions of the VS, showing that changes in the VS can be used to guide the selection of diverse and informative samples in experimental design settings. Similarly, Askari Hemmat et al. (2024) leverage incremental changes to the VS to guide image generation toward underrepresented regions of the output space. The VS has also been used for OOD detection: the Vendi Novelty Scores (VNS) detect OOD samples by measuring how much a test sample increases the diversity of a reference dataset by class-conditional novelty estimates derived from a trained classifier ( Pasarkar and Dieng, 2026 ) . VNS relies on incremental changes to diversity, but it is designed for inference-time OOD detection relative to a fixed training distribution and leverages model-dependent signals. 3 Method We review the Vendi Scores (VS), and introduce our method for leveraging them in unsupervised AD. The Vendi Scores. Let 𝑿 ∈ ℝ N × D \boldsymbol{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D} denote a dataset of N N samples. Given a positive semidefinite kernel k ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) k(\cdot,\cdot) , we construct the similarity matrix 𝑲 ∈ ℝ N × N \boldsymbol{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} with entries K i ​ j = k ⁡ ( x i , x j ) K_{ij}=k(x_{i},x_{j}) . The VS ( Friedman and Dieng, 2022 ) measures the diversity of 𝑿 \boldsymbol{X} via the entropy of the eigenvalues of 𝑲 \boldsymbol{K} , normalized such that Tr ​ ( 𝑲 ) = 1 \text{Tr}(\boldsymbol{K})=1 . This definition can be generalized using the Rényi entropy ( Pasarkar and Dieng, 2023 ) . The order- q q is defined as VS q ​ ( 𝑲 ) = exp ⁡ ( 1 1 − q ​ log ​ ∑ i = 1 N λ i ​ ( 𝑲 ) q ) . \text{VS}_{q}(\boldsymbol{K})=\exp\left(\frac{1}{1-q}\log\sum_{i=1}^{N}\lambda_{i}(\boldsymbol{K})^{q}\right). items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.12869 (cs) [Submitted on 9 Nov 2026] Title: Where Does Alignment Emerge and What Does It Mean? A Closer Look at the Platonic Representation Hypothesis Authors: Julia Herbst , Simon Roschmann , Quentin Bouniot , Zeynep Akata View a PDF of the paper titled Where Does Alignment Emerge and What Does It Mean? A Closer Look at the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, by Julia Herbst and Simon Roschmann and Quentin Bouniot and Zeynep Akata View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that neural networks are converging toward similar representation spaces. As language models become more capable, their representations are aligning with those of vision models. However, recent work has questioned whether this trend continues to hold for newer language models. Moreover, it has been shown that representation similarity metrics can be confounded by model depth and width, requiring appropriate baselines for interpretation. In this work, we first investigate where alignment emerges between unimodal models across model layers and representation dimensions. Next, we find that the PRH capability-alignment trend persists for newer models as long as the captions are sufficiently clean and informative. Finally, we contextualize cross-modal alignment, introducing unimodal and multimodal baselines on various datasets. Our results show that the cross-modal representational alignment of unimodal models can surpass that of explicitly aligned vision-language models, but remains substantially behind the alignment observed for models of the same modality. A Closer Look at the Platonic Representation Hypothesis Authors: Julia Herbst , Simon Roschmann , Quentin Bouniot , Zeynep Akata View a PDF of the paper titled Where Does Alignment Emerge and What Does It Mean? A Closer Look at the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, by Julia Herbst and Simon Roschmann and Quentin Bouniot and Zeynep Akata View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that neural networks are converging toward similar representation spaces. As language models become more capable, their representations are aligning with those of vision models. However, recent work has questioned whether this trend continues to hold for newer language models. Moreover, it has been shown that representation similarity metrics can be confounded by model depth and width, requiring appropriate baselines for interpretation. In this work, we first investigate where alignment emerges between unimodal models across model layers and representation dimensions. Next, we find that the PRH capability-alignment trend persists for newer models as long as the captions are sufficiently clean and informative. Finally, we contextualize cross-modal alignment, introducing unimodal and multimodal baselines on various datasets. Our results show that the cross-modal representational alignment of unimodal models can surpass that of explicitly aligned vision-language models, but remains substantially behind the alignment observed for models of the same modality. Code is available at this https URL . items.summary: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.12865 (cs) [Submitted on 9 Nov 2026] Title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning Authors: Xinjie Shen View a PDF of the paper titled Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning, by Xinjie Shen View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent's task capability while reinforcing behavior that violates contextual execution requirements. We study this reward-driven misalignment, including reward hacking, through verifiable reward--context conflicts, where compliant task completion remains feasible while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task dynamics lets us generate diverse interactive environments at scale and derive compliance feedback from execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real productivity
items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.12865 (cs) [Submitted on 9 Nov 2026] Title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning Authors: Xinjie Shen View a PDF of the paper titled Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning, by Xinjie Shen View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent's task capability while reinforcing behavior that violates contextual execution requirements. We study this reward-driven misalignment, including reward hacking, through verifiable reward--context conflicts, where compliant task completion remains feasible while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task dynamics lets us generate diverse interactive environments at scale and derive compliance feedback from execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real productivity through unauthorized resource use or raises reported scores while actual work declines. Controlled changes in the training distribution show that minority conflict exposure can still lead to widespread shortcut acquisition, reaching 97.9\% certified profitable violations on an API task under a 25\% conflict mixture after 128 updates. The same contextual checks supply a simple binary penalty that supports joint capability and compliance gains and partially mitigates acquired violations. Learned safety adapts to expanded authorization and transfers across mechanisms into workflows with evolving evidence and approval requirements. We study this reward-driven misalignment, including reward hacking, through verifiable reward–context conflicts, where compliant task completion remains feasible while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task dynamics lets us generate diverse interactive environments at scale and derive compliance feedback from execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real productivity through unauthorized resource use or raises reported scores while actual work declines. Controlled changes in the training distribution show that minority conflict exposure can still lead to widespread shortcut acquisition, reaching 97.9% certified profitable violations on an API task under a 25% conflict mixture after 128 updates. The same contextual checks supply a simple binary penalty that supports joint capability and compliance gains and partially mitigates acquired violations. These results connect a verifiable account of reward-driven misalignment with scalable task construction and safety learning that remains useful under changing execution requirements. 1 Introduction Capable and reliable language-model agents are increasingly expected to repair software, schedule resources, and complete complex workflows over long horizons while following human requirements. To develop these capabilities, reinforcement learning (RL) commonly uses task reward based on the quality or amount of work accomplished at the end of an episode, providing a direct, scalable training signal across diverse tasks [ Guo et al., 2025 , Shen et al., 2026a , Wei et al., 2025a ] . However, whether the work meets human expectations also depends on the context in which it is carried out [ Levy et al., 2026 ] . This context includes user intent, interaction history, and specific constraints such as authorization or organizational rules, which determine which actions are appropriate and which constraints apply [ Ruan et al., 2024 , Xiang et al., 2025 , Yao et al., 2024 ] . Following these contextual requirements becomes more challenging as execution horizons grow [ Chen et al., 2026 ] . Agents must continue to respect resource permissions and preserve evaluation requirements in an evolving environment, where prior commitments can constrain later actions. A finite instruction list may leave requirements and their interactions implicit or unspecified, so compliance can depend on basic safety judgment that cannot be taken for granted in LLM agents [ Zhang et al., 2025 , Chen et al., 2026 ] . Even when requirements are explicitly stated, their applicability can change as actions alter the state and create or invalidate obligations [ Shen et al., 2026b , Asif et al., 2026 ] . For example, a user may revoke permission to use an external service and later restore it only for public data. Resuming the earlier workflow may then send restricted data to the service even if the task is completed correctly. Task reward may not fully capture these conditions, leaving room for RL-induced misalignment of the kind observed in studies using production training environments [ Anthropic, 2025 , Qi et al., 2026 ] . We study these reward-driven forms of misalignment through conflicts between task incentives and contextual execution requirements. Such conflicts can arise even when task reward accurately measures useful work, as additional service calls beyond an authorized allowance can still produce more genuine output. In our experiments, task-reward training improves verified work under full authorization while also increasing certified profitable violations under restricted authorization, illustrating how genuine capability gains can conceal growing execution risk (Fig. 4 ). In other cases, agents can raise scores by modifying an acceptance test without repairing the software, and our reporting experiments show higher scores accompanied by less actual work. We interpret these reward-seeking departures from expectations, including behaviors commonly studied as reward hacking [ Taufeeque et al., 2026 , Qi et al., 2026 ] , as shortcuts that bypass contextual requirements of task completion. We construct tasks in which compliant completion remains feasible, while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than any compliant strategy (Fig. 1 ). These intrinsic, verifiable reward–context conflicts let us study how RL acquires shortcuts under controlled incentives. Figure 1: Reward–context conflicts. (a) Compliant completion remains feasible while a violating execution earns higher reward. (b) A binary violation penalty can change the preferred ideal optimum. (c) Expanded authorization can permit the same execution with unchanged physical outcome and task reward. The geometry is schematic. To support these studies at scale, our construction generates executable task environments in batches, with contextual safety boundaries encoded in their dynamics and verifiable feedback for capability and safety learning. Using these environments, we find that profitable violations can become frequent even when conflict tasks form a minority of the training data. Simple reward shaping with the same feedback supports joint capability and compliance gains and mitigates acquired violations. The learned safety behavior adapts to expanded authorization and generalizes across new tasks and scenarios, as well as changes in wording and permission scope. Cross-task cases further document capability transfer and violation emergence, alongside protection that carries over to workflows whose evidence and approval requirements change during execution. 2 Formulation We consider language-model agents trained through reinforcement learning (RL) in executable task environments. Task dynamics determine which executions are possible by specifying how tool calls change the environment’s state and return observations. Contextual requirements distinguish compliant executions within this space, while task reward assigns value to the resulting outcomes. We formalize conflicts between these requirements and task reward as verifiable task properties. This lets us construct tasks for studying shortcut acquisition and use the same execution checks to learn contextual compliance. 2.1 Contextual execution and task reward For a task instance, let τ \tau denote an execution trajectory ending in a terminal state and T T the set of trajectories executable under its dynamics. A context c c specifies requirements on how the task is carried out, and C ⁡ ( c ) ⊆ T C(c)\subseteq T contains the trajectories that satisfy them. Trajectories in T ∖ C ⁡ ( c ) T\setminus C(c) remain executable despite falling outside contextual expectations (Fig. 1 a). Within an execution, earlier actions can change which requirements apply later, so compliance is defined over the full history. Across authorization contexts, expanded permission can make the same physical execution compliant without changing its outcome or task reward (Fig. 1 c). Section 3 describes how these boundaries are implemented in executable environments. Let R task ​ ( τ ) R_{\mathrm{task}}(\tau) denote native task reward and b b a fixed task-value baseline. We use the bounded, graded value V ⁡ ( τ ) = R task ​ ( τ ) − b V(\tau)=R_{\mathrm{task}}(\tau)-b , whose zero marks this value baseline. The score and b b are fixed before interaction and shared by paired authorization contexts, so centering preserves reward ordering and reward gaps. Task completion follows the instance’s own requirements and is checked separately (Appendix B.2 ). 2.2 Verifiable reward–context conflicts We call a reward-seeking route that bypasses contextual requirements of task completion a shortcut . Excess resource use can increase real output; altering a measurement channel can increase the score without such progress. To study how agents acquire these behaviors during RL, we construct instances with two verifiable properties. P1: Compliant feasibility. There exists a reference execution τ c \tau_{c} meeting the basic task goal and satisfying τ c ∈ C ⁡ ( c ) , V ⁡ ( τ c ) ≥ 0 . \tau_{c}\in C(c),\qquad V(\tau_{c})\geq 0. (1) P1 makes the required completion feasible within the contextual boundary. P2: Reward conflict. The best compliant reward is strictly below the best executable reward outside the compliant set: max τ ∈ C ⁡ ( c ) ⁡ V ⁡ ( τ ) < max τ ∈ T ∖ C ⁡ ( c ) ⁡ V ⁡ ( τ ) . \max_{\tau\in C(c)}V(\tau)<\max_{\tau\in T\setminus C(c)}V(\tau). (2) The two trajectory classes are nonempty, and the bounded task reward attains a maximum on each. Together, P1 and P2 describe tasks that can be completed as required, while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Executable references certify these properties. We execute τ c \tau_{c} through the same tool interface available to the agent to verify compliant task completion at or above the value baseline. Its reward is recorded alongside independently checked work. For P2, let V c ∗ = max τ ∈ C ⁡ ( c ) ⁡ V ⁡ ( τ ) V_{c}^{*}=\max_{\tau\in C(c)}V(\tau) denote the compliant optimum and let U c U_{c} be a certified upper bound on it. A violating witness τ s ∈ T ∖ C ⁡ ( c ) \tau_{s}\in T\setminus C(c) certifies the conflict when its execution through this interface establishes V c ∗ ≤ U c < V ⁡ ( τ s ) ≤ max τ ∈ T ∖ C ⁡ ( c ) ⁡ V ⁡ ( τ ) . V_{c}^{*}\leq U_{c}<V(\tau_{s})\leq\max_{\tau\in T\setminus C(c)}V(\tau). (3) When the exact compliant optimum is available, set U c = V c ∗ U_{c}=V_{c}^{*} . These references establish a reward advantage for an executable shortcut over all compliant strategies (Fig. 2 ). Applying the same feasibility and conflict criteria across task instances supplies a basis for batch construction and controlled studies of RL behavior. Figure 2: Feasible completion and a certified shortcut. (a) A compliant reference τ c \tau_{c} meets the task goal and attains the value baseline, while an executable shortcut τ s \tau_{s} crosses the contextual boundary. (b) Every compliant value is at most the certified bound U c U_{c} . A witness with V ⁡ ( τ s ) > U c V(\tau_{s})>U_{c} guarantees a positive reward gap (Eq. ( 3 )). The zero line marks the task-value baseline; contours increase toward the shortcut endpoint. Curves and reward levels are schematic. 2.3 Learning and evaluating contextual compliance With contextual violations made verifiable by construction, a simple mitigation is to penalize them in the training reward. Let I c ​ ( τ ) I_{c}(\tau) equal zero when τ ∈ C ⁡ ( c ) \tau\in C(c) and one otherwise, and let λ ≥ 0 \lambda\geq 0 weight the penalty. We compare: Task-trained: R task ( τ ) , Safety-trained: R task ( τ ) − λ I c ( τ ) , λ = 1 . \text{Task-trained: }R_{\mathrm{task}}(\tau),\qquad\text{Safety-trained: }R_{\mathrm{task}}(\tau)-\lambda I_{c}(\tau),\qquad\lambda=1. (4) Let V s ∗ = max τ ∈ T ∖ C ⁡ ( c ) ⁡ V ⁡ ( τ ) V_{s}^{*}=\max_{\tau\in T\setminus C(c)}V(\tau) and λ × = V s ∗ − V c ∗ > 0 \lambda_{\times}=V_{s}^{*}-V_{c}^{*}>0 . The binary penalty leaves every compliant reward unchanged and subtracts the same λ \lambda from each violating reward. The two ideal optima tie at λ = λ × \lambda=\lambda_{\times} ; the compliant optimum is strictly preferred exactly when λ > λ × = V s ∗ − V c ∗ . \lambda>\lambda_{\times}=V_{s}^{*}-V_{c}^{*}. (5) Figure 1 b shows this ideal change in preference. Policy training then tests how the same contextual feedback shapes useful execution and compliance. Evaluation compares task reward with independently verified actual work. We track historical violations over the execution and certify them as profitable only when their reward exceeds the compliant optimum or a valid upper bound on it. Other boundary-crossing trajectories can raise a policy’s score while remaining below that reference. Historical checking retains these events, while independent work verification distinguishes unauthorized productivity from changes to the measurement channel. The constructed tasks thus connect learned behavior to a verifiable incentive conflict, while the same execution checks provide feedback for learning contextual compliance alongside capability. Section 3 constructs executable task environments following VHD’s mechanism-first approach [ Shen et al., 2026a ] . We ground task reward and contextual checks in the state-update mechanism before realizing its tool interface, so each instance retains a verified incentive structure. 3 Scalable construction of verifiable task environments In real workflows, executable behavior can exceed contextual permission. This gap provides a practical source of reward–context conflicts. We turn it into reusable task mechanisms by encoding contextual requirements as checks on the states and execution histories maintained by task dynamics, while keeping boundary-crossing actions executable. Following VHD, we then render these dynamics into interactive environments [ Shen et al., 2026a ] . Figure 3 illustrates how familiar operational rules give rise to these mechanisms. Under a shared resource allowance, a tool call can produce more work while pushing cumulative use beyond the authorized total, including when calls are spread across accounts. The dynamics record both work and resource consumption, allowing productive execution to register a contextual violation. In a versioned workflow, publication requires evidence for the current artifact, even though the interface may still allow an archived report to be selected. Renewing the evidence restores its current validity, while an earlier invalid publication remains part of the execution history. Figure 3: From encoded dynamics to tool execution. (a) Shared resource permission and (b) current-version evidence pair agent-facing tool calls with their state transitions and contextual boundaries. (c) A schematic trajectory projection with illustrative reward contours increasing toward the violating endpoint. Teal denotes compliant execution; orange denotes a violation. Shading shows current evidence validity; the returning path renews evidence after an invalid publication while retaining that breach in history. Calls remain executable, and v a v_{a} and v r v_{r} denote artifact and report revisions. Mechanism sources and sampling. These examples draw on requirements already present in practical workflows. Input-validity rules provide further candidates, as in an ordering interface that accepts negative quantities despite a nonnegative-quantity requirement. Unforeseen weaknesses in real systems can expose similar gaps. In the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident, agents seeking task solutions exploited infrastructure vulnerabilities to circumvent network isolation and access third-party systems [ OpenAI, 2026 ] . Even when the intended boundary is clear, the operations and combinations that allow an agent to cross it may not have been anticipated. We construct candidate mechanisms by retaining a contextual requirement while relaxing its enforcement in the executable dynamics. In a resource workflow, for example, sampling varies physical capacity and job demands together with the authorized allowance. The same accounting rules track resource use across these instances. A reference procedure verifies a compliant trajectory that meets the task goal (P1) and an executable violating trajectory whose reward exceeds the compliant optimum or a valid upper bound (P2). We retain instances satisfying both properties. Changing authorization can also produce an ordinary counterpart with the same physical task and reward, supporting controlled mixtures of ordinary and conflict tasks. Together with corpus grounding, parameter sampling provides diverse environments under shared verification rules. Table 4 gives the core mechanism catalogue. Corpus-grounded realization. For a sampled instance with parameters θ \theta , an LLM setter renders its executable dynamics D ⁡ ( θ ) D(\theta) into an agent-facing environment. The setter also receives an independently sampled corpus passage x x , which supplies the operational setting and domain language. Stateful tools implement the underlying transitions, while the work order presents the applicable contextual requirements. Through the mapping D ⁡ ( θ ) → E ⁡ ( θ , x ) D(\theta)\to E(\theta,x) , admitted realizations preserve the instance’s task reward and contextual checks across different scenarios and interfaces. Parameter sampling changes the instance, while corpus grounding diversifies its realization. The setter has access to the mechanism and instance parameters, while the solver encounters the realized environment through task instructions and tool observations. The underlying implementation and reference outcomes remain private. Execution checks follow the VHD realization approach [ Shen et al., 2026a ] , with replay and admission criteria detailed in Appendix A.3 . Table 1 presents representative workflows alongside task coverage and mechanism construction results. Beyond sampling existing families, an automated proposal study produced seven verified workflows from 24 requests by pairing newly authored dynamics with constrained-search verification. These workflows compose state changes with contextual requirements, as when editing a document invalidates an earlier approval. The same compositional approach underlies the release tasks evaluated in Section 4.3 , where changing vendor permissions interacts with evidence and approval requirements. In one such workflow, an approval response revises the evidence rule and commitment, creating new obligations before publication (Fig. 13 a). Such compositions make compliance depend on how earlier operations change the requirements governing later ones. The resulting environments support controlled studies of shortcut acquisition and useful contextual safety. Their execution histories provide the binary violation feedback in Eq. ( 4 ), allowing the same task mechanisms to support both task-only optimization and safety-aware RL. Table 1: Representative workflows and construction scale. Task instances cover training and evaluation. Admission rates and estimated costs are measured on sampled realizations, including repair. Cohort release is an unseen composed target in RQ3. Workflow Useful work Contextual requirements API-assisted computation Complete jobs using local computation and external requests Cumulative requests must respect the authorized allowance across accounts. Software repair and certification Repair an artifact and publish validation evidence Published evidence must apply to the current artifact and required checks. Cohort release Complete dependency-linked processing and release a verified artifact Vendor permission can be revoked and reissued with a new scope; publication requires current evidence and approval. Construction summary Value Core mechanism families 8 Constructed task instances > > 800 First-pass / final executable admission 91.7% / 100% Estimated API cost per admitted realization ≈ \approx $0.019 New workflow proposals passing verification 7 of 24 4 Experiments We study how reward–context conflicts shape behavior during RL and whether feedback grounded in the same contextual requirements supports useful, transferable compliance. RQ1. What does task reward optimization learn when profitable shortcuts are available despite explicitly stated contextual requirements? RQ2. Can context-dependent feedback train useful safety behavior, both from Base and after shortcut acquisition? RQ3. How far do capability, shortcut behavior, and contextual safety generalize? Experimental setup. The starting policy is Qwen3.5-4B (Base). We optimize policies with GRPO using their own group rollouts from admitted task environments. In the constructed tasks, public task instructions explicitly provide the applicable contextual requirements and authorization conditions during training and evaluation. Task-trained optimizes task reward; Safety-trained adds the binary history penalty in Eq. ( 4 ). Policies share evaluation instances, authorization conditions, tools, and inference budget within each comparison. Prevention starts from Base; mitigation continues from a common Task-trained parent. Training sources for each comparison are specified in Appendix B.1 . Shared measurements. We report task reward, independently verified real work, historical violations, and certified profitable violations. Certification requires a contextual violation and reward strictly above the compliant optimum or a valid upper bound. Paired contexts change authorization while preserving the physical task and score. Independent work checks assess the original task requirements; mechanism-specific completion criteria are in Appendix B.2 . Safe completion requires task completion with no historical violation. 4.1 RQ1: Learning capability and profitable shortcuts 4.1.1 Capability gains and shortcut acquisition Task optimization can improve real work while increasing profitable violations. On the API resource task, Task-trained improves verified work in both authorized and restricted contexts, while certified profitable violations rise sharply under restricted authorization. Higher reward here reflects additional work, including work obtained through unauthorized resource use (Fig. 4 a). Validation shows the opposite work pattern: the reported score approaches its maximum while current-state repair progress declines and certified profitable violations increase. Together, the two panels distinguish unauthorized productivity from manipulation of the measurement channel (Fig. 4 b). Figure 4: Two routes to higher reward. Open circles are Base; filled circles are Task-trained. Each directed span shows the gap between the observed endpoints. (a) API reward measures verified output. (b) Validation reward reads reports and can diverge from actual repair. Violation rates use 48 attempts per context. To distinguish amplification from newly observed violations, we examine the acquisition patterns across mechanisms and fixed cases. The panels show amplification from both low and established Base risk. On an API subset with no observed Base events, Task-trained additionally exhibits historical and certified profitable violations (Fig. 5 ). Appendix C.1 defines panel-level and instance-level emergence and reports the counts. Figure 5: Amplification and emergence of historical and certified profitable violations. Full panels use 48 attempts per endpoint; the API subgroup uses 36 attempts on nine cases. Exact counts are in Appendix C.1 . 4.1.2 Conflict prevalence and continued optimization A multi-mechanism Task-trained policy exposed to both authorized ordinary tasks and restricted conflict tasks improves authorized real work on both resource mechanisms, alongside an increase in restricted certified profitable violations (Fig. 6 ). We then use paired authorization conditions to vary conflict exposure within the same resource mechanisms. At matched training dose, a 25% conflict mixture produces fewer restricted violations than 100% conflict training. On API, certified profitable violations are 18.8% versus 81.3%, while authorized real work is .999 versus .983. Restricted safe completion also increases on both resource mechanisms (Table 2 ). This lets us construct tasks for studying shortcut acquisition and use the same execution checks to learn contextual compliance. 2.1 Contextual execution and task reward For a task instance, let τ \tau denote an execution trajectory ending in a terminal state and T T the set of trajectories executable under its dynamics. A context c c specifies requirements on how the task is carried out, and C ⁡ ( c ) ⊆ T C(c)\subseteq T contains the trajectories that satisfy them. Trajectories in T ∖ C ⁡ ( c ) T\setminus C(c) remain executable despite falling outside contextual expectations (Fig. 1 a). Within an execution, earlier actions can change which requirements apply later, so compliance is defined over the full history. Across authorization contexts, expanded permission can make the same physical execution compliant without changing its outcome or task reward (Fig. 1 c). items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.12825 (cs) [Submitted on 9 Nov 2026] Title: MaxIM: Maximally Informative Incremental Summarization via Reinforcement Learning Authors: Jihwan Jeong , Guy Tennenholtz , Yinlam Chow , Chih-Wei Hsu , Craig Boutilier View a PDF of the paper titled MaxIM: Maximally Informative Incremental Summarization via Reinforcement Learning, by Jihwan Jeong and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: AI systems must often maintain bounded memory of unbounded interaction histories. However, optimizing the memory representation, and its updates, for downstream task utility is difficult for standard reinforcement learning (RL) due to severe credit assignment bottlenecks induced by sparse, delayed rewards. We introduce MaxIM (Maximally Informative Incremental Memory), a framework that formulates incremental summarization as a capacity-constrained, information-theoretic reward-shaping problem. Grounded in value suboptimality bounds, we show that bounding sequential information loss motivates maximizing the predictive log-likelihood of future, task-relevant targets, a variational lower bound on predictive sufficiency. We introduce a recursive consistency condition to ensure summaries are grounded by maximizing mutual information (MI) with the observed history. We mitigate credit assignment issues with a parameterized asymmetric critic that computes step-wise variational MI bounds for dense reward shaping. Empirical evaluation on long-horizon scientific reading and multi-turn dialogue benchmarks shows that MaxIM outperforms RL, supervised fine-tuning, and prompt-focused baselines on factual grounding, comprehensive autorater metrics, and downstream task utility across strict token budgets and extended horizons, without the need for expensive human preference labels. items.content: MaxIM: Maximally Informative Incremental Summarization via Reinforcement Learning Jihwan Jeong Affiliation: Google Research Guy Tennenholtz † † thanks: Work done while at Google. Affiliation: Noetive Yinlam Chow Affiliation: Google DeepMind {jihwanjeong, yinlamchow, cwhsu, cboutilier}@google.com , guytenn@gmail.com Chih-Wei Hsu Affiliation: Google Research Craig Boutilier Affiliation: Google Research Abstract AI systems must often maintain bounded memory of unbounded interaction histories. However, optimizing the memory representation, and its updates, for downstream task utility is difficult for standard reinforcement learning (RL) due to severe credit assignment bottlenecks induced by sparse, delayed rewards. We introduce MaxIM (Maximally Informative Incremental Memory) , a framework that formulates incremental summarization as a capacity-constrained, information-theoretic reward-shaping problem. Grounded in value suboptimality bounds, we show that bounding sequential information loss motivates maximizing the predictive log-likelihood of future, task-relevant targets, a variational lower bound on predictive sufficiency . We introduce a recursive consistency condition to ensure summaries are grounded by maximizing mutual information (MI) with the observed history. We mitigate credit assignment issues with a parameterized asymmetric critic that computes step-wise variational MI bounds for dense reward shaping. Empirical evaluation on long-horizon scientific reading and multi-turn dialogue benchmarks shows that MaxIM outperforms RL, supervised fine-tuning, and prompt-focused baselines on factual grounding, comprehensive autorater metrics, and downstream task utility across strict token budgets and extended horizons, without the need for expensive human preference labels. 1 Introduction A critical challenge facing AI agents in continuous, streaming environments—from real-time personalization [ 1 , 2 ] to long-horizon dialogue [ 3 , 4 ] —is the inability to retain unbounded context. Despite the expanded context windows of modern large language models (LLMs), processing ever-growing interaction logs frequently degrades reasoning performance due to “lost in the middle” phenomena [ 5 ] . While heuristic memory buffers (e.g., MemGPT [ 6 ] ) and RL-based memory models (e.g., MemAgent [ 7 ] , Mem- α \alpha [ 8 ] ) offer practical mechanisms for context management, agents ultimately need rigorous methods to actively compress these streams into a fixed-capacity working memory. We assume a trainable history/context summarization policy manages this bounded memory state, while a separate, frozen action agent uses it to choose how to act in the environment. In this setting, the objective of a memory system is to maximize downstream task utility, R task R_{\text{task}} . In principle, optimizing a summarizer using reinforcement learning (RL) on R task R_{\text{task}} yields an optimal compression strategy. However, in long-horizon settings, task rewards are notoriously sparse and delayed, inducing extreme credit assignment failures in RL—the policy receives insufficiently granular feedback to learn which observation-stream features are predictive of task success. Conversely, optimizing for surface-level text reconstruction [ 9 , 10 ] discards deeper latent intents needed for effective future inference. Figure 1: The MaxIM framework. Streaming Inference (Solid Lines): A trained actor policy incrementally compresses prior summaries z t − 1 z_{t-1} and incoming observations o t o_{t} into a bounded memory z t z_{t} . This memory, alongside recent observations, provides the context for a frozen downstream agent interacting with the environment with zero critic calls at test time. Asymmetric Training (Dotted Lines): During training, a pretrained critic q ϕ q_{\phi} evaluates the actor’s summary using oracle context Y t Y_{t} and the immediate history ( z t − 1 , o t ) (z_{t-1},o_{t}) . It computes dense, information-theoretic shaping rewards (predictive sufficiency and recursive consistency) that step-wise guide the policy, bypassing the credit assignment bottleneck of the sparse terminal task reward R task R_{\text{task}} . To bridge this gap, we develop MaxIM (Maximally Informative Incremental Memory) , a novel RL framework that addresses credit assignment with dense information-theoretic reward shaping. Leveraging bounds from state abstraction theory, we show that the performance gap induced by constrained memory is bounded by sequential information loss. We show that bounding this loss motivates maximizing the predictive log-likelihood of future, task-relevant target variables Y t Y_{t} , a variational lower bound on predictive sufficiency . items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.12816 (cs) [Submitted on 9 Nov 2026] Title: Automated Knowledge Acquisition Pipeline for Disassembly Instructions: A Comparison of NLP and Generative AI Frameworks Authors: Tim Schnieders , Tareq Maximilian Gabriel Ahrari , Oliver Petrovic , Christian Brecher View a PDF of the paper titled Automated Knowledge Acquisition Pipeline for Disassembly Instructions: A Comparison of NLP and Generative AI Frameworks, by Tim Schnieders and 3 other authors View PDF Abstract: The push towards circularity and Re-X principles presents a challenge to SMEs, particularly due to increasing product complexity that impedes the adoption of disassembly automation. This paper introduces and compares two frameworks for extracting disassembly instructions from unstructured information sources, such as disassembly manuals. Our goal is to transform natural language text into a structured, curated and machine-readable format. We implemented and tested a rule-based Natural Language Processing (NLP) framework against a generative AI framework leveraging LLMs. The performance of both approaches was compared using real-world disassembly manuals. This work provides the necessary data foundation for developing and automating future disassembly processes. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.12775 (cs) [Submitted on 9 Nov 2026] Title: LogCDM: Interpretable Log Anomaly Detection via Behavioral Graph Drift and Adaptive Signal Fusion Authors: Suryansh Talukdar , Taha Sarwat , Jin Soung Yoo View a PDF of the paper titled LogCDM: Interpretable Log Anomaly Detection via Behavioral Graph Drift and Adaptive Signal Fusion, by Suryansh Talukdar and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Log-based anomaly detection is increasingly dominated by large pretrained models, from BERT-scale encoders to 8B-parameter language models, which require GPUs at inference time and are difficult to deploy on the monitoring nodes where logs are produced. We present LogCDM, a compact detector that scores each log session using three complementary signals: the next-event surprise of a small causal Transformer, the distance between a graph-attention embedding of the session's own transition graph and that of a normal reference graph, and a transition-drift statistic that we show is exactly a frequency-weighted chi-squared divergence between transition kernels. The divergence view yields an asymptotic null distribution, a length-standardized score, and a per-edge decomposition that explains each alarm. A sigmoid gate fuses the three signals; under a shared-covariance Gaussian model, this gate is the Bayes posterior, and its learned weights indicate which signal each dataset relies on. With 8.1-8.8M parameters and no GPU required at inference, LogCDM reaches F1 scores of 0.984 on HDFS, 0.870 on chronologically split BGL, and 0.850 on Thunderbird, within 0.013-0.12 of an 8.1B-parameter LLM detector evaluated under the same protocol and above all compact baselines on BGL. It scores a session in 5.5-10.5 ms on a CPU. Ablations show that the structural signals add 0.025-0.030 F1 on BGL and Thunderbird but almost nothing on HDFS, consistent with the learned fusion weights. Ablations show that the structural signals add 0.025-0.030 F1 on BGL and Thunderbird but almost nothing on HDFS, consistent with the learned fusion weights.
