items.content: LogCDM: Interpretable Log Anomaly Detection via Behavioral Graph Drift and Adaptive Signal Fusion Suryansh Talukdar talusb01@pfw.edu Affiliation: Purdue University Fort Wayne Taha Sarwat sarwt01@pfw.edu Affiliation: Purdue University Fort Wayne Jin Soung Yoo jyoo@pfw.edu Affiliation: Purdue University Fort Wayne Abstract Log-based anomaly detection is increasingly dominated by large pretrained models, from BERT-scale encoders to 8B-parameter language models, which need GPUs at inference time and are hard to deploy on the monitoring nodes where logs are produced. We present LogCDM, a compact detector that scores each log session with three complementary signals: the next-event surprise of a small causal Transformer, the distance between a graph-attention embedding of the session’s own transition graph and that of a normal reference graph, and a transition-drift statistic that we show is exactly a frequency-weighted χ 2 \chi^{2} divergence between transition kernels. The divergence view yields an asymptotic null distribution, a length-standardized score, and a per-edge decomposition that explains each alarm. A sigmoid gate fuses the three signals; under a shared-covariance Gaussian model this gate is the Bayes posterior, and its learned weights indicate which signal each dataset relies on. With 8.1–8.8M parameters and no GPU at inference, LogCDM reaches F1 of 0.984 on HDFS, 0.870 on chronologically split BGL and 0.850 on Thunderbird, within 0.013–0.12 of an 8.1B-parameter LLM detector evaluated under the same protocol and above all compact baselines on BGL. It scores a session in 5.5–10.5 ms on a CPU. Ablations show that the structural signals add 0.025–0.030 F1 on BGL and Thunderbird but almost nothing on HDFS, consistent with the learned fusion weights. 1 Introduction Modern distributed systems, from Hadoop pipelines to supercomputers and cloud microservices, record their runtime behavior in system logs. Hardware faults, stalled jobs and cascading service failures all leave traces in the order and structure of logged events, and the volume of these logs rules out manual inspection ( He et al., 2021 ; Landauer et al., 2023 ) . Log-based anomaly detection (LAD) asks whether a session or window of log events deviates from normal behavior, given historical logs and, in the semi-supervised setting, a small set of labeled anomalies. Three properties make LAD hard. Raw log lines are free text whose surface form changes across software versions, so detectors first parse them into templates ( He et al., 2017 ) , and parsing errors bound what any downstream model can achieve ( Shin et al., 2021 ) . Anomalies are rare, from about 3% of HDFS sessions to about 1% of Thunderbird windows, which makes threshold-based decisions fragile ( Le and Zhang, 2022 ) . Finally, anomalies are heterogeneous: some insert a forbidden event, some change event counts, and some change how events follow one another across a whole session without introducing any unusual event locally ( Meng et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Limitations of prior work. Most deep LAD methods score a session by how surprising its event sequence is under a model of normal sequences. DeepLog uses an LSTM next-event predictor ( Du et al., 2017 ) ; LogRobust and NeuralLog use semantic template embeddings with recurrent or Transformer encoders ( Zhang et al., 2019 ; Le and Zhang, 2021 ) ; LogBERT and LogFormer adapt masked-language-model pretraining ( Guo et al., 2021 ; Guo et al., 2024 ) . Recent detectors push accuracy further with large language models: LogLLM combines BERT with Llama-3-8B ( Guan et al., 2024 ) , CoLA routes hard cases from a small model to a fine-tuned 8B LLM ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , and LogLLaMA fine-tunes a LLaMA-2 architecture with reinforcement learning ( Yang and Harris, 2025 ) . This trend leaves two gaps. First, cost . LLM-based detectors need a GPU to score each session and gigabytes of memory to hold the model, while the nodes that most need monitoring (edge devices, cluster managers, on-premise servers) often have neither. Evaluation studies have long argued that time and resource cost belong next to accuracy when judging LAD systems ( Le and Zhang, 2022 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) , yet model size has grown by three orders of magnitude. Second, structure and explanation . Sequence surprise is computed locally, one next event at a time. It can miss sessions whose events are individually plausible but whose overall pattern of transitions has shifted, and it gives the operator a single number with no account of which transitions caused the alarm. Graph-based detectors model transition structure ( Li et al., 2024 ) , but they usually replace sequence models instead of combining with them, and their scores lack a statistical interpretation. Our approach. LogCDM (Log Contextual Dual-pathway Model) combines three signals in one small model (Figure 1 ). A 6-layer causal Transformer gives a sequence score. A graph attention network ( Veličković et al., 2018 ) embeds the session’s own transition graph and compares it with an embedding of a normal reference graph. A closed-form Structural Transition Drift Score (STDS) compares the session’s transition frequencies with the reference. A sigmoid gate fuses the three scores. Template embeddings are computed once offline, so the deployed model never calls a language model. Contributions. 1. A compact three-signal detector. LogCDM has 8.1–8.8M parameters, roughly 1,000 × \times fewer than LLM-based detectors, and runs on a CPU (Section 3 ). 2. A statistical account of structural drift. We prove that STDS equals a frequency-weighted χ 2 \chi^{2} divergence between transition kernels, and equivalently a weighted norm of the difference of random-walk Laplacians. This yields a total-variation lower bound, a bounded score under smoothing, an asymptotic χ 2 \chi^{2} null distribution, a length-standardized score, and a per-edge decomposition for explaining alarms (Section 4 ). 3. An interpretable fusion gate. Under a shared-covariance Gaussian model the gate is the Bayes posterior, so its standardized weights reflect each signal’s class separation. We also show that a common way of feeding an adapted adjacency matrix to a GAT passes no gradient to the adapter, and give a support-preserving adapter that does (Section 4 ). 4. A protocol-aware evaluation. We evaluate on HDFS, BGL and Thunderbird with random and chronological splits, five seeds, AUC-PR, bootstrap intervals, CPU latency, nine ablations, label-noise tests and fusion-weight analysis (Section 5 ). Raw logs Drain3 templates MiniLM (once, offline) Normal reference graph A ~ ref \tilde{A}_{\mathrm{ref}} Causal Transformer p e p_{e} Session GAT vs. ref. s graph s_{\mathrm{graph}} STDS ( χ 2 \chi^{2} drift) z z Sigmoid gate y ^ = σ ⁡ ( 𝐰 ⊤ ​ 𝐬 + b ) \hat{y}=\sigma(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{s}+b) Alarm + top edges Figure 1: LogCDM overview. Grey boxes run once offline; blue boxes run per session on a CPU. The three scores are fused by a sigmoid gate, and the STDS term decomposes over transitions to explain each alarm. 2 Related Work Sequence models for log anomaly detection. DeepLog frames LAD as next-event prediction with an LSTM trained on normal sessions ( Du et al., 2017 ) . LogAnomaly adds template semantics and count features ( Meng et al., 2019 ) , LogRobust uses FastText embeddings with an attention Bi-LSTM to tolerate evolving log statements ( Zhang et al., 2019 ) , and Lu et al. (2018) use a CNN over embedded event sequences. NeuralLog skips parsing and encodes raw messages with BERT ( Le and Zhang, 2021 ) . LogBERT ( Guo et al., 2021 ) trains a small Transformer with masked log-key prediction and a hypersphere objective, and LogFormer ( Guo et al., 2024 ) pretrains on one system and adapts to another with adapters. LightLog targets edge devices with a temporal convolutional network ( Wang et al., 2022 ) , and LogMamba uses state-space models with a frequency branch ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . LogDA combines SBERT template vectors with dual attention for imbalanced data ( Zhang and Fu, 2025 ) . These models score order and content but not session-level transition structure, and none gives a statistical meaning to its score. Large language models for logs. LogLLM feeds BERT message embeddings into Llama-3-8B and reports the strongest results under a common protocol ( Guan et al., 2024 ) . CoLA lets a mixture-of-experts Bi-LSTM defer uncertain sessions to a fine-tuned Llama3-8B ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , and LogLLaMA fine-tunes a LLaMA-2 architecture with reinforcement learning ( Yang and Harris, 2025 ) . These methods set the accuracy frontier but require GPUs and billions of parameters at inference. LogCDM targets the opposite end of this trade-off. Graph-based detection. Logs2Graphs converts sessions to attributed directed graphs and detects anomalies with a one-class digraph convolutional network, showing that transition topology carries signal beyond event order ( Li et al., 2024 ) . We keep this insight but embed each session’s graph next to a sequence model, compare it with a reference graph, and add a closed-form divergence with known statistical properties. Pearson-type tests on Markov transition counts go back to Anderson and Goodman (1957) ; our contribution is to connect that classical test to a learned detector, use it for length standardization and explanation, and fuse it with neural scores. Parameter-efficient adaptation and score fusion. LoRA adapts frozen weights with low-rank updates ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , and GraphLoRA brings low-rank adaptation to graph neural networks ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . We use a low-rank, support-preserving correction of the reference adjacency matrix instead of the network weights. Our two-phase training, normal-only pretraining followed by a small labeled set, follows semi-supervised anomaly detection ( Ruff et al., 2020 ; Ruff et al., 2021 ) , and our fusion gate is the discriminative counterpart of linear discriminant analysis ( Hastie et al., 2009 ; Ng and Jordan, 2002 ) . Lightweight and explainable detection. Compact detectors for constrained hardware include LightLog’s temporal convolutions ( Wang et al., 2022 ) and LogFormer’s adapter tuning, which trains about 0.4M–1M parameters ( Guo et al., 2024 ) . Neither reports CPU latency together with accuracy under a chronological protocol, which is the comparison Xiao et al. (2026) argue for. Explanations for log anomalies are usually post hoc, for example subgraph explanations of a graph detector’s output ( Li et al., 2024 ) . In LogCDM the explanation is part of the score: the STDS term decomposes exactly over transitions, so the evidence behind an alarm is available without an extra explainer. Evaluation practice. Random splits leak future information and inflate scores, while chronological splits lower them and can reorder methods ( Le and Zhang, 2022 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) . Common benchmarks also contain sessions that are trivially separable ( Landauer et al., 2024 ) . We therefore report chronological splits, AUC-PR ( Saito and Rehmsmeier, 2015 ) , seed variance and bootstrap intervals, and separate same-protocol from different-protocol comparisons. 3 Methodology 3.1 Problem setup Definition 1 (Sessions and vocabulary) . A parser π \pi maps each log line to a template in a finite vocabulary 𝒱 = { 1 , … , V } \mathcal{V}=\{1,\dots,V\} , with 0 0 reserved for padding. A session is a sequence x ( i ) = ( e 1 ( i ) , … , e T ( i ) ) ∈ ( 𝒱 ∪ { 0 } ) T x^{(i)}=(e_{1}^{(i)},\dots,e_{T}^{(i)})\in(\mathcal{V}\cup\{0\})^{T} grouped by block ID (HDFS) or by a fixed window of log lines (BGL, Thunderbird), with label y ( i ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } y^{(i)}\in\{0,1\} . Definition 2 (Leakage-free partition) . Sessions are split into disjoint sets ℐ tr , ℐ val , ℐ te \mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{tr}},\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{val}},\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{te}} , either chronologically or by stratified random sampling. items.raw_text: LogCDM: Interpretable Log Anomaly Detection via Behavioral Graph Drift and Adaptive Signal Fusion Suryansh Talukdar talusb01@pfw.edu Affiliation: Purdue University Fort Wayne Taha Sarwat sarwt01@pfw.edu Affiliation: Purdue University Fort Wayne Jin Soung Yoo jyoo@pfw.edu Affiliation: Purdue University Fort Wayne Abstract Log-based anomaly detection is increasingly dominated by large pretrained models, from BERT-scale encoders to 8B-parameter language models, which need GPUs at inference time and are hard to deploy on the monitoring nodes where logs are produced. We present LogCDM, a compact detector that scores each log session with three complementary signals: the next-event surprise of a small causal Transformer, the distance between a graph-attention embedding of the session’s own transition graph and that of a normal reference graph, and a transition-drift statistic that we show is exactly a frequency-weighted χ 2 \chi^{2} divergence between transition kernels. The divergence view yields an asymptotic null distribution, a length-standardized score, and a per-edge decomposition that explains each alarm. A sigmoid gate fuses the three signals; under a shared-covariance Gaussian model this gate is the Bayes posterior, and its learned weights indicate which signal each dataset relies on. With 8.1–8.8M parameters and no GPU at inference, LogCDM reaches F1 of 0.984 on HDFS, 0.870 on chronologically split BGL and 0.850 on Thunderbird, within 0.013–0.12 of an 8.1B-parameter LLM detector evaluated under the same protocol and above all compact baselines on BGL. It scores a session in 5.5–10.5 ms on a CPU. Ablations show that the structural signals add 0.025–0.030 F1 on BGL and Thunderbird but almost nothing on HDFS, consistent with the learned fusion weights. 1 Introduction Modern distributed systems, from Hadoop pipelines to supercomputers and cloud microservices, record their runtime behavior in system logs. Hardware faults, stalled jobs and cascading service failures all leave traces in the order and structure of logged events, and the volume of these logs rules out manual inspection ( He et al., 2021 ; Landauer et al., 2023 ) . Log-based anomaly detection (LAD) asks whether a session or window of log events deviates from normal behavior, given historical logs and, in the semi-supervised setting, a small set of labeled anomalies. Three properties make LAD hard. Raw log lines are free text whose surface form changes across software versions, so detectors first parse them into templates ( He et al., 2017 ) , and parsing errors bound what any downstream model can achieve ( Shin et al., 2021 ) . Anomalies are rare, from about 3% of HDFS sessions to about 1% of Thunderbird windows, which makes threshold-based decisions fragile ( Le and Zhang, 2022 ) . Finally, anomalies are heterogeneous: some insert a forbidden event, some change event counts, and some change how events follow one another across a whole session without introducing any unusual event locally ( Meng et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Limitations of prior work. Most deep LAD methods score a session by how surprising its event sequence is under a model of normal sequences. DeepLog uses an LSTM next-event predictor ( Du et al., 2017 ) ; LogRobust and NeuralLog use semantic template embeddings with recurrent or Transformer encoders ( Zhang et al., 2019 ; Le and Zhang, 2021 ) ; LogBERT and LogFormer adapt masked-language-model pretraining ( Guo et al., 2021 ; Guo et al., 2024 ) . Recent detectors push accuracy further with large language models: LogLLM combines BERT with Llama-3-8B ( Guan et al., 2024 ) , CoLA routes hard cases from a small model to a fine-tuned 8B LLM ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , and LogLLaMA fine-tunes a LLaMA-2 architecture with reinforcement learning ( Yang and Harris, 2025 ) . This trend leaves two gaps. First, cost . LLM-based detectors need a GPU to score each session and gigabytes of memory to hold the model, while the nodes that most need monitoring (edge devices, cluster managers, on-premise servers) often have neither. Evaluation studies have long argued that time and resource cost belong next to accuracy when judging LAD systems ( Le and Zhang, 2022 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) , yet model size has grown by three orders of magnitude. Second, structure and explanation . Sequence surprise is computed locally, one next event at a time. It can miss sessions whose events are individually plausible but whose overall pattern of transitions has shifted, and it gives the operator a single number with no account of which transitions caused the alarm. Graph-based detectors model transition structure ( Li et al., 2024 ) , but they usually replace sequence models instead of combining with them, and their scores lack a statistical interpretation. Our approach. LogCDM (Log Contextual Dual-pathway Model) combines three signals in one small model (Figure 1 ). A 6-layer causal Transformer gives a sequence score. A graph attention network ( Veličković et al., 2018 ) embeds the session’s own transition graph and compares it with an embedding of a normal reference graph. A closed-form Structural Transition Drift Score (STDS) compares the session’s transition frequencies with the reference. A sigmoid gate fuses the three scores. Template embeddings are computed once offline, so the deployed model never calls a language model. Contributions. 1. A compact three-signal detector. LogCDM has 8.1–8.8M parameters, roughly 1,000 × \times fewer than LLM-based detectors, and runs on a CPU (Section 3 ). 2. A statistical account of structural drift. We prove that STDS equals a frequency-weighted χ 2 \chi^{2} divergence between transition kernels, and equivalently a weighted norm of the difference of random-walk Laplacians. This yields a total-variation lower bound, a bounded score under smoothing, an asymptotic χ 2 \chi^{2} null distribution, a length-standardized score, and a per-edge decomposition for explaining alarms (Section 4 ). 3. An interpretable fusion gate. Under a shared-covariance Gaussian model the gate is the Bayes posterior, so its standardized weights reflect each signal’s class separation. We also show that a common way of feeding an adapted adjacency matrix to a GAT passes no gradient to the adapter, and give a support-preserving adapter that does (Section 4 ). 4. A protocol-aware evaluation. We evaluate on HDFS, BGL and Thunderbird with random and chronological splits, five seeds, AUC-PR, bootstrap intervals, CPU latency, nine ablations, label-noise tests and fusion-weight analysis (Section 5 ). Grey boxes run once offline; blue boxes run per session on a CPU. The three scores are fused by a sigmoid gate, and the STDS term decomposes over transitions to explain each alarm. 2 Related Work Sequence models for log anomaly detection. DeepLog frames LAD as next-event prediction with an LSTM trained on normal sessions ( Du et al., 2017 ) . LogAnomaly adds template semantics and count features ( Meng et al., 2019 ) , LogRobust uses FastText embeddings with an attention Bi-LSTM to tolerate evolving log statements ( Zhang et al., 2019 ) , and Lu et al. (2018) use a CNN over embedded event sequences. NeuralLog skips parsing and encodes raw messages with BERT ( Le and Zhang, 2021 ) . LogBERT ( Guo et al., 2021 ) trains a small Transformer with masked log-key prediction and a hypersphere objective, and LogFormer ( Guo et al., 2024 ) pretrains on one system and adapts to another with adapters. LightLog targets edge devices with a temporal convolutional network ( Wang et al., 2022 ) , and LogMamba uses state-space models with a frequency branch ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . LogDA combines SBERT template vectors with dual attention for imbalanced data ( Zhang and Fu, 2025 ) . These models score order and content but not session-level transition structure, and none gives a statistical meaning to its score. Large language models for logs. LogLLM feeds BERT message embeddings into Llama-3-8B and reports the strongest results under a common protocol ( Guan et al., 2024 ) . CoLA lets a mixture-of-experts Bi-LSTM defer uncertain sessions to a fine-tuned Llama3-8B ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , and LogLLaMA fine-tunes a LLaMA-2 architecture with reinforcement learning ( Yang and Harris, 2025 ) . These methods set the accuracy frontier but require GPUs and billions of parameters at inference. LogCDM targets the opposite end of this trade-off. Graph-based detection. Logs2Graphs converts sessions to attributed directed graphs and detects anomalies with a one-class digraph convolutional network, showing that transition topology carries signal beyond event order ( Li et al., 2024 ) . We keep this insight but embed each session’s graph next to a sequence model, compare it with a reference graph, and add a closed-form divergence with known statistical properties. Pearson-type tests on Markov transition counts go back to Anderson and Goodman (1957) ; our contribution is to connect that classical test to a learned detector, use it for length standardization and explanation, and fuse it with neural scores. Parameter-efficient adaptation and score fusion. LoRA adapts frozen weights with low-rank updates ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , and GraphLoRA brings low-rank adaptation to graph neural networks ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . We use a low-rank, support-preserving correction of the reference adjacency matrix instead of the network weights. Our two-phase training, normal-only pretraining followed by a small labeled set, follows semi-supervised anomaly detection ( Ruff et al., 2020 ; Ruff et al., 2021 ) , and our fusion gate is the discriminative counterpart of linear discriminant analysis ( Hastie et al., 2009 ; Ng and Jordan, 2002 ) . Lightweight and explainable detection. Compact detectors for constrained hardware include LightLog’s temporal convolutions ( Wang et al., 2022 ) and LogFormer’s adapter tuning, which trains about 0.4M–1M parameters ( Guo et al., 2024 ) . Neither reports CPU latency together with accuracy under a chronological protocol, which is the comparison Xiao et al. (2026) argue for. Explanations for log anomalies are usually post hoc, for example subgraph explanations of a graph detector’s output ( Li et al., 2024 ) . In LogCDM the explanation is part of the score: the STDS term decomposes exactly over transitions, so the evidence behind an alarm is available without an extra explainer. Evaluation practice. Random splits leak future information and inflate scores, while chronological splits lower them and can reorder methods ( Le and Zhang, 2022 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) . Common benchmarks also contain sessions that are trivially separable ( Landauer et al., 2024 ) . We therefore report chronological splits, AUC-PR ( Saito and Rehmsmeier, 2015 ) , seed variance and bootstrap intervals, and separate same-protocol from different-protocol comparisons. 3 Methodology 3.1 Problem setup Definition 1 (Sessions and vocabulary) . The 30-year Treasury constant maturity series was discontinued on February 18, 2002, and reintroduced on February 9, 2006. From February 18, 2002, to February 9, 2006, the U.S. Treasury published a factor for adjusting the daily nominal 20-year constant maturity in order to estimate a 30-year nominal rate. The historical adjustment factor can be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . Source: U.S. Treasury. 10. Yields on Treasury inflation protected securities (TIPS) adjusted to constant maturities. Source: U.S. Treasury. Additional information on both nominal and inflation-indexed yields may be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . 11. Note: Current and historical H.15 data, along with weekly, monthly, and annual averages, are available on the Board's Data Download Program (DDP) at www.federalreserve.gov/datadownload/Choose.aspx?rel=H15 ). Weekly, monthly and annual rates are averages of business days unless otherwise noted. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: November 10, 2026 Back to Top
